title: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development
section: Why a truncated eigendecomposition is a component solution
text:
Why a truncated eigendecomposition is a component solution
For a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix, \(\mathbf R=\mathbf V\mathbf D\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\) with orthonormal eigenvectors. Retaining the first \(m\) eigenpairs gives \(\mathbf R_m=\mathbf V_m\mathbf D_m\mathbf V_m^{\mathsf T}\). Its trace is the sum of the retained eigenvalues. Among unrestricted rank-\(m\) approximations, this truncation minimizes squared Frobenius error. The omitted diagonal is not required to be a diagonal residual covariance from a latent-variable measurement model. That is the key reason a convenient low-rank approximation and common-factor estimation answer different questions.
Replacing the diagonal by communality estimates changes the eigenproblem. The reduced matrix need not be positive semidefinite: its diagonal is no longer the full variance of an observed random vector. In a principal-axis iteration, the retained positive roots define a current common part whose diagonal supplies the next communality estimates. Convergence of that iteration and its sensitivity to starts are numerical questions separate from whether the resulting factors make sense.
crumbs: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development

title: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development
section: Other retention summaries are not interchangeable votes
text:
Other retention summaries are not interchangeable votes
The minimum average partial (MAP) idea progressively removes component directions and examines the remaining partial-correlation structure. It is not the same reference comparison as parallel analysis. Very simple structure (VSS) compares approximations obtained by simplifying loading patterns to a small number of entries per row; it consequently depends on the kind of simplicity one is prepared to impose. Sequential model tests target exact covariance restrictions under their reference conditions. Information criteria trade likelihood against parameter count but also require a carefully specified likelihood and admissible candidate family.
These methods can disagree because they target different features. A useful extension would state each target, its tuning choices, and the implications of disagreement, rather than assemble a majority-vote factor count. Newer eigenvalue corrections likewise require their own derivation and calibration; they should not be introduced merely by renaming the eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule.
crumbs: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development

title: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development
text:
Two explicit oblique criteria
Ignoring a positive multiplicative constant, the quartimin objective is
\[
Q_{\mathrm{quartimin}}(\mathbf P)
=\sum_{j=1}^p\sum_{a<b}p_{ja}^2p_{jb}^2.
\]
Large coefficients in two columns of the same row increase this objective. A geomin objective takes the form
\[
Q_{\mathrm{geomin}}(\mathbf P)
=\sum_{j=1}^p
\left[\prod_{a=1}^m(p_{ja}^2+\delta)\right]^{1/m},
\qquad\delta>0.
\]
The small positive \(\delta\) regularizes behavior near zero. These criteria may have several local optima. Convergence checks, multiple starts, and sensitivity comparisons are therefore part of a complete rotation report. Neither objective supplies a probability that a factor name is correct, and neither changes the fitted common covariance when implemented as an equivalent rotation.
crumbs: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development

title: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development
text:
Factor-score indeterminacy in one equation
If factors and indicators are jointly normal, a model-based conditional mean score in the standardized metric is
\[
E(\boldsymbol\eta\mid\mathbf z)
=\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf P^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol\Sigma_z^{-1}\mathbf z.
\]
The conditional variance generally remains positive. Thus knowing the model parameters does not identify each person’s latent value without error. Other scoring criteria lead to other point estimates. This appendix supplies the conceptual warning; Chapter 4 develops scoring and its uncertainty after the CFA model has been evaluated.
crumbs: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
This reference gives one agreed meaning for each concept the twelve chapters of Part Two use. It exists so that a reader who meets a term in Chapter 3 can find the chapter and section that explains it, and so that the chapters need not define a term again each time they use it. The concept tables gather related terms into broad groups and give each term’s meaning or essential distinction; the closing table records the notation the chapters share. It is written for lookup rather than for reading through. Chapters 1–4 are available on the website; references to Chapters 5–12 point forward to chapters that are not yet available.
A row is read from left to right. The preferred name comes first, with the common alternatives a reader will meet elsewhere beside it. The meaning cell states the essential distinction rather than a full explanation. The final cell of a concept table, Main explanation, is a destination: the chapter and section where the term is principally explained, with a first use elsewhere noted where one exists. In the notation table the Main use column carries that destination and a further column records alternative symbols and the cautions attached to them. Terms that name the same concept in context share an entry, related concepts with different meanings have separate entries, and a symbol whose preferred form carries a qualifier takes a row of its own that names its other uses. This reference records the vocabulary rather than teaching it: first-use explanations, worked examples and the reasons behind each distinction stay in the chapters themselves.

title: Part Two Concept Reference
section: Latent Variables and the Common-Factor Model
text:
Latent Variables and the Common-Factor Model



Table 1: Latent variables and the common-factor model.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Latent-variable modeling
Latent variable (common factor, \(\eta_k\))
An unobserved random variable introduced by a model and given a distribution over units. It is not a parameter, not a score, and not made observable by being named.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1


Latent-variable modeling
Construct
A substantive idea in the research question. Its meaning comes from theory, item content, response processes, population and intended use, none of which a covariance matrix supplies.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1


Latent-variable modeling
Indicator (item, observed response \(Y_j\))
An observed variable proposed to bear on a factor; an item response is the value recorded for one unit.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1


Latent-variable modeling
Domain sampling (content or behavioral domain coverage)
Defensible coverage of the domain a construct names. It supports a broad construct interpretation and is usually systematic rather than a literal probability sample; it is a different question from sampling units from a population.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1


Latent-variable modeling
Reflective direction (formative alternative)
The modelling choice that writes each indicator as a function of the factors plus a residual. It states a direction of representation, not a causal finding, and it fails for constructs whose indicators produce them.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1


Latent-variable modeling
Classical true score (\(X_{ir}=T_i+E_{ir}\))
The expected score of a person over repetitions of a specified procedure. It is a property of a person and a procedure, so a stable irrelevant influence stays inside it; it equals a common factor only under added assumptions.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.2


Common-factor model
Common-factor model (linear factor model)
\(\mathbf y_i=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\eta_i+\boldsymbol\epsilon_i\) with the moment assumptions on \(\boldsymbol\eta_i\) and \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_i\). Its predictors are not columns of the dataset, which is what separates it from a regression.
Chapter 1, Sec. 2.1–2.2


Common-factor model
Loading (pattern coefficient, \(\lambda_{jk}\))
A fixed unknown parameter relating indicator \(j\) to factor \(k\) on a chosen factor metric. It is not a person’s score and not a direct measure of how much attribute a person has.
Chapter 1, Sec. 2.1


Common-factor model
Residual (unique part, \(\epsilon_j\)) and residual covariance \(\theta_{jk}\)
The part of an indicator the declared factors do not represent, which may hold random fluctuation, item-specific content, method or occasion effects, an omitted factor, or misspecification. A residual covariance is a pair-specific relation outside the common part.
Chapter 1, Sec. 2.3


Common-factor model
Factor covariance matrix (\(\boldsymbol\Phi\))
The \(m\times m\) variance-covariance matrix of the factors, symmetric and positive semidefinite. It is total latent covariance, distinct from a disturbance covariance in a later structural model.
Chapter 1, Sec. 2.2


Common-factor model
Local independence (conditional independence)
Indicators being independent given the factors. It is stronger than zero conditional residual covariance, which is stronger than the zero unconditional covariance a diagonal \(\boldsymbol\Theta\) supplies; none of the three says the observed items are unrelated.
Chapter 1, Sec. 2.3


Specification
Simple structure and cross-loading
A loading pattern in which each indicator relates to one factor, the remaining entries being fixed at zero; a cross-loading is a nonzero entry outside that pattern. Each zero is a restriction, not a drawing convenience. As a rotation criterion the same pattern favours relatively few substantial relations per item and identifiable indicator groups; it is not a criterion of fit to the observed covariance matrix, and rotation does not improve \(F_{\mathrm{ML}}\).
Chapter 1, Sec. 3.1; as a rotation criterion Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2


Specification
Fixed, free and constrained parameter (parameter restriction)
Three distinct statuses an entry of \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\), \(\boldsymbol\Phi\) or \(\boldsymbol\Theta\) can hold: fixed at a declared value, freely estimated, or tied to another parameter. A path diagram does not distinguish them.
Chapter 1, Sec. 3.2


Factor scale
Scale setting (marker variable, fixed factor)
Supplying a metric to a factor that has none, either by fixing one loading per factor or by fixing the factor variance. Neither convention is superior, and the implied covariance among indicators is the same under both.
Chapter 1, Sec. 4.1


Factor scale
Sign indeterminacy
Reversing a factor’s direction and every one of its loadings leaves every product, and therefore the implied covariance, unchanged. A negative sign is a convention, and a sign flip between equivalent solutions is not a change in results.
Chapter 1, Sec. 4.2


Factor scale
Location convention (latent intercept \(\boldsymbol\alpha\))
Fixing the origin of the factors, usually by setting the single-group factor means at zero, because observed means cannot determine unrestricted intercepts and unrestricted factor means together. \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) is a latent intercept and coincides with \(E(\boldsymbol\eta_i)\) only without structural paths.
Chapter 1, Sec. 4.2


Factor scale
Observed-unit change
Re-expressing recorded indicators in different units, which changes loadings, residual variances and implied covariances coherently and predictably. Nothing is indeterminate; this is not a latent-coordinate convention.
Chapter 1, Sec. 4.3


Factor scale
Rotational freedom (coordinate change, \(\mathbf Q\))
The freedom, with two or more factors, to replace the axes while corresponding changes to \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\) and \(\boldsymbol\Phi\) leave the observed covariance unchanged. It resolves a representation choice and establishes nothing substantive.
Chapter 1, Sec. 4.1 and 7


Covariance structure
Model-implied covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)\) (covariance structure analysis)
\(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Theta\): the covariance the model implies, split into a common and a residual part. It needs finite second moments and the stated moment restrictions, not normality.
Chapter 1, Sec. 5


Covariance structure
Pattern matrix and structure matrix (\(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\))
\(\boldsymbol\Lambda\) holds the coefficients of the indicator equations; \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\) holds indicator-factor covariances. They coincide under orthogonal unit-variance factors and must be read side by side in an oblique solution.
Chapter 1, Sec. 5; oblique reading Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1


Covariance structure
Communality (\(h_j^{2}\))
The common part of an indicator’s variance, \(\boldsymbol\lambda_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\lambda_j\), under the declared model. The shortcut \(\lambda_j^{2}\) holds only for one nonzero loading on a unit-variance factor; correlated factors add a cross term.
Chapter 1, Sec. 5.1


Covariance structure
Uniqueness (residual variance; Heywood case)
\(\theta_{jj}=1-h_j^{2}\) for a standardized indicator: variance the declared common factors do not represent, which is not the same as random error. A negative estimate is an improper, or Heywood, solution.
Chapter 1, Sec. 5.1


Covariance structure
Moment structure (\(\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)\))
The modeled object is the mean and covariance pair; \(\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\alpha\). Analysing covariances alone sets the mean structure aside, which is a choice rather than an absence.
Chapter 1, Sec. 5.2


Covariance structure
Distinct moment and degrees of freedom (\(u=p(p+1)/2\), \(df=u-t\))
The number of distinct entries a covariance matrix supplies, and its difference from the free-parameter count. More respondents estimate the same moments more precisely; \(df\ge0\) is necessary for, and never proof of, identification.
Chapter 1, Sec. 5.3


Covariance structure
Tetrad restriction
The vanishing of \(\sigma_{jk}\sigma_{lm}-\sigma_{jm}\sigma_{lk}\), which one common factor with uncorrelated residuals forces for every four indicators. A nonzero tetrad refutes exact reproduction by that model, whatever its loadings.
Chapter 1, Sec. 6.3


Covariance structure
SS loading (column sum of squared loadings)
A summary of one factor column across indicators, read after rotation as a column statistic of the oriented solution. It is not in general an eigenvalue of the analysed correlation matrix, the matrix being decomposed must always be named, and with correlated factors it gives no unique additive partition of common variance.
Chapter 1, Sec. 6.1; post-rotation reading Chapter 2, Sec. 3.2


Neighboring objects
Factor-score estimate (\(\widehat{\eta}_{ik}\))
A prediction of an unobserved factor value from responses, a fitted model and a scoring rule. Different rules give different numbers from the same fit, and no rule makes it an error-free measurement.
Chapter 1, Sec. 6.5


Neighboring objects
Principal component and prespecified composite
Weighted composites of observed variables, one chosen to capture observed variance and one declared as a rule such as a sum or mean. Neither decomposes covariance into common and residual parts, so neither answers the common-factor model’s question.
Chapter 1, Sec. 6.5


Analytic orientation
Exploratory, confirmatory and hybrid orientation
Names for how much is declared before the focal analysis, not for unrelated models. Both use the same covariance decomposition; the restrictions and the history of the decisions separate them.
Chapter 1, Sec. 1.4 and 6.6


Analytic orientation
Analytic status (development versus confirmation evidence)
The record of which body of evidence informed each decision. A specification chosen on one body of evidence receives a genuinely new test only from evidence not used to choose it; analyses move from confirmatory to exploratory status and never back.
Chapter 1, Sec. 6.6–6.7

title: Part Two Concept Reference
section: Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development
text:
Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development



Table 2: Exploratory factor analysis and model development.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Exploratory analysis
Exploratory factor analysis (EFA)
A common-factor analysis that leaves most loading restrictions open while seeking a comparatively low-dimensional representation of shared covariation. It is not assumption-free: the indicator set, population, association matrix, residual restriction, dimensional range and rotation criterion all shape what it can reveal.
Chapter 2, Sec. 1


Exploratory analysis
Development sample (development record)
The sample whose inspection produces a model. A model developed after inspecting these observations is exploratory with respect to them whatever fitting function is used, so the same records cannot confirm it.
Chapter 2, Sec. 1


Extraction
Squared multiple correlation (SMC)
For indicator \(j\), the \(R^2\) from regressing it on all other indicators, computed as \(1-1/(\mathbf R^{-1})_{jj}\). It is a regression summary of the observed matrix used as a communality start, not a known common variance.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3


Extraction
Reduced correlation matrix (SMC-reduced matrix)
The correlation matrix with communality estimates replacing the unit diagonal. It need not be positive semidefinite, and its eigenvalues are on a different scale from the full matrix’s.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3


Extraction
Principal-axis factoring (PAF)
Iterative extraction that decomposes a reduced matrix, forms loadings from its leading positive roots and updates the diagonal from row sums of squared loadings. The diagonal start, nonpositive-root handling and stopping rule are implementation choices.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3


Extraction
Minimum-residual extraction (minres)
Extraction minimizing the sum of squared off-diagonal correlation residuals, giving each displayed discrepancy equal weight. It is a common-factor method but not another name for PAF.
Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4


Retention
Kaiser–Guttman rule (eigenvalue-greater-than-one)
Retaining roots above one in a unit-diagonal correlation analysis. Sampling variation alone produces roots above one, and applying the threshold to a reduced matrix changes the comparison.
Chapter 2, Sec. 3.3


Retention
Scree plot
An ordered plot of eigenvalues read for where large decreases give way to a flatter sequence. It supplies no sampling reference, and full- and reduced-matrix plots need not agree.
Chapter 2, Sec. 3.3


Retention
Parallel analysis (permutation parallel analysis)
Comparing each observed eigenvalue with the same-rank eigenvalues of datasets built to have no common factors but the same sample size and marginal distributions, and retaining the leading consecutive run that clears its reference. The eigenvalue basis, the null generator, the reference statistic and the replication count and seed all belong to the specification.
Chapter 2, Sec. 3.4


Retention
Empirical Kaiser criterion (EKC)
A sample-adjusted repair of Kaiser–Guttman using the Marchenko–Pastur bound \((1+\sqrt{p/n})^2\) for the first root, correcting later roots for variance already accounted for and flooring the reference at one.
Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5


Retention
Sequential model tests
Fitting successive factor counts and stopping at the first non-significant exact-fit test. The sequence is trustworthy only while still under-fitting, because the \(\chi^2\) reference fails once the count exceeds the true number.
Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5


Retention
Combination rule
Using two criteria with different references together, and treating their disagreement as evidence that the dimensions are hard to detect rather than as a tie to be broken by vote.
Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5


Counting
Effective EFA parameter count (\(t_m\))
\(pm+p-m(m-1)/2\) for an unrestricted common-factor covariance model at regular points, with \(df_m=p(p+1)/2-t_m\). The subtraction removes rotational redundancy; an oblique rotation adds no parameters because it re-expresses the same fitted covariance.
Chapter 2, Sec. 4.1


Counting
Ledermann bound
The largest factor count the covariance moments can generically support, \(m\le(2p+1-\sqrt{8p+1})/2\). It is a counting limit, not a recommendation, a positive-root count or a proof of identification.
Chapter 2, Sec. 4.1


Rotation
Inverse-paired transformation
The general nonsingular change of factor coordinates \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf T^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf T\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf T^{\mathsf T}\), which leaves the fitted common covariance unchanged. Multiplying loadings while leaving \(\boldsymbol\Phi\) alone is not an equivalent oblique rotation.
Chapter 2, Sec. 5.1


Rotation
Varimax
An orthogonal criterion maximizing the dispersion of squared loadings within columns. A clean varimax pattern does not establish that the substantive attributes are unrelated.
Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2


Rotation
Direct oblimin (quartimin at \(\gamma=0\))
An oblique criterion discouraging large squared coefficients in several columns of one row while permitting factor correlations. The name alone is not a specification: \(\gamma\), normalization, tolerance, iteration limit, starts and seed all matter.
Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2


Rotation
Kaiser normalization
Dividing each loading row by its communality-based length before optimizing and restoring the scale afterward, which reweights indicators in the criterion. It is not the same operation as standardizing the observed variables.
Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2


Reading an oblique solution
Pattern coefficient (pattern matrix \(\mathbf P\))
The coefficient of a factor in the simultaneous decomposition of a standardized indicator, read conditional on the other factors in the same representation.
Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1


Reading an oblique solution
Structure correlation (structure matrix \(\mathbf C=\mathbf P\boldsymbol\Phi\))
The zero-order indicator–factor correlation, which can be appreciable where the pattern coefficient is near zero because part of the relation travels through the factor correlation. Pattern and structure coincide only in an orthogonal solution.
Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 (defined as \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\) in Chapter 1, Sec. 5)


Reading an oblique solution
Oblique communality as a quadratic form
\(h_j^2=\mathbf p_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf p_j\), whose factor-correlation cross-products are part of the common variance. A row sum of squared pattern coefficients omits them and is a different quantity.
Chapter 2, Sec. 6.2


Residual evidence
Correlation residual matrix (\(\mathbf E\)) and off-diagonal RMS
Observed minus reproduced correlations, summarized by \(\sqrt{2\sum_{j<k}e_{jk}^2/[p(p-1)]}\), which excludes variances. The largest absolute residual and the location of discrepancy carry information an average conceals, and this summary is not automatically any software statistic named RMSR or SRMR.
Chapter 2, Sec. 7.1


Residual evidence
Uniqueness boundary (bound-constrained uniqueness)
A fitted uniqueness at the implementation’s lower bound rather than in the interior. It can signal too many factors, a redundant pair, sampling fluctuation or misspecification, and is different evidence from an interior estimate.
Chapter 2, Sec. 4.3


Preliminary summaries
KMO (Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy)
The ratio of summed squared zero-order correlations to that sum plus the summed squared partial correlations. It describes the input; it selects no factor count and is no minimum-sample-size calculation.
Chapter 2, Sec. 7.2


Preliminary summaries
Bartlett’s test of sphericity
A normal-theory test of \(H_0:\mathbf R_{\mathrm{population}}=\mathbf I\) on \(p(p-1)/2\) df. Rejection says the indicators are not mutually uncorrelated, not that a low-dimensional factor model fits.
Chapter 2, Sec. 7.2


Analytic sensitivity
Tucker’s congruence coefficient
The cosine between two loading-column vectors, compared after column order and sign are aligned. It compares coefficient directions, not participant scores, and near-one congruence can hide an important difference for one item.
Chapter 2, Sec. 7.3


Analytic sensitivity
Analytic sensitivity comparison
Changing one declared analytic choice at a time on the same records and comparing aligned solutions. It is same-sample evidence about analytic robustness, never an independent replication or a sampling interval.
Chapter 2, Sec. 7.3


Analytic status
Frozen candidate specification
The exact item order, free and fixed relations, scaling, covariance and mean settings, estimation family and named rivals recorded before any confirmation evidence is inspected. This separates a planned confirmation from a comparison developed after inspection, whose interpretation must acknowledge that selection.
Chapter 2, Sec. 8


Analytic status
Planned rival model
A restriction or broader alternative named before the confirmation outcome, distinguished from a post-hoc change, which changes analytic status and requires new evidence.
Chapter 2, Sec. 8

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Confirmatory Specification, Identification, and Estimation



Table 3: Confirmatory specification, identification, and estimation.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Confirmatory specification
Confirmatory factor analysis (restricted factor model; CFA)
A common-factor model whose loading, residual, and factor-covariance entries are restricted before estimation, giving testable implications beyond the number of factors. The label describes restrictions and analytic history, not a favorable conclusion or a function name.
Chapter 3, Sec. 1


Confirmatory specification
Exclusion restriction (fixed zero loading; absent arrow)
A loading entry set to zero as a substantive claim that the indicator has no direct relation to that factor. It does not state that the indicator and factor are uncorrelated, because correlated factors still induce a nonzero structure coefficient.
Chapter 3, Sec. 1


Parameter status
Free, fixed, equality-constrained, bounded, and defined parameter
Estimated under the other restrictions; assigned a constant; required to share a value; restricted to a range; or computed from fitted parameters without adding freedom. A diagram shows which relations exist, not which status each has.
Chapter 3, Sec. 3


Parameter status
Residual covariance (correlated residual; correlated uniqueness)
A freely estimated off-diagonal entry of \(\boldsymbol\Theta\), occupying two symmetric cells and adding one free parameter. It changes one indicator pair’s implied covariance, unlike a cross-loading, which changes a whole row and column.
Chapter 3, Sec. 3


Latent metric
Marker scaling (reference indicator; unit loading identification)
Fixing one loading per factor at one, so the factor is expressed in that indicator’s units and the factor variance is estimated. It does not set the factor variance to one and does not make the marker error-free.
Chapter 3, Sec. 4


Latent metric
Fixed-factor scaling (unit variance identification; std.lv = TRUE)
Fixing each factor variance at one and estimating every target loading, so a factor unit is one model standard deviation in a single-group model. It does not standardize the observed indicators.
Chapter 3, Sec. 4


Latent metric
Factor-scale reparameterization (\(\mathbf D\) transformation)
The diagonal rescaling \(\boldsymbol\Lambda^*=\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf D^{-1}\), \(\boldsymbol\Phi^*=\mathbf D\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf D^{\mathsf T}\), which leaves the implied covariance and \(\boldsymbol\Theta\) unchanged. Equivalence fails if a constraint is not transformed with the metric or a factor variance is on a boundary.
Chapter 3, Sec. 4


Observed units
Observed-unit rescaling (\(\boldsymbol\Delta\) rescaling)
Replacing \(\mathbf y\) by \(\mathbf b+\boldsymbol\Delta\mathbf y\), which multiplies an indicator’s intercept and loading by its factor, its variance and residual variance by that factor squared, and its covariance with an unchanged indicator by the factor. It changes the record, not the latent coordinates, and leaves fit unchanged under a consistently transformed model.
Chapter 3, Sec. 4


Observed units
Correlation reparameterization (standardized-indicator model)
Writing \(\mathbf R=\mathbf D_y^{-1/2}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf D_y^{-1/2}\) with rescaled loading and residual matrices. It standardizes the indicators, not the factors, and its moment count differs from the covariance form because the unit diagonal is fixed.
Chapter 3, Sec. 4


Coefficient metrics
Latent-standardized and fully standardized loading (std.lv; std.all)
\(\lambda\sqrt{\phi_{aa}}\) expresses a factor change in standard-deviation units in the indicator’s raw unit; \(\lambda\sqrt{\phi_{aa}}/\sqrt{\sigma_{jj}}\) standardizes both. A raw standard error is not the standardized coefficient’s standard error, because the transformation uses estimated quantities.
Chapter 3, Sec. 4


Moment accounting
Observed moments, free parameters, and model degrees of freedom (\(u\), \(t\), \(df=u-t\))
The distinct sample moments a declared representation supplies, the free coordinates the model estimates, and their difference. Necessary bookkeeping for one stated representation; neither identification nor quality, and unique covariance entries are not observations.
Chapter 3, Sec. 6


Moment accounting
Unrestricted-EFA dimension
The count of distinct covariance-model axes in an unrestricted \(m\)-factor solution, \(pm+p-m(m-1)/2\) at regular full-rank points, which subtracts the continuous rotational freedom that changes the display without changing the reproduced covariance.
Chapter 3, Sec. 6


Identification
Identification (global, local, and generic; empirical or weak identification)
Whether the moments determine the parameters: uniquely over the admissible space, in a neighborhood, or except at exceptional values. Weak identification describes a recoverable model whose parameters are poorly distinguished, showing as unstable estimates and very large standard errors rather than an error message.
Chapter 3, Sec. 6


Identification
Two- and three-indicator sufficient conditions (connectedness)
A factor with at least three exclusive indicators is identified under a fixed scale and diagonal residuals; a factor with two exclusive indicators needs a nonzero covariance with another identified factor. Both are sufficient and neither is necessary, and the second depends on an estimated quantity.
Chapter 3, Sec. 6


Identification
Moment Jacobian rank check
Full column rank of \(\partial\mathbf s/\partial\boldsymbol\vartheta^{\mathsf T}\) at a regular fitted point, a local diagnostic that supports local identification. It does not prove global uniqueness or uniform stability, and it is a check on the fitted solution rather than a structural proof.
Chapter 3, Sec. 6


Model relations
Nested, nonnested, and equivalent models (observational equivalence)
Nesting requires that every covariance matrix one model generates belongs to the other’s set, shown by the restrictions producing the inclusion. Equal degrees of freedom imply neither nesting nor equivalence, and observational equivalence limits what covariance data can distinguish.
Chapter 3, Sec. 6


Estimation
Normal-theory ML discrepancy (\(F_{\mathrm{ML}}\))
\(\log|\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)|+\operatorname{tr}\{\mathbf S\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)^{-1}\}-\log|\mathbf S|-p\), minimized over the admissible parameter space and normalized to zero at \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf S\). The covariance equation needs no normality; the conventional standard errors and test do.
Chapter 3, Sec. 7 (first used Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4)


Estimation
Covariance divisor convention (\(\mathbf S_N\) against \(\mathbf S_{N-1}\); normal against Wishart)
\(\mathbf S_N=\{(N-1)/N\}\mathbf S_{N-1}\) is the normal-likelihood convention; the Wishart convention uses an \(N-1\) covariance and multiplier. A supplied covariance matrix communicates neither the sample size nor the divisor, so the convention must be disclosed and never applied twice.
Chapter 3, Sec. 7


Mean structure
Indicator intercepts and the latent location convention
Free indicator intercepts with latent intercepts fixed at zero add \(p\) moments and \(p\) parameters, leaving the covariance restrictions and degrees of freedom unchanged. Freeing both at once identifies no latent origin, because \(\boldsymbol\alpha+\mathbf c\) with \(\boldsymbol\nu-\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf c\) reproduces the same means.
Chapter 3, Sec. 5


Solution quality
Convergence, admissibility, and the Heywood case
Convergence is an optimizer’s stopping statement; admissibility requires positive residual variances and positive definite factor and implied covariance matrices. A negative or zero residual variance is a symptom of the whole decomposition and is neither a cosmetic warning nor something to replace by zero in a report.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8


Inference
Wald test of a linear restriction (\(\mathbf R\boldsymbol\vartheta=\mathbf r\))
A \(\chi^2_q\) test computed from the estimates and their covariance matrix, requiring the covariance between estimates and not only their variances. It tests the stated restriction conditional on the rest of the model; it is not a global-fit test and need not equal a refitted likelihood-ratio statistic.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8


Transition record
Evaluation transition record (handoff record)
The auditable record of evidence identity, model, parameter conventions, estimation settings, numerical checks, parameter uncertainty, global/local evaluation and its limits, and reproduction metadata. It preserves what was fixed, inspected, or revised so a later comparison cannot silently change the analysis.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8


Observed system
Parceling (item aggregation)
Fitting \(\mathbf z=\mathbf A\mathbf y\) with \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf z)=\mathbf A\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf A^{\mathsf T}\). Reducing dimension lets different item-level patterns give the same parcel covariance, so a well-fitting parcel model does not establish the item-level restrictions.
Chapter 3, Appendix

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Evaluation, Comparison, Reliability, and Extensions



Table 4: Evaluation, comparison, reliability, and extensions.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Global fit
Model chi-square (exact-fit test; likelihood-ratio model test)
\(T_M=N\widehat F_{\mathrm{ML}}\) referred to \(\chi^2_{df_M}\), testing whether some admissible parameter vector reproduces the population moment structure exactly. Nonrejection is not acceptance of the model, and rejection at large \(N\) is evidence against exact fit rather than a measure of its magnitude.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 2


Global fit
RMSEA (root mean square error of approximation) with its 90% interval
Estimated discrepancy per degree of freedom, \(\sqrt{\max\{(T_M-df_M)/(N\,df_M),0\}}\), whose behavior also depends on model size and degrees of freedom, with an interval obtained by inverting a noncentral chi-square reference. A zero estimate is a truncation, not zero residuals; the convention (\(N\) or \(N-1\)) must be named.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 2


Global fit
Incremental fit index (CFI; TLI or NNFI) with its independence baseline
Improvement of the model relative to a stated reference rather than relative to exact fit. The usual baseline frees the observed variances and fixes all covariances to zero, so a high value depends on how poor that baseline is; TLI is not bounded by one.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 2


Global fit
SRMR (standardized root mean square residual)
Root mean square of observed-SD-standardized covariance residuals over one triangle including the diagonal. Not a mean absolute residual; a small value can hide a few large cells among many near-zero ones.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 3


Local diagnosis
Covariance residual (raw; observed-SD-standardized; correlation residual)
Observed minus implied covariance, either in the product of the two indicators’ units, divided by the product of observed SDs, or as a difference of separately formed correlations. None is a residual divided by its sampling standard error, so none is automatically a \(z\) statistic.
Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 3


Local diagnosis
Modification index (score statistic; Lagrange multiplier) and expected parameter change (EPC; standardized EPC)
A local one-parameter approximation to the improvement from releasing one fixed restriction, with the approximate value the released parameter would take. Read with the residual pattern, the parameter’s meaning, and the status of the search; not the exact LR change, and not an instruction.
Chapter 4, Sec. 6


Comparison
Nested difference test (\(\chi^2\) difference; likelihood-ratio difference test)
\(\Delta T=T_R-T_U\) on \(\Delta df=df_R-df_U\) for regularly nested, compatible ML fits on identical cases, outcomes, scale, mean structure, and likelihood convention. A smaller parameter count is not proof of nesting, and failure to reject is not equivalence.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4


Comparison
Information criteria for covariance structures (AIC; BIC) eligibility
\(-2\ell+2q\) and \(-2\ell+q\log N\) with \(q\) the effective free-parameter count. They rank eligible candidates fitted to the same observations and outcomes under one likelihood convention, including nonnested ones; neither is a test or an adequacy index.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4


Comparison
Score, Wald, and likelihood-ratio views of one restriction
Three statistics for one null: slope and information at the restricted fit; distance of the unrestricted estimate from the restriction relative to its uncertainty; difference of optimized likelihoods. Asymptotic equivalence is not finite-sample equality.
Chapter 4, Sec. 4


Comparison
Equivalent models (covariance-equivalent representation)
Distinct specifications with the same set of admissible implied covariance matrices, so that each is nested in the other: every covariance matrix one can reproduce, the other can also reproduce, as an exact parameter mapping shows. On any data they therefore give the same fitted covariance matrix, statistic, df, and fit indices. Identical fit in one sample is a consequence, not a test, and no covariance data can choose between them; only theory and evidence beyond reproduced covariance can.
Chapter 4, Sec. 5


Extensions
Higher-order factor model (second-order factor; first-order disturbance)
A model in which one further latent variable accounts for the covariances among first-order factors, \(\boldsymbol\Phi_l=\boldsymbol\gamma\boldsymbol\gamma^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Psi_h\). The first-order disturbances are distinct from indicator residuals. With diagonal first-order disturbances, the generic covariance-equality restriction count is \(m(m-3)/2\) for \(m\ge3\): three factors add no equality degrees of freedom, but nonnegative disturbance variances still restrict the admissible correlations.
Chapter 4, Sec. 5


Extensions
Bifactor model (general plus orthogonal specific or group factors)
Every item loads directly on one general factor and one assigned specific factor, all factors mutually orthogonal. A specific factor is common variance among its items after the general factor is held constant, not an item residual, and the model is generally nonnested against a correlated-factor model of the same items.
Chapter 4, Sec. 5


Extensions
Schmid-Leiman transformation and the proportionality restriction
The algebraic rewriting of a higher-order model as an orthogonal general factor with loadings \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_l\boldsymbol\gamma\) and specific factors with loadings \(\boldsymbol\Lambda_l\boldsymbol\Psi_h^{1/2}\). Because both come from one loading matrix, each simple-structure item in a domain has the same general-to-specific loading ratio \(\gamma_k/\psi_{h,k}^{1/2}\); a freely estimated bifactor model is not bound by that ratio.
Chapter 4, Sec. 5


Extensions
Method effect; testlet effect
Common variance among items sharing a format (reverse keying, response scale, informant) or a stimulus (passage, vignette, apparatus). Both are design-known groupings and the least controversial motivation for a specific factor, which generalizes a freed residual covariance to several items.
Chapter 4, Sec. 5


Reliability
Cronbach’s alpha for a declared unit-weighted score, \(\alpha_C\)
A coefficient computed from item variances and their total-score variance. Interpreting it as reliability requires additional measurement assumptions; it is not a universal lower bound when residual dependence is allowed.
Chapter 4, Sec. 8


Reliability
Model-based omega for a declared score, \(\omega(\mathbf w)\) (composite reliability)
The proportion of a declared weighted composite’s model-implied variance attributable to all modeled common factors. It retains cross-loadings, factor correlations, and modeled residual covariances, and is conditional on model, weights, and sample.
Chapter 4, Sec. 8


Reliability
Omega-hierarchical, \(\omega_h(\mathbf w)\)
The share of a declared score’s variance attributable specifically to a bifactor general factor. Its complement within total omega is modeled reliable specific-factor variance, not error, and a substantial value does not establish essential unidimensionality.
Chapter 4, Sec. 5


Reliability
Average variance extracted (AVE) and coefficient \(H\) as bounded neighbours
AVE summarizes average communality for a simple fully-standardized single-factor item set; \(H=a/(1+a)\) with \(a=\boldsymbol\lambda^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Theta^{-1}\boldsymbol\lambda\) is a maximum over optimally weighted composites. Neither is the reliability of a stated unit-weighted score, and neither applies unqualified to a cross-loading subscale.
Chapter 4, Appendix


Scores
Factor score (regression or conditional-mean score; Bartlett score) and factor-score determinacy
A model-dependent linear prediction of a latent variable from the indicators, whose weights use the whole fitted structure; determinacy is the model-based correlation between factor and prediction. A score is a prediction with nonzero conditional variance, not an observed latent value.
Chapter 4, Sec. 8


Analytic history
Pseudo-true (population-ML) parameter and population discrepancy (\(F_0\); population RMSEA)
The optimum of a misspecified model fitted to the exact generating covariance, and the discrepancy remaining there. Displacement at this optimum is deterministic under two stated specifications, not sampling fluctuation and not finite-sample estimator bias.
Chapter 4, Sec. 7


Analytic history
Post-selection revision and independent revalidation
A change suggested by inspecting a body of evidence is exploratory with respect to that evidence, whatever function fits it; only records not used to suggest it can support it, and a retest that fails to support it does not prove the parameter is zero.
Chapter 4, Sec. 6

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Observed Structural Systems



Table 5: Observed Structural Systems.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Structural systems
Structural equation
An equation representing an outcome as a function of its designated predictors and a disturbance, within a declared system. Its causal interpretation requires assumptions beyond covariance fit.
Chapter 5, Sec. 1


Structural systems
Endogenous variable
A variable explained by another variable in the structural system. This model role differs from econometric endogeneity, which concerns dependence between a regressor and its equation’s disturbance.
Chapter 5, Sec. 1; Sec. 3


Structural systems
Exogenous variable
A variable whose distribution is supplied without modeling incoming structural paths in the declared system. The label alone does not establish independence from every unmeasured cause.
Chapter 5, Sec. 1


Structural systems
Structural disturbance (\(\zeta\))
Variation in a structural outcome not represented by its designated predictors. Covariances among disturbances and with exogenous variables are part of the model’s assumptions.
Chapter 5, Sec. 1


Structural systems
Reduced form
The structural equations solved in terms of the exogenous inputs and disturbances, when the required inverse exists. Reduced-form coefficients combine direct and transmitted relationships.
Chapter 5, Sec. 1; Sec. 7


Structural systems
Direct, indirect and total effect
A direct coefficient belongs to one structural equation; an indirect contribution follows a directed route. In an acyclic linear system, the total sums the compatible directed-route products. Feedback requires the inverse-system response. A causal reading requires the declared causal assumptions.
Chapter 5, Sec. 2; Sec. 7


Structural systems
Saturated structural system
A structural parameterization that leaves the modeled variables’ covariance unrestricted. Its coefficients can be estimated with uncertainty even though its global covariance test has zero degrees of freedom.
Chapter 5, Sec. 3; Sec. 4


Structural systems
Recursive and nonrecursive system
Under the chapter’s convention, a recursive linear system has an acyclic ordering, mutually uncorrelated disturbances, and disturbances uncorrelated with exogenous inputs. Feedback or relaxed disturbance assumptions require a separate identification analysis.
Chapter 5, Sec. 1; Sec. 7


Feedback
Feedback (reciprocal system)
A directed cycle in a simultaneous structural system. Its equilibrium interpretation differs from an observed lagged relationship across measurement occasions.
Chapter 5, Sec. 7


Feedback
Equilibrium stability
For the declared repeated linear adjustment, the condition \(\rho(\mathbf B)<1\) that makes departures decay. Existence of \((\mathbf I-\mathbf B)^{-1}\) alone does not establish stability.
Chapter 5, Sec. 7


Reproducibility
Summary-statistic reconstruction
Analysis using the published moments, variable definitions, sample information and model restrictions actually available. Distinguish a numerical reproduction from a changed reanalysis or an independent empirical replication.
Chapter 5, Sec. 5; Sec. 8

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Causal Models, Interventions and Identification



Table 6: Causal Models, Interventions and Identification.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Causal interpretation
Structural causal model (SCM)
Structural assignments and a distribution for their disturbances, with an intervention defined by replacing an assignment while retaining the other declared mechanisms.
Chapter 6, Sec. 1


Causal interpretation
Conditioning
Comparing or selecting observations at a recorded value of a variable. It generally changes the distribution of related variables and is different from intervening on the variable.
Chapter 6, Sec. 1


Causal interpretation
Intervention
Replacing a variable’s structural assignment by a specified value or policy under the model’s invariance assumptions. Setting a value removes that variable’s incoming causal arrows.
Chapter 6, Sec. 4


Causal interpretation
Collider
A variable at which two arrows on a path meet head to head. Conditioning on it or its descendant can open an otherwise blocked path.
Chapter 6, Sec. 2


Causal interpretation
d-separation
A graph criterion that blocks every path between two sets under a conditioning set and implies conditional independence under the graph’s Markov assumptions. An open path permits dependence but does not guarantee it for every parameter value.
Chapter 6, Sec. 2


Identification
Instrumental variable
A source of regressor variation requiring relevance, exclusion from the outcome equation, and the stated independence or orthogonality to its disturbance. A first-stage association tests neither exclusion nor exogeneity.
Chapter 6, Sec. 6


Identification
Instrument relevance
Association with the endogenous regressor after the included controls are accounted for. Weak conditional association makes the identifying covariance ratio unstable.
Chapter 6, Sec. 6


Identification
Exclusion restriction
A restriction removing a direct route from an instrument to the outcome in the stated structural equation and control set. It needs substantive support distinct from first-stage strength.
Chapter 6, Sec. 6


Identification
Causal identification
Whether the stated causal target is uniquely determined by the observed distribution together with the declared causal assumptions; statistical parameter recovery within one chosen model does not establish this.
Chapter 6, Sec. 1; Sec. 6


Adjustment
Backdoor adjustment
Recovering an intervention distribution by averaging conditional outcome distributions over a stated target covariate distribution when the covariates satisfy the causal adjustment requirements, with consistency and positivity.
Chapter 6, Sec. 4


Counterfactuals
Counterfactual outcome
The outcome under a specified replacement of a structural assignment while retaining the unit’s relevant disturbances; factual evidence determines what is known or uncertain about those disturbances.
Chapter 6, Sec. 5


Counterfactuals
Abduction, action and prediction
Updating disturbance information using factual evidence, replacing the specified assignment, and propagating that retained information through the altered system.
Chapter 6, Sec. 5


Sensitivity
Exclusion sensitivity
Re-estimating a target under explicitly fixed alternative direct instrument-outcome effects; conditional sampling intervals and the across-assumption sensitivity range answer different questions.
Chapter 6, Sec. 7

text:
Joint Measurement and Structural Modeling



Table 7: Joint Measurement and Structural Modeling.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Full SEM
Joint measurement model
One model containing all relevant measurement blocks, with their factors allowed to covary before structural restrictions are imposed.
Chapter 7, Sec. 1


Full SEM
Two-step SEM workflow
Evaluation of a joint measurement specification followed by joint estimation of its measurement and structural parameters in the full SEM.
Chapter 7, Sec. 1


Full SEM
Structurally saturated model
A model whose structural component reproduces an unrestricted covariance among its latent variables; measurement restrictions may still leave the complete model with positive degrees of freedom.
Chapter 7, Sec. 2; Sec. 4


Exploratory measurement
ESEM
A structural equation model containing an exploratory factor block whose estimated loadings are oriented by rotation, potentially alongside confirmatory blocks and structural regressions.
Chapter 7, Sec. 5


Exploratory measurement
Target rotation
Rotation toward a declared loading pattern whose target entries guide orientation rather than necessarily fixing corresponding loadings to exact values.
Chapter 7, Sec. 5


Measurement representation
Causal indicator
An observed variable proposed to contribute to a latent variable whose disturbance represents additional causes. Identification requires more than assigning arrows to its predictors.
Chapter 7, Sec. 6


Measurement representation
Exact composite
A variable defined as a specified weighted combination of observed components, with no disturbance in that defining equation.
Chapter 7, Sec. 6


Means and covariates
Mean structure
The model’s specification of expected observed levels through intercepts, latent means, and predictor means.
Chapter 7, Sec. 7


Means and covariates
MIMIC model
A model combining observed predictors of a latent variable with multiple indicators of that latent variable.
Chapter 7, Sec. 7

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Indirect and Conditional Relationships



Table 8: Indirect and Conditional Relationships.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Indirect relationships
Specific indirect effect
The product of coefficients along one directed indirect route between a stated source and outcome in the declared linear structural system.
Chapter 8, Sec. 1


Indirect relationships
Total indirect effect
The sum of the specified directed indirect-route contributions between the same source and outcome. Contributions with opposite signs can cancel.
Chapter 8, Sec. 2


Indirect relationships
Indirect-effect contrast
A difference or other declared comparison of indirect effects whose uncertainty retains the dependence between their estimated component paths.
Chapter 8, Sec. 2


Conditional relationships
Conditional slope
The rate of change in a modeled conditional mean with a predictor at stated values of the moderator and other conditioned variables. Its value depends on the declared scale and origin.
Chapter 8, Sec. 6


Conditional relationships
Latent interaction
A product relationship involving latent predictors represented through explicit measurement models. A latent outcome alone does not turn an observed predictor product into a latent interaction.
Chapter 8, Sec. 5


Conditional relationships
Product indicator
An observed product of indicators used to represent a latent product under specified measurement-error and centering assumptions. Its measurement error contains more than the product of the two original errors.
Chapter 8, Sec. 5


Conditional relationships
Conditional indirect effect
A specified indirect-effect function evaluated at stated moderator values, with its uncertainty propagated through the joint parameter estimates.
Chapter 8, Sec. 7


Conditional relationships
Index of moderated mediation
The coefficient describing change in a specified indirect effect per unit of a moderator when that indirect-effect function is linear in the moderator. Its formula depends on the structural model.
Chapter 8, Sec. 7

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Measurement Comparability and Group Comparisons



Table 9: Measurement Comparability and Group Comparisons.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Comparability
Measurement invariance
Equality of the conditional response distribution across groups at the same latent values. Particular loading, intercept and residual restrictions express aspects of this requirement within a declared measurement model.
Chapter 9, Sec. 1; Sec. 3


Comparability
Configural model
A joint group model with the same designated factor-loading pattern and separately estimated group parameters under declared scale and location constraints. The shared pattern alone does not establish a common factor unit or origin.
Chapter 9, Sec. 2


Comparability
Metric invariance (loading invariance)
Equality of the designated factor loadings across groups, supporting a common factor unit through the stated anchors. It does not impose common indicator intercepts or residual structures.
Chapter 9, Sec. 3


Comparability
Scalar invariance (intercept invariance)
Equality of the designated indicator intercepts as well as loadings, supporting a common origin for the specified latent-mean comparison. The comparison group’s latent means remain free when they are the target.
Chapter 9, Sec. 3


Comparability
Strict invariance
Equality of the measurement residual covariance structure in addition to the scalar restrictions. It is not generally required for a latent-mean comparison and does not alone guarantee equal reliability.
Chapter 9, Sec. 3


Comparability
Partial invariance
A declared model that retains specified cross-group equality restrictions while allowing selected measurement parameters to differ. Its interpretation depends on the remaining anchors and the evidence supporting them.
Chapter 9, Sec. 4


Identification and comparison
Anchor
A retained measurement restriction that supplies a common reference for the latent scale or origin. A numerically identifying anchor can still lack substantive comparability.
Chapter 9, Sec. 4


Identification and comparison
Anchor sensitivity
Variation in an interpreted factor comparison when the declared parameters linking its scale or origin across groups are changed.
Chapter 9, Sec. 4


Group targets
Latent-mean contrast
A difference or other declared comparison of latent means on a supported common scale and origin. Its standardized form additionally depends on the chosen reference variance.
Chapter 9, Sec. 5


Group targets
Multigroup SEM
Joint estimation of group-specific measurement and structural systems with explicit restrictions on which parameters are shared and which can differ.
Chapter 9, Sec. 2; Sec. 5


Group targets
Conditional group contrast
A comparison at specified covariate values under the fitted model. It can differ from the marginal group difference because the groups’ covariate distributions differ.
Chapter 9, Sec. 5; Sec. 6


Item comparisons
Intercept differential item functioning (uniform DIF)
A group difference in an indicator’s conditional expected response at the same latent values, represented by an intercept difference or a group-to-indicator direct path in the stated model. It is distinct from loading noninvariance.
Chapter 9, Sec. 6

text:
Incomplete Data and Robust Inference



Table 10: Incomplete Data and Robust Inference.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Observation process
Missingness pattern
The combination of observed and missing variables in a record.
Chapter 10, Sec. 1


Observation process
MCAR
Missingness does not depend on the observed or unobserved values in the analysis.
Chapter 10, Sec. 2


Observation process
MAR
Conditional on the observed information included in the analysis, missingness does not depend on the unobserved values.
Chapter 10, Sec. 2


Observation process
MNAR
Missingness still depends on unobserved values after conditioning on the observed information in the analysis.
Chapter 10, Sec. 2


Observation process
Ignorability
Conditions under which inference for the data-model parameters can omit an explicit missingness model; for likelihood inference these include MAR and distinct parameters.
Chapter 10, Sec. 2


Observed-data estimation
Observed-data likelihood
A likelihood formed from the values actually observed, integrating over the missing values under the specified model.
Chapter 10, Sec. 3


Observed-data estimation
FIML
Joint maximum-likelihood estimation using each record’s observed variables and the corresponding model-implied distribution.
Chapter 10, Sec. 3


Additional information
Auxiliary variable
An additional variable included to supply information about incomplete values or missingness without assigning it a substantive structural role.
Chapter 10, Sec. 6


Robust inference
Sandwich covariance
A parameter covariance estimate combining likelihood curvature with the empirical variability of individual score contributions.
Chapter 10, Sec. 5


Robust inference
Scaled difference test
A model-comparison test that adjusts the difference in compatible unscaled fit statistics using information from the fitted models.
Chapter 10, Sec. 5


Additional information
Sensitivity parameter
A quantity fixed at substantively considered values to examine how conclusions depend on an assumption the observed data do not identify.
Chapter 10, Sec. 6

title: Part Two Concept Reference
text:
Latent Growth Models



Table 11: Latent Growth Models.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Trajectory components
Latent intercept
A person-specific level of the modeled trajectory at the declared time origin. Its unit and location depend on the outcome or measurement scale.
Chapter 11, Sec. 2


Trajectory components
Latent slope
A person-specific change per unit of coded time in a linear growth model; its meaning changes when the time unit or growth basis changes.
Chapter 11, Sec. 2


Trajectory components
Mean slope
The population mean of the latent slope in an unconditional model; with predictors, the structural slope intercept describes the mean at the stated predictor reference.
Chapter 11, Sec. 2


Trajectory components
Slope variance
Between-person variance of the latent slope under the specified trajectory model, distinct from uncertainty in the estimated mean slope.
Chapter 11, Sec. 2


Time and shape
Intercept–slope covariance
Covariance between the latent level at a declared time origin and the latent slope; changing that origin can change its value or sign without changing the modeled trajectories.
Chapter 11, Sec. 4


Time and shape
Time centering
Replacing time by time minus a stated constant, changing the intercept meaning and its moments while preserving the same trajectory model.
Chapter 11, Sec. 4


Time and shape
Latent basis
A growth model that fixes two basis loadings to set the origin and unit and estimates the remaining loadings; people share the basis shape while their levels and amplitudes vary.
Chapter 11, Sec. 4


Time and shape
Piecewise growth
A trajectory represented by distinct functions over prespecified time segments, with explicit restrictions on the knot, continuity and the meaning of each slope.
Chapter 11, Sec. 4


Longitudinal measurement
Occasion disturbance
An occasion-specific latent deviation from the growth curve, distinguished from an indicator-specific measurement residual in a multiple-indicator growth model.
Chapter 11, Sec. 5


Longitudinal measurement
Longitudinal measurement comparability
Support for measurement restrictions that make the intended construct comparison meaningful across occasions, including suitable loading and intercept anchors for latent mean growth.
Chapter 11, Sec. 5

text:
Study Planning and Power Analysis



Table 12: Study Planning and Power Analysis.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
text:
NoteChapter overview



One research question can need several statistical answers before its substantive answer is justified. A study can also owe several separately reportable answers whose support depends on one another. This chapter teaches how to distinguish these arrangements, read their supporting records, evaluate their conclusions, and coordinate construction and revision. An invented feedback study and an invented confidence-and-belonging study develop the ideas. Historical occupation records and a published working-from-home experiment provide transfers.
A report may contain a dozen models but answer only one question. Another may fit a single model while answering two questions that have different evidential obligations. Counting models, coefficients or significant tests therefore gives little guidance about the structure of the study. Start with what the report promises to answer, and ask which results that answer actually needs.
The examples supply the study information and explain the selected output locally. Familiarity with regression and intervals helps, but the reading tasks do not require completing every earlier chapter or fitting a factor or mixed model. Full method instruction has a different purpose: here the task is to understand what a result contributes and what its conditions allow a researcher to say. Calculated values are rounded to four decimals, dropping unnecessary trailing zeros; software or intermediate rounding can produce small differences.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
section: Recognizing Separate Questions and Statistical Strands
text:
Recognizing Separate Questions and Statistical Strands

Begin with the answer owed
An argument connects a question to its bounded answer through evidence, justification and inference. Evidence is the information used; justification comprises the reasons and conditions offered for using it; inference is the analytical and interpretive work; the claim is the resulting answer with its limits. Each question-answer pair has one argument with linked statistical and substantive layers. The statistical layer concerns quantities, models and uncertainty. The substantive layer concerns what those quantities mean in the study’s setting.
For example, a mean difference is a statistical result. Reading it as a worthwhile change in retained learning also needs information about the assessment, its timing and a defensible benchmark. Neither layer substitutes for the other. A calculation can be correct while the interpretation reaches beyond the measured outcome, and a compelling educational question can remain unanswered because its uncertainty is large.



Table 1: The promised answer, rather than the number of models, determines the arrangement.










Arrangement
What the report promises
What the reader follows




Independent questions
Separate answers whose support does not depend on one another
Each question’s argument


One integrated question
One answer that jointly requires distinct estimands, such as worthwhile learning with acceptable time burden
Several statistical strands within one argument


Coordinated questions
Separately owed answers, with support or qualifications passed between them
Each argument and the dependency between answers






A statistical strand is an estimand-specific statistical chain inside one argument. Two strands arise when sibling estimands are jointly required for one integrated substantive answer; each has its own inference and conclusion. Several estimators or sensitivity checks for the same target can remain within one strand. Conversely, two outcomes become separate arguments when the report promises a separate substantive answer for each.
Suppose a college asks, “Does this feedback format produce worthwhile sustained learning without an unacceptable increase in students’ study time?” The performance and time comparisons jointly serve that one answer. If the college instead commissions a learning-effect report and a separate workload report, two answers are owed. The data may be identical; the question-answer contract differs. A reader should identify when this organization is supplied by the report and when it is the reader’s proposed reconstruction of an unclear report.


Share information without sharing every reason
A class-allocation record contributes evidence about assignment to both the performance and time comparisons. The validity of a score interpretation and the completeness of time logs are different matters. They need different measurement information even when the same students provide both outcomes. Shared data also make the two estimated effects statistically dependent; distinct strands do not imply independent samples.
A recorded item can perform more than one function. The allocation procedure is evidence about what happened and can supply a reason for an assignment-effect interpretation. The fitted model and its estimates are analytical work in Inference; the reasons offered for its adjustment set and uncertainty calculation belong to Justification. A weak reason is still an identifiable reason. Reading records what the authors invoke before evaluation judges whether it is adequate.
Within a layer, evidence together with justification supports inference, and inference supports the claim. The substantive-to-statistical links have four functions: substantive evidence situates statistical records; substantive reasons augment and contextualize statistical justification; substantive interpretation interprets statistical inference; and the substantive claim bounds its question-facing reach. A dependency between separately owed answers is a different relationship. Its arrow must name the support received rather than imply that one result causes another.
Two auxiliary reading tasks help organize this work. First identify the argument’s organization: which questions receive their own answers, which estimands jointly support one answer, and which records are shared. Then follow reporting across the abstract, methods, results and discussion. Ask whether the final wording retains the same outcome, time, population, uncertainty and question. These are practical reading tasks, not additional argument components.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
section: Reading One Complex Argument with Multiple Statistical Strands
text:
Reading One Complex Argument with Multiple Statistical Strands

A declared joint question
The following extension is invented. Its setting has 480 eligible students in 24 classes, with 20 students per class. Twelve classes receive explanatory feedback and twelve receive the comparison format, allocated across the full class pool. This is class assignment, not individual assignment or paired assignment within schools. Classes are treated as independent; no additional school grouping is stipulated. The assignment-effect interpretation invokes consistent implementation and no relevant spillovers between classes; actual attendance would be a different exposure. Repeated scores from the same student and scores from students in the same class remain dependent.
The six-week program has an assessment two weeks after it ends and another twelve weeks after it ends. Students record time spent studying outside scheduled instruction during the program. The burden outcome is their average weekly minutes across those six weeks. It is neither teacher workload nor all time spent in education.
The earlier supplied feedback report concerned its two-week assessment and stipulated an estimate of 2.5 with interval [1, 4]. The new generated records below are a separate teaching realization of the extended design. They do not reproduce that earlier fitted result. Its original answer remains attached to its original occasion and report.



Table 2: A protocol packet makes the integrated answer assessable.









Protocol item
Prospective commitment in this invented extension




Question
Does assignment improve twelve-week performance by more than 2 points while increasing weekly outside-class study time by less than 30 minutes?


Targets
Average assignment effects on the named twelve-week assessment and on weekly study time for these eligible students


Benchmarks
Teachers judge 2 assessment points educationally worthwhile; a student panel judges an additional half-hour per week the largest acceptable burden in this setting. These are stipulated local reasons, not universal cutoffs.


Weighting
Each eligible student receives equal weight; the equal class sizes also make equal-class and equal-student target weighting agree.


Success rule
Both benchmark conditions must receive the declared directional support. Failure to establish one leaves overall success unresolved.


Production
Preserve the allocation record, score rubric, assessment times, time-log instructions, completeness accounting and model/check record.






The model is chosen to represent the question and dependence, rather than to make every recorded variable a predictor. For student \(i\) in class \(j\) at occasion \(t\), let \(G_j=1\) denote explanatory feedback, \(L_t=1\) denote the twelve-week occasion, and \(B_{ij}\) denote a centered baseline score. The working model is
\[
Y_{ijt}=\beta_0+\beta_B B_{ij}+\beta_G G_j+\beta_L L_t+
\beta_{GL}G_jL_t+u_j+v_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ijt}.
\]
Here \(u_j\) is a class deviation, \(v_{ij}\) a student deviation shared across occasions, and \(\varepsilon_{ijt}\) an occasion-specific deviation. The supplied fit uses independent, mean-zero Normal random intercepts and residuals, with common variances for each component, and restricted maximum likelihood for the variance components. These are working conditions, not facts proved by a diagram or by software convergence. Baseline adjustment is included for precision; it does not create the randomized assignment.
The assignment contrast at twelve weeks is \(\theta_Y=\beta_G+\beta_{GL}\). With no assignment-by-baseline interaction and mean-zero random effects, that fixed contrast also gives the model’s marginal assignment contrast for the declared weighting. The interaction coefficient by itself asks how the assignment contrast changes between the two occasions. It is not the twelve-week effect. Two occasions also do not identify an unrestricted growth trajectory.


Read the supplied results
The generated complete-data fit gives \(\widehat\beta_G=2.4793\) and \(\widehat\beta_{GL}=1.3093\). Their sum, calculated before rounding, is a twelve-week contrast of 3.7886 points. Its SE uses their covariance; adding the two coefficient SEs would be incorrect. Burden is analyzed through the 24 class means, comparing twelve classes with twelve classes. This avoids treating 480 students as independent assignment units.



Table 3: Supplied model-based comparisons for the invented extension.












Strand
Estimate
SE

The bounds use a \(t\) reference with 22 class degrees of freedom. For the mixed-model contrast this is a declared approximate class-level calibration; for the equal-variance comparison of independent class means it is the usual reference. The lower gain bound and upper time bound answer different directional questions. Both must pass for the joint success claim. This is an intersection-union decision: when at least one benchmark condition is false, declaring success requires incorrectly passing that condition’s test. Subject to the calibrations, the overall false-success probability is therefore at most .05. The two marginal bounds are not being presented as a 95% simultaneous confidence region.








Figure 1: The joint answer needs support on both sides of the protocol: worthwhile performance and acceptable burden.





The time estimate is below 30, but the uncertainty extends above it. A test against zero would ask whether there is any change in time. That is a different question from whether the increase stays below the acceptable margin. Equally, failing to establish acceptability does not establish that the program is too burdensome.
A calibrated answer is: the model-based evidence supports a worthwhile twelve-week performance gain, while the acceptable-burden condition remains unresolved; the declared joint success criterion is not established. The findings are useful precisely because they identify the unresolved part. Calling the program successful merely because its learning p-value is small would discard one of the promised obligations.


Trace how the strands contribute








Figure 2: Two estimand-specific statistical strands contribute to one integrated substantive answer.








Table 4: One integrated answer retains both strands’ contributions.

Fit the repeated-score model, form the later contrast with covariance, compare class-average time and compute the declared directional bounds
Equation and results table


Statistical claims
Gain exceeds its benchmark under the model; acceptable burden remains unresolved
Benchmark column and interpretation


Substantive evidence and justification
The assessment measures the intended course performance; outside-class minutes express the chosen burden; local reasons support the two benchmarks
Rubric, log instructions and protocol

Calibrated answer above






The table locates the promised supporting documents; their adequacy still requires examination. A rubric would need evidence for its score interpretation, and a time log could miss unrecorded studying. A small model residual does not verify either measurement. The generated residuals illustrate a calculation, not empirical evidence that a real educational intervention satisfies these conditions.


A focused missingness sensitivity
Now change the record: suppose the last two listed students in each class lack the twelve-week assessment. This is an invented missingness scenario, with 48 missing outcomes and 432 observed outcomes. It does not alter the original target of all 480 eligible students. For a transparent sensitivity calculation, fill each missing value first with its observed class mean. Then lower the missing feedback students’ values by \(\delta\) points while leaving the comparison reference values unchanged.
The reference is a within-class completion scenario, not a claim that missing scores equal those means. Class weighting is preserved, and only the hypothesized unobserved feedback outcomes change. Because 10% of feedback outcomes are missing, the resulting unadjusted assignment difference changes by \(0.1\delta\):
\[
\widehat\Delta(\delta)=3.9992-0.1\delta,
\]
where calculations use the unrounded reference difference. This is a point-estimate sensitivity for the class-weighted completed outcome, not a re-estimated mixed-model confidence interval. A proper inferential missing-data analysis must also account for imputation uncertainty and the dependence structure (Little & Rubin, 2019; National Research Council, 2010).



Table 5: A missingness assumption can change a benchmark comparison without changing an observed score.

The point comparison reaches 2 at a shortfall of 19.9916 points. This is a tipping point for that particular sensitivity estimand and completion rule. Whether such a shortfall is plausible needs reasons about absence and the assessment scale. It is not a test that establishes the missingness mechanism, and it cannot resolve the original time-burden uncertainty.
Predict and explain. If the assumed shortfall doubled from 5 to 10 while the observed data remained fixed, the completed difference would fall by 0.5 points. The change comes from an assumption about the missing tenth of the feedback group. A correct answer names that source, rather than saying that the treatment suddenly became less effective in the observed records.
