title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
section: Reading Coordinated Questions and Their Dependencies
text:
Reading Coordinated Questions and Their Dependencies

A measurement answer and a substantive answer
A second invented study observes 400 students in one educational setting. It records three continuously scored indicators of learning confidence and three of belonging at entry, followed by an achievement score at the end of term. These are separate generated participants, not an undocumented extension of the feedback sample. The six indicators are invented measurement summaries, not a validated questionnaire.
The investigators promise two answers. First, does a proposed two-factor representation provide a defensible summary of the six indicators in this setting? Second, how do those two factors relate to later achievement under a joint model? The first supplies part of the support the second needs, but the second still requires achievement measurement, timing, model form and substantive reasoning of its own.



Table 6: Measurement meaning precedes a factor label.










Recorded indicator
Intended meaning in the invented instrument
Model assignment




c1
Confidence in explaining a solution
Confidence factor


c2
Confidence in attempting unfamiliar work
Confidence factor


c3
Confidence in recovering after an error
Confidence factor


b1
Feeling accepted in the learning group
Belonging factor


b2
Feeling able to seek help
Belonging factor


b3
Feeling part of the class
Belonging factor






A confirmatory factor model represents each indicator as an intercept plus a loading times its assigned factor plus a measurement residual. A loading expresses how an indicator varies with the factor. The model allows the two factors to covary, assigns each indicator to its named factor, and fixes residual covariances to zero. These restrictions have substantive implications: for example, shared wording might create residual association not represented by the two factors.
The first loading of each factor is fixed to 1 to define its unit; factor means are fixed to zero in this single-group model. Other loadings and factor variances are estimated. A one-unit change in a factor is therefore expressed on its marker indicator’s scale, not automatically one standard deviation. Scale setting makes the model interpretable and identified under its other conditions. It is not evidence that the first indicator is perfectly reliable.








Figure 3: A two-factor measurement model is retained when the later-achievement association is added. Arrows express model relations, not established causal effects.





The factor-to-indicator arrows represent the measurement loadings. Adding the two arrows to later achievement retains that measurement representation while asking a new question. Residual variation remains in every indicator and in achievement; the diagram is a model specification, not evidence of causal direction.


Read a fit result without turning it into a certificate
The six-indicator two-factor model is fitted by maximum likelihood with a mean structure. It has 8 degrees of freedom and gives \(\chi^2=8.4265\), \(p=.393\), CFI = 0.9996, RMSEA = 0.0115 and SRMR = 0.0158. The CFI compares with a baseline model, RMSEA summarizes discrepancy per degree of freedom, and SRMR summarizes standardized residual discrepancies. The small discrepancies are compatible with this deliberately generated process; they do not establish the validity of a real confidence or belonging interpretation (Bollen, 1989; Kane, 2013).
Two separate three-indicator one-factor models would each be just identified under their usual unconstrained covariance specification. Perfect global fit there would test no covariance restriction. The joint two-factor model here has testable restrictions. A reader should therefore ask what the reported fit actually tests before treating a favorable index as evidence.



Table 7: One restriction can have an implementation, a reason, and a test; these are different functions.










Statement in a model report
Function to identify
What evaluation still asks




“The loading of c1 is fixed to 1.”
Implemented scale constraint in statistical Inference
Does the model have adequate identification and a clear unit?


“A scale must be set because factor units are otherwise arbitrary.”
Justification for the scale constraint
Does that reason apply to this specification?


“We compare a model with two loadings equal against the less restricted model.”
A tested restriction and comparison in Inference
Is the comparison eligible, and what does equality mean on these scales?


“The fit is acceptable, so both constructs are measured without error.”
A substantive claim based on the fit
The conclusion is too strong: the model explicitly includes measurement error and does not establish construct meaning alone.








Follow support into the later-achievement model
The substantive model retains the six-indicator measurement structure and adds
\[
Y_i=\alpha+\gamma_C\eta_{Ci}+\gamma_B\eta_{Bi}+\zeta_i,
\]
where \(\eta_C\) and \(\eta_B\) denote the confidence and belonging factors, \(Y\) is later achievement and \(\zeta\) its remaining variation. The coefficients compare expected achievement at the same value of the other factor under the model. They are associations: neither confidence nor belonging was randomly assigned, and temporal order alone does not remove confounding.



Table 8: Jointly fitted measurement and later-achievement model on 400 invented records.











Conditional association
Estimate
SE
Model-based 95% interval




Confidence, holding belonging fixed
3.1068
0.5152
[2.0971, 4.1166]


Belonging, holding confidence fixed
1.9208
0.5061
[0.9289, 2.9127]






These unstandardized coefficients use the marker scales defined above. Their standard errors arise from joint estimation of the measurement and regression parameters. Treating estimated factor scores as perfectly measured predictors in a second ordinary regression would be a different analysis, with different uncertainty and potentially different targets. A dependency in the argument does not require fitting its models in separate chronological steps.








Figure 4: A measurement answer supplies specified support to a separately owed substantive answer.





The measurement answer supports how the later question represents its explanatory variables, and supplies reasons for interpreting the estimated relations as involving confidence and belonging. It does not supply a randomization argument or a verified causal mechanism. The substantive conclusion remains conditional on the measurement specification, association model, selection and timing of the observed students.


A qualification can have a selective consequence
Suppose the instrument has been examined within each of two programs, but equality of item intercepts across programs remains unresolved. A within-program association can still be examined under its own supported measurement model. A claim that one program has a higher latent confidence mean requires additional comparability information. It should not inherit approval from an adequate within-program model. Equally, the unresolved mean comparison is not a reason to reject every within-program association.
Now suppose a residual association between two similarly worded confidence indicators is substantively justified and added to the model. Refit the measurement and substantive model, then trace which estimates and claims change. An unchanged later-achievement conclusion might survive the sensitivity; a changed conclusion needs revision. The arrow transfers conditions as well as support.
This logic also helps with indirect effects. A significant overall treatment effect is not a general prerequisite for asking about an indirect effect. However, randomizing treatment does not by itself randomize a mediator or establish the mediator-outcome comparison. Likewise, moderation asks how a specified association or effect varies; it does not establish the mechanism responsible for that variation. The questions and their design support, rather than a ritual sequence of significant tests, determine what must be justified.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
section: Evaluating Answers and Their Cross-Question Coherence
text:
Evaluating Answers and Their Cross-Question Coherence

Judge the answer actually offered
Reading identifies the evidence, reasons, analytical steps and claims. Evaluation then asks whether they support the answer. The six question-level checks are Question alignment, Evidence integrity, Justification adequacy, Inferential adequacy, Transition fidelity, and Claim calibration. Each receives a reasoned judgment: adequate for this purpose, needs revision, insufficient information to judge, or not applicable. These are judgments about particular functions, not scores to total.
A whole argument can then be supported as stated, supported only after narrowing or revision, not supported, or not assessable from the accessible record. An explicitly unresolved answer can be supported as stated. A study need not produce a decisive positive result to complete its question honestly.
For the feedback case, the statement that gain clears its benchmark while burden remains unresolved matches the supplied evidence and conditions. The stronger claim that the declared joint success criterion has been met does not. The originating problem is an unjustified transition from the time estimate to its acceptability, with consequences for the integrated claim. Penalizing the same mistake under several labels adds little to this diagnosis.
For the measurement study, a supported single-setting interpretation cannot silently become a cross-program mean comparison. That limitation passes to the particular later question requiring cross-program comparability. If a report promises both answers, add Cross-question coherence: does their synthesis retain each answer’s target, population, uncertainty and qualifications? This seventh check concerns joining separately owed answers. Multiple strands within one argument still use the six checks.
Consider the offered reason, “Because the SEM fits well, the predictor was effectively randomized.” Reading records an identifiable reason in Justification; evaluation judges it inadequate. Model fit concerns agreement with restrictions on the observed distribution. It does not supply the missing design argument. Recording the reason as absent would conceal the actual error.


Three answers from the same occupation records
The historical Canadian occupation data provide a complete transfer (Fox & Weisberg, 2019). An occupation is the unit, income is in thousand 1971 Canadian dollars, education is average years, prestige comes from an earlier rating survey, and the remaining predictors are percentage of women and three occupation types. Of 102 records, 98 have a recorded type. All three comparisons below retain those same 98 records.
The additive working model regresses income on education, prestige, percentage of women and two type indicators. Its education slope compares expected occupation income at the same values of the other predictors within supported combinations. It is neither an individual return to schooling nor automatically a causal effect. The supplied record is sufficient for the argument task even if these data are unfamiliar.



Table 9: Three separately owed answers in the occupation teaching study.










Pair and role
Question
Estimand and owed answer




1. Contextual description
How does income vary linearly with education across the 98 retained occupations?
The finite-record marginal least-squares slope; a descriptive answer for these records


2. Primary conditional association
How does income differ with education at the same prestige, percentage of women, and type, within support?
The linear conditional-mean coefficient \(\beta_E\) under the declared working model; fitted \(b_E\) is its estimate from the 98 retained records


3. Secondary prediction analysis
Does the full additive learning rule predict eligible same-source occupation records with lower expected absolute error than the education-only rule?
Difference in expected absolute error of the two learning procedures at the declared training sizes; an internal validation answer








Read the supplied teaching report

R0 – Common record and declared scope. We analyzed the 98 complete occupation records described above. Income was scaled to thousand 1971 Canadian dollars. Education and income were historical occupational averages; prestige came from an earlier rating survey. We retained the same rows for all three questions and make no claim of verified probability sampling or randomized education.
R1 – Marginal answer. Across these records the education-only least-squares slope was 0.883 thousand dollars per year. This is a descriptive linear summary: occupations with more education tended to have higher average income. It is not an individual or causal effect.
R2 – Conditional answer. The intended estimand was the linear conditional-mean education coefficient \(\beta_E\), comparing education at the same prestige, percentage of women, and occupational type. Its fitted estimate was \(b_E=0.1164\), with a classical 95% interval [\(-0.4302\), 0.6631] under the independent linear conditional-mean working model with common variance and the Normal-error reference for the classical interval. HC3 gave [\(-0.6429\), 0.8758]. Influence, functional-form, and support checks limit that model’s interpretation. The direction and practically relevant magnitude remain unresolved under these calculations; the result does not establish no conditional relationship.
R3 – Prediction answer. The two fixed OLS learning rules were compared with the shared ten-fold protocol specified here: a fixed pair of rules, balanced folds from seed 80806, identical rows and units, training sets containing every type with full column rank, and pooled case-level errors. The full rule had MAE 1.5412 versus 2.4031 for education-only, difference \(-0.8619\). The examined resplits all favored the full rule. This is internal evidence about learning procedures trained on 88/89 eligible records under the stated same-source exchangeability assumptions. Lower expected error is a provisional conclusion because new-sample uncertainty is not quantified; this is not external validation of a final 98-record equation.
R4 – Synthesis. Education has a positive marginal linear association with income in these historical records. Its conditional association is imprecisely resolved by the specified additive model, while the full learning rule predicts the held-out records more accurately than the education-only rule. These conclusions answer different questions and do not establish that changing education would change income.

The report is an invented teaching reconstruction of these real records, not a statement about the original investigators’ intentions. Its ten-fold comparison uses two fixed learning rules, common balanced folds, seed 80806, complete training types and pooled case errors. The row count and declared protocol are part of the evidence, not incidental software settings.



Table 10: Reading the linked-layer functions without three duplicate maps.










Function
Shared or pair-specific content
Trace in this teaching record




STAT-E
Named 98 rows, variables, exclusions, and computations’ inputs
R0; the supplied 102-to-98 audit and Chapter 8, Section 2.1


SUB-E
Occupations rather than workers; historical dollars, education, ratings, and types
R0; variable/source descriptions


STAT-J
Pair 1: fixed-record least-squares definition. Pair 2: declared stochastic model and uncertainty conditions. Pair 3: held-out fitting, fixed rules, loss, and exchangeability
R1–R3; model and protocol declarations above; Chapter 8, Sections 1–6


SUB-J
Reasons connecting those measurements and comparisons to historical occupational income, with limits on individual, current, and causal interpretations
R0–R3; unit/time explanations and prediction-opportunity definition


STAT-I
Pair 1’s 0.883 slope; Pair 2’s 0.1164 estimate, intervals, coefficient test and checks; Pair 3’s case-level errors, MAEs, and split sensitivity
Supplied results; Chapter 8, Sections 2–6; R1–R3


STAT-C
Descriptive positive marginal slope; unresolved conditional slope under the model; smaller internal error for the full rule under the protocol
R1, R2, and R3 respectively


SUB-I
Interpret years, income units, conditioning, and prediction errors in the named historical occupation setting
The supplied unit definitions and held-out errors; R1–R3


SUB-C
Each question-facing answer with its own limits; none supplies a causal or individual-earnings answer
R1–R3; their distinctions preserved in R4






R2 explicitly offers independence as a model condition, but R0 does not establish a probability selection process. The dollar translation follows from scaling income by 1,000. These distinctions let a reader identify a stated reason without treating its empirical support as established. The same passage may perform several functions; the table avoids reproducing three nearly identical maps.


Evaluate each answer and its synthesis



Table 11: Apply the six questions before evaluating the study-level synthesis.









Quality-evaluation question
Application to these arguments




Question alignment
R1 matches its finite-record slope. R2 names \(\beta_E\), its fitted estimate, the conditioning set, and the model extension. R3 names the learning procedure, loss, and training sizes rather than substituting a coefficient test.


Evidence integrity
The 102-to-98 accounting and common rows are explicit. Missing type still limits what is represented. CV excludes held-out outcomes from fitting; source selection is not repaired by that procedure.


Justification adequacy
Least squares is sufficient for the declared finite description. Pair 2’s model conditions and Pair 3’s same-source exchangeability remain assumptions with incomplete empirical support. Statistical computation alone cannot establish them.


Inferential adequacy
The slope, intervals, error arithmetic, and comparisons are reproducible. Neither zero-crossing nor a large p-value proves absence; repeated folds are not independent replication. Substantive reasoning must retain those distinctions.


Transition fidelity
Occupation-level average income remains occupation-level average income; partial adjustment is not a causal intervention, and model fit is not held-out performance.


Claim calibration
R1 remains finite and historical; R2 reports unresolved magnitude/direction rather than no relationship; R3 remains internal and procedure-specific. No claim extends to individual workers or modern populations.






Each question receives a judgment with a reason: adequate for this purpose, needs revision, insufficient information to judge, or not applicable. The record is adequate, for example, to check Pair 3’s held-out computations, but it gives insufficient information to establish exchangeability with an external population.
Each whole pair then receives its own conclusion:

Pair 1: supported as stated, as an accurate bounded description of the retained records.
Pair 2: supported as stated, as the explicitly conditional, unresolved working-model answer about \(\beta_E\) actually reported. This certifies neither the model nor a population relationship, and a claim that the true national conditional slope is zero would not be supported.
Pair 3: supported as stated, as a qualified internal comparison with its assumptions and limits. External superiority of the final all-record fitted equation is not assessable from the accessible record, and it is not the answer being accepted.

The other whole-pair conclusions are supported only after narrowing or revision, not supported, and not assessable from the accessible record. A correctly reported inconclusive answer can be supported as stated; it is not rejected for failing to answer a stronger question.
Cross-question coherence.
Coordinated questions add one evaluation question, Cross-question coherence: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions, estimands, methods, priority, analysis timing, uncertainty, and limits of the separate answers? Apply it here after reading and evaluating each of the three answers.
R4 is coherent because it reports three distinct outcomes: a positive marginal slope, an unresolved conditional slope, and better internal prediction can hold together without contradiction. Now consider this alternative:

Once the other predictors were controlled, education had no effect; nevertheless, the significant full regression proves it will predict workers’ incomes accurately.

Reading first identifies the inference and claim it offers. Evaluation then finds three failures: “no effect” substitutes a causal null for the conditional-association answer, an omnibus significance test is not held-out validation, and occupations have become workers. The corrected synthesis is R4, not an overarching fourth argument that erases the separate conclusions.
The distinctions matter: a stated model assumption is identifiable Justification even when its empirical support is incomplete; an explicitly unresolved answer can be reported and supported accurately; and lower internal error does not establish external performance. “Not located” describes the accessible record, not proof that investigators did nothing. A wrong reason remains the offered reason and is then judged inadequate; do not silently replace it with a more defensible one.


Transfer a changed model claim
An argument reading can expose a problem without requiring a complete new methods course. The following small changes each alter a specific link between the reported computation and its interpretation.



Table 12: A changed analytical claim should change the relevant reason or qualification.









Supplied report or change
What the reader can already decide




An ordered outcome has three categories. The report says this ordering guarantees the same predictor slope at both cumulative cutpoints.
Ordering defines the thresholds; a common slope is an additional model restriction. Read its checks and the fitted category probabilities before accepting that interpretation.


The same departure from common slopes is easier to detect in a much larger sample.
A smaller p-value can reflect greater precision. Judge the consequences through predicted category probabilities at meaningful predictor values, not through significance alone.


Two clinics have equal visit counts, but one was observed for twice as long.
Equal counts are not equal rates. A rate comparison needs the exposure period and its role in the model.


A prediction model has a lower internal validation error and a significant treatment coefficient.
These are different answers. Neither establishes external-cohort performance, and internal accuracy does not supply causal identification.






The first two rows preserve a useful distinction from ordinal regression: an assumption may matter little for one prediction and greatly for another. An adequate argument names the decision-facing contrast and shows the consequence. Requiring a ritual sentence that “assumptions were checked” would reveal much less about the research reasoning.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
section: Coordinating Construction and Revision Across Questions
text:
Coordinating Construction and Revision Across Questions

Plan shared commitments while preserving each question
Construction is an auxiliary use of the approach, distinct from reading or evaluating a completed report. A single multi-strand question has one six-stage cycle because its estimands and integrated answer are planned together. Several coordinated questions retain separate question-level cycles. Their planning aligns common records, measurement and analysis choices, and their completion adds an explicit study-level synthesis.








Figure 5: Each question retains its six-stage cycle; coordinated questions also require synthesis of their outcomes. The planning-to-production handoff stays one-way within a cycle.







A complete construction history for the occupation study
The records were collected for earlier purposes. The following chronology is an invented teaching reconstruction of how the three analyses could be planned and completed. It is not a claim that the source investigators registered this plan. Each of the three questions retains its own target and bounded answer.



Table 13: Separate question-level cycles share planning and end in an explicit synthesis.









Phase and stage
Commitment in the occupation teaching study




Understand and plan: 1. Review
Review the historical records, their units and measurements, the source-selection information and plausible uses of an occupation-level analysis.


2. Frame
Pose a finite-record descriptive question, a conditional-association question and a prediction question. Name a candidate answer and its scope for each; a causal effect is not one of these targets.


3. Plan and align prospectively across questions
Fix the common 98 rows and income units. Plan a descriptive least-squares slope for the first question, the additive model and its uncertainty/checks for the second, and the two fixed learning rules, loss, shared folds and training sizes for the third. Align shared evidence without giving the three questions identical justifications.


Produce and complete: 4. Produce or acquire and document evidence
Acquire the source records, retain and document the four missing-type exclusions, apply the fixed unit conversion and preserve the source/protocol record. Do not infer a historical probability sample or prospective registration.


5. Estimate, check, and analyse
Fit the declared models; inspect form, influence, spread and support; compare classical and HC3 uncertainty under their conditions; compute predictions without using held-out outcomes in fitting; report sensitivity without relabelling it as a new study.


6. Contextualize, interpret, and complete the bounded answer
Complete each answer, including an unresolved conditional slope and a qualified internal prediction result. A contrary or inconclusive result can complete its question.


7. Give explicit outcomes and synthesize
State the separate outcomes and join them as R4, preserving their units, estimands, uncertainty, analytic history and limits. The synthesis introduces no causal or worker-level claim.






Iteration stays within a phase. Correcting a coding error under the same question and estimand, or repairing an uncertainty calculation on a justified basis, can reopen production work. A newly preferred outcome, question mode or estimand needs a revised or additional cycle, with its timing and reused evidence stated. This respects the one-way planning-to-production handoff within a cycle; it does not prohibit researchers from asking a new question.



Table 14: An invented chronology distinguishes repairs from changed research commitments.










Point in the teaching reconstruction
Decision and reasoning
Consequence for the questions




Before the comparison
Declare common rows and units, three questions, model conditions and validation protocol
The questions share evidence while retaining different targets and assumptions.


During computation
Discover that income was divided by 100 twice in a copied calculation; restore the declared division by 1,000
A same-target error repair: recompute affected estimates, errors and dollar statements, then recheck the synthesis.


During checks
Unequal spread motivates a disclosed HC3 sensitivity alongside the classical interval
The coefficient target stays fixed; the covariance estimator and its justification change. HC3 still needs independent observations and does not repair a wrong mean or selection.


After reading results
Ask whether increasing an individual’s education causes higher earnings
A new question, unit and causal target require a revised or additional cycle and suitable design/evidence. The occupation association cannot be relabelled as that answer.


After internal validation
Want a claim about occupations in another country or period
A new deployment target needs evidence for transport or new validation. A new fold allocation of the original records supplies no external outcomes.








Follow revisions through their dependencies
Correcting a measurement-model coding error retains the question but changes the inputs to its answer. A later SEM using that measurement representation must be refitted and its claim re-evaluated. In contrast, deciding after inspection to compare latent means between programs adds a target with new comparability requirements. It needs a revised or additional planning cycle, not a new label on the original association result.
An explicit decision history makes this distinction visible. A researcher’s final report may be neatly organized even when decisions changed during the work. The reader should locate statements about timing in the protocol, analysis record or disclosed amendments; the final section order is not evidence of prospective planning. “Not located in the accessible record” identifies an information limit. It does not prove that the investigators never considered the issue.
The same principle applies when AI supplies a model, a table or a paragraph. Those products are analytical proposals until their target, data, conditions and interpretation have been checked. An investigator remains responsible for recognizing a changed question, retaining the record of a correction, and revising dependent claims. A polished paragraph that merges incompatible targets can be less trustworthy than a short explicit statement that one answer remains unresolved.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
section: Transferring the Reading to a Published Study
text:
Transferring the Reading to a Published Study

Read the record before borrowing its conclusion
Bloom and colleagues’ Ctrip experiment provides a real published case (Bloom et al., 2015). Eligible volunteers in a Chinese call center were allocated to a nine-month home-working arrangement or office work. Appendix Table A.II records 131 assigned to home working and 118 to the office. The intervention included four home days and one office day per working week. These details define the comparison; they do not automatically describe all remote workers or all possible home-working arrangements.
Two reader-formulated questions will organize this transfer: what happened to performance under the assigned arrangement, and what happened to employee retention? These separately owed answers can inform a shared organizational decision. Retention also affects the later performance record, because an employee who leaves no longer contributes the same subsequent work observations. That connection needs attention when the findings are synthesized.



Table 15: The published argument is distributed across several documentary locations.










Source location
Information to trace
Function in the reading




Article pp. 169–174 and Appendix Table A.II, p. 214
Eligibility, volunteered participation, birth-date allocation, and the 131/118 group counts
Evidence about study entry and assignment; support and limits for an assigned-arrangement comparison


Table II, column 4 and notes, p. 187
Logged weekly calls, employee and week fixed effects, employee-clustered uncertainty and the analysis sample
Statistical specification, computation and output


Interpretation, p. 188
The published approximately 13% performance reading
Translation of the fitted log-scale contrast into a substantive statement


Figure IX and Section V.B
Leaving employment and its relationship with performance
A separate outcome and a qualification for the evolving performance record


Author replication files, Tables2014.do, Table 2 block
Selection conditions and fitting commands for each displayed column
A reproducible trace of the implemented analysis, distinct from its rationale






The article and author’s research page provide the source and replication links. The following calculations were reproduced from the author-linked data, rather than inferred from the abstract. The original records remain at their source; the displayed summaries suffice for the reading task.


Preserve the analysis denominator and uncertainty
Table II, column 4 concerns 134 order takers with the required call measures, not all 249 randomized employees. Its 9,426 observations are person-weeks across 85 distinct weeks. The analysis excludes the transition week and applies the authors’ outcome-availability and call-count conditions. Employee fixed effects represent stable employee differences, week effects represent common week differences, and the uncertainty is clustered by employee to accommodate within-employee dependence.
The reproduced assignment-by-experiment-period coefficient is 0.1198, with clustered SE 0.025. It matches the paper’s displayed 0.120 (0.025), whose published precision is retained here. Exponentiating the unrounded coefficient gives a 12.7304% relative contrast on the fitted logged scale, consistent with the paper’s rounded approximately 13%. A log-scale coefficient does not by itself establish the same ratio for arithmetic mean calls; that translation also depends on the residual distribution and the target being reported.
The raw retention record has 21 of 131 home-assigned employees leaving, compared with 41 of 118 office-assigned employees: proportions 0.1603 and 0.3475. This is a directly reproduced raw comparison from quit_data.dta; the article’s Section V.B summarizes attrition as 17% and 35%. The file-based home proportion is not an exact reconstruction of that published summary, so the two are kept distinct. It is distinct from the paper’s adjusted probit analyses and supplies no independent estimate of a particular psychological mechanism.
A statistical trace identifies the selected rows, variables, fixed effects, coefficient and cluster calculation. A substantive trace identifies the employees, the home-working arrangement, what call performance represents and the scope of retention. The reason supplied by randomized assignment is different from the implementation of the regression. Treating the fixed effects themselves as proof of randomization would confuse the model with the design.


A short exploratory moderation extension
Now ask a new question: does the log-call assignment contrast differ between the two categories of the replication file’s recorded men indicator, coded 0 for women and 1 for men? This is a teaching reanalysis of the same source data, selected here after the main results. It is exploratory and is not a result being attributed to the original authors. The same selected rows, employee and week effects, and employee-clustered covariance are retained; an assignment-by-experiment-period-by-indicator term allows the contrast to vary. The model also includes the experiment-period-by-indicator term, allowing the groups to have different background changes across the experimental period. The remaining lower-order terms are absorbed by the employee and week effects.



Table 16: A new exploratory question uses the original records but has its own answer.











Recorded group
Fitted log-call assignment contrast
SE
Pointwise 95% interval




Women (0)
0.1414
0.0358
[0.0706, 0.2122]


Men (1)
0.0994
0.0342
[0.0316, 0.1671]






Both subgroup intervals exclude zero, yet the estimated difference between contrasts is \(-0.042\) with SE 0.0495. A \(t\) comparison on 133 cluster degrees of freedom leaves its direction unresolved. The subgroup intervals are pointwise, not a simultaneous claim over an unrestricted set of possible probes. The correct comparison uses the covariance of the two estimated contrasts; comparing their separate p-values does not test their difference.
This is effect-pattern description conditional on the design and observation process, not a causal effect of gender or an explanation of why a difference would occur. A mechanism claim would need additional evidence and identification. A resampling sensitivity, if undertaken, would preserve the assignment and dependence units by resampling employees rather than individual weeks. Bootstrapping alone would not supply causal or measurement support.


Evaluate a coherent synthesis
A coherent synthesis can say that the source supports improved call performance under the experimental home-working arrangement for its stated analysis and lower observed departure in the randomized sample, while the teaching reanalysis leaves the contrast difference between recorded groups unresolved. It retains the different denominators, outcomes and analysis histories. It does not turn a later choice to work at home into the original randomized comparison.
The trial’s voluntary eligibility conditions constrain transport to other employees. Outcome availability and attrition constrain interpretation of later performance records. These are places to examine the article’s sensitivity and selection discussion, not automatic reasons to discard every result. They also illustrate why a procedure can reproduce exactly while a stronger causal or generalization claim still needs additional support.
Predict and explain. If the employee count stayed fixed but each person contributed twice as many weeks, a calculation treating all weeks as independent would exaggerate the added independent information. More repeated observations can improve precision, but the change depends on within-person dependence. The research explanation must identify the repeated unit, not just quote the larger row count.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
text:
Summary and Reading Bridge
One integrated question can require several estimand-specific statistical strands. Several separately owed answers retain separate arguments, even when one fitted model serves them all. A dependency transfers particular support and its qualifications; it is neither a causal arrow nor a command to perform a ritual sequence of significant tests.
The feedback example shows why a favorable performance result cannot settle an unresolved burden requirement. The measurement example shows why one supported interpretation can inform a later association while leaving a different mean-comparison claim unresolved. The occupation example shows how a positive marginal slope, an unresolved conditional slope and better internal prediction can coexist. The published experiment shows how allocation, repeated outcomes, selected analysis samples and exploratory extensions must retain their own documentary traces.
Reading is the primary task: identify the question, answer and support. Evaluation asks whether that support warrants the answer. Construction uses the same distinctions to plan commitments, document changes and revise dependent claims. Organizing the argument and following reporting across the report are auxiliary reading tasks, not additional components. The framework draws on argument, statistical-reasoning and validation traditions (Kane, 2013; LeMire, 2010; Toulmin, 2003), while the quantitative methods supply the technical detail needed in each setting.
The selected models here are explained sufficiently for the reading. Regression, generalized linear models, prediction and causal design develop their calculations and conditions in the relevant method chapters. Factor and structural models have their full treatment in Part Two. Argument Chapter C will develop the additional measurement layer; understanding this chapter’s supplied results does not require completing that future unit.

Key terms



Table 17: Selected terms introduced in Argument Chapter B.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Argument-based reading
Statistical strand
An estimand-specific statistical chain inside one argument. Two strands arise only when sibling estimands are jointly required for one integrated substantive answer; each has its own statistical inference and conclusion.
Arg. B, Sec. 1


Argument-based reading
Coordinated questions
Several question-answer pairs in one study whose support depends on one another. Each answer is read on its own, and their coherence across questions is judged separately.
Arg. B, Sec. 3






Evidence, justification, inference and bounded claim retain their shared meanings. The Part One Concept Reference gathers these terms; Argument Chapter A develops the documentary reading of individual components and evaluation questions.

title: Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
text:
Exercises


Exercise 1: Questions and strands (Foundational)
Three reports use the same classroom data. Report A promises one answer about worthwhile learning without unacceptable time burden. Report B promises separate answers about learning and burden. Report C promises a measurement answer and a later-achievement answer that uses that measurement representation. (1) Identify the arrangement in each report and explain why the number of fitted models does not settle it. (2) Report A adds a second estimator for its same learning target. Does this necessarily create another strand? (3) Name one piece of allocation information that A’s two strands share, and one measurement issue they do not share.



Exercise 2: Read the integrated answer (Foundational)
An invented feedback study assigns twelve of 24 classes to each format, with 20 students per class and repeated scores. Its later-performance contrast is 3.7886 points, with one-sided 95% lower bound 2.6285. Its weekly study-time contrast is 20.2128 minutes, with one-sided 95% upper bound 30.9011. The declared success rule requires gain greater than 2 points and extra time below 30 minutes. (1) Read each strand and give the integrated answer. (2) Explain why a test of time difference against zero would answer the wrong burden question. (3) In a separate invented language record, two learners score 58, 65, 68, 76 and 62, 63, 67, 68 at four equally spaced occasions. Explain why an average gain per interval of 6 or 2 is neither a constant observed slope nor the assignment effect at the last occasion.



Exercise 3: Follow measurement support (Integrative)
A two-factor CFA uses six continuous indicators, three per factor. It fixes one loading per factor to 1 and gives chi-square 8.4265 on 8 degrees of freedom, p = .393. A jointly estimated later-score SEM gives a confidence coefficient 3.1068 with interval [2.0971, 4.1166], holding belonging fixed. The report has not examined item-intercept comparability between programs. (1) Separate the implemented scale constraint, its identification reason, and a test of an eligible equality restriction. (2) State what the measurement answer contributes to the later-score answer and what additional support the latter needs. (3) Explain why these results do not establish that one program has higher latent confidence or that increasing confidence causes achievement to improve.



Exercise 4: Evaluate coordinated answers (Integrative)
On 98 historical occupation records, a report gives a positive marginal education slope 0.883, a conditional slope 0.1164 with interval [-0.4302, 0.6631], and ten-fold mean absolute errors 1.5412 for a full additive rule and 2.4031 for an education-only rule. A summary says, “Education has no effect, but the significant full regression proves accurate prediction of individual workers in a future country.” (1) Identify three changes of target or support in that summary. (2) Write a coherent replacement that retains the unresolved answer. (3) Explain when the six question-level evaluations suffice and when Cross-question coherence is added. (4) A separate supplied student-prediction rule has lower held-out error in its source records, but no later-cohort outcomes are available. What evidence is still needed for a future-cohort performance claim?



Exercise 5: Predict and explain a revision (Integrative)
An occupation-study plan declares income in thousand dollars, a conditional-association question, and two fixed prediction rules. During computation an analyst finds that a copied calculation divided income by 100 twice instead of by 1,000. Later the team asks whether increasing an individual worker’s education causes higher pay. (1) Predict which numerical outputs need rechecking after the scale repair and explain why this is not automatically a new question. (2) Explain why the later causal question needs a revised or additional construction cycle. (3) In a separate SEM, a corrected measurement-model coding error changes a confidence loading. Identify a later answer that must be revisited and one reason its numerical conclusion might nevertheless survive.



Exercise 6: Read the published-study trace (Integrative)
Bloom and colleagues’ working-from-home experiment allocated 131 eligible volunteers to home work and 118 to the office. Table II, column 4 (p. 187), analyzes logged weekly calls from 134 order takers, using 9,426 person-weeks, employee and week fixed effects, and employee-clustered uncertainty. It reports coefficient 0.120 and SE 0.025. A separate teaching reanalysis adds a recorded-group interaction; its two log-call contrasts are 0.1414 and 0.0994, with a direct difference -0.042 and SE 0.0495. (1) Explain the different roles of 249, 134 and 9,426. (2) Identify where to locate the implemented sample restriction and where to locate the published interpretation. (3) Explain why positive separate subgroup contrasts do not establish moderation. (4) Distinguish reading a stated causal reason from evaluating whether it also justifies generalization to all remote workers. The supplied study details are paraphrased from the article and the authors’ replication record; the interaction analysis is exploratory teaching work, not their reported finding.

title: Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty
text:
NoteChapter overview



Chapter 8 wrote one regression model for the occupation records. This chapter extends it in two directions: Sections 1–4 change or compare the mean part; Sections 5–7 recompute uncertainty when spread differs or pupils share a school. By the end, you will be able to read indicator coefficients and a declared contrast, explain covariance adjustment, compare models and predictors, interpret curvature and a logged outcome, and choose an uncertainty calculation for a stated reason. The occupation records, a randomized reading study, and Project STAR connect each method with the question it answers and the conditions it needs.
Chapter 8 asked how income differs with education when prestige, the percentage of women, and occupational type are held fixed. A report on the same 98 records usually needs more. How do the three types compare? Does a group of predictors add anything once the others are in? Is a straight line in prestige adequate, and should income be analyzed on its own scale? How far can the standard errors be trusted when professional incomes spread much more widely? We answer these questions on the same records, with income in thousand 1971 Canadian dollars and the type levels bc, prof, and wc. Two further studies join where these records cannot serve: a randomized reading study with a pretest (Section 2) and Project STAR (Section 7).
Recall Chapter 8’s model, with the conditions Chapter 7, Section 1.1, first stated for one predictor:
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_jx_{ij}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad
E(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=\sigma^2.
\]
Its mean part gives the expected outcome at stated predictor values. Its error part says that errors average zero at every predictor profile, share one variance, and are independent across records; Normal errors additionally supply the exact \(t\) and \(F\) references. For the occupation model m2, with blue-collar as reference, the mean part is
\[
E(\mathrm{income}_k\mid e,p,w,\mathrm{type})=\beta_0+\beta_Ee+\beta_Pp
+\beta_Ww+\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}
+\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\]
Here \(e\), \(p\), and \(w\) are education, prestige, and the percentage of women; the two \(D\) columns indicate professional and white-collar types.
We work on these two parts in turn: indicators, covariance adjustment, model comparisons and transformations first; unequal spread and school-level dependence second. Short R demonstrations connect the model to its fitted comparisons and uncertainty.

title: Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty
text:
Predictors That Are Categories

One indicator, then several
Chapter 7, Section 3.3, fitted a single 0/1 predictor to 24 invented feedback-by-practice scores. The fitted line passed through the two group means, its slope was their difference, 4 with SE 1.6967 and \(t=2.3575\) on 22 df, and that test was the equal-variance two-sample test written as a regression. The same idea extends to more than two groups.
A factor with \(J\) levels enters a regression as \(J-1\) indicator columns. One level is omitted and becomes the reference: the intercept is its fitted mean, and each indicator coefficient is a difference from it. With three occupation types and blue-collar as the reference,
\[
\widehat y_g=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}
+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}},\qquad
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{bc}}=\widehat\beta_0,\quad
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{prof}}=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}},\quad
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{wc}}=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\]
Two indicators, not three, carry three means. A third column would equal the intercept column minus the other two, so the design matrix would lose full rank and no coefficient would be separately estimable. Which level is omitted is a choice of coordinates, not a choice of model.
The working data d retain the 98 occupations in carData::Prestige with a recorded type. Income divided by 1,000 gives income_k in thousand 1971 Canadian dollars, and the factor order is blue-collar, professional, then white-collar, so blue-collar is the reference. On these same rows, m0, m1, and m2 name the education-only, the education-and-prestige, and the full additive models:

m0 <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = d)
m1 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige, data = d)
m2 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type, data = d)

The 98 records hold 44 blue-collar, 31 professional, and 23 white-collar occupations, and the full model fits six coefficients, leaving 92 residual degrees of freedom. The rows were chosen because their records are complete, not sampled at random from a labour market (Fox et al., 2022; Fox & Weisberg, 2019).


What the indicator coefficients mean
Fit income on type alone and read the coefficients against Figure 1. A blue-collar occupation carries 0 in both indicator columns, a professional one a 1 in the first, and a white-collar one a 1 in the second, so each type’s fitted value is the intercept plus that type’s coefficient.

group_fit <- lm(income_k ~ type, data = d)
coef(group_fit)

(Intercept)    typeprof      typewc 
   5.374136    5.185315   -0.321832 










Figure 1: Income of the 98 occupations by type. Bars mark the group means; the dashed line is the blue-collar mean, the intercept, and the arrows are the two indicator coefficients, 5.1853 and −0.3218.





The coefficients are 5.3741, 5.1853, and \(-0.3218\). The intercept is the blue-collar mean, the dashed line in the figure, and each coefficient is an arrow from that line to another type’s mean: professional occupations average 5.1853 thousand dollars more, white-collar occupations 0.3218 less. The fitted means, 5.3741, 10.5595, and 5.0523, are exactly the observed means, for the reason Chapter 8, Appendix A, gave: with one free parameter per group, least squares returns each group’s own mean. A group-only regression is therefore a description of three means, with no adjustment in it. The figure also shows the wide spread of professional incomes, from about 4.6 to 25.9 thousand dollars, which Section 5 takes up.
Keep this description apart from the full model. In m2 the professional and white-collar coefficients are 0.3242 and 0.2353: they compare fitted incomes at the same education, prestige, and percentage of women. The raw professional advantage of 5.1853 and the adjusted 0.3242 answer different questions, and neither is “the effect of occupational type”.


Changing the reference level
Releveling makes a different level the reference. Refit the group-only model with white-collar as the reference:

group_fit_wc <- lm(income_k ~ relevel(type, ref = "wc"), data = d)
coef(group_fit_wc)

                  (Intercept)   relevel(type, ref = "wc")bc 
                     5.052304                      0.321832 
relevel(type, ref = "wc")prof 
                     5.507147 


The coefficients are now 5.0523, 0.3218, and 5.5071: the intercept is the white-collar mean, and the two coefficients measure the blue-collar and professional means from it. The fitted values and residuals are unchanged (Chapter 8, Appendix A); the same three means are reported in new coordinates. Releveling m2 in the same way gives intercept 0.6559, blue-collar \(-0.2353\), and professional 0.0889, while the education, prestige, and women coefficients stay exactly as they were.
Centering a continuous predictor (Chapter 7, Section 2.5, and Chapter 8, Appendix A), subtracting a constant such as its mean, is the same kind of change: it moves the profile the intercept describes and leaves every fitted value, residual, and substantive contrast alone. Neither operation adds information, such as the cross-type support the records lack, and “the professional coefficient” always means professional minus whichever level is currently the reference.


One-way analysis of variance as a regression
Chapter 4, Sections 2.2–2.4, compared one common mean with separate group means through between-group and within-group variation. In the group-only regression, equal means says that both indicator coefficients are zero. The between-group sum of squares is \(SS_B=595.9562\) on \(J-1=2\) degrees of freedom. The within-group sum of squares is the group-only model’s residual sum of squares, \(SS_W=1138.123\) on \(N-J=95\) degrees of freedom. The familiar calculation is
\[
F=\frac{MS_B}{MS_W}=\frac{SS_B/(J-1)}{SS_W/(N-J)}
=\frac{595.9562/2}{1138.123/95}=24.8725,\qquad
\eta^2=\frac{SS_B}{SS_T}=.3437.
\]
The regression and ANOVA describe the same fitted means, so eta squared is also the group-only regression’s \(R^2\). Chapter 6, Sections 1.3 and 3.2, fitted and compared these kinds of models in R. Here the reduced model has only an intercept and the fuller one has two indicators; Section 3.1 generalizes their comparison.

anova(lm(income_k ~ 1, data = d), group_fit)





Res.Df
RSS
Df

F
Pr(>F)

aov() returns the same statistic from the same fitted means, residual sum of squares, and degrees of freedom. The equality is algebraic: it holds whether or not group membership was randomized, so it supplies no causal warrant of its own. As in Chapter 4, the omnibus \(F\) says that the three means are not all equal but not which differ, and a comparison chosen after seeing it needs Chapter 4’s family calibration. A declared comparison needs no significant omnibus result first; the next subsection gives its calculation.


A contrast and its standard error
A linear contrast writes a comparison as a linear combination of coefficients, \(C=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\). For a comparison declared before the results are read, the estimate is that same combination of the fitted coefficients, and its variance uses the whole coefficient covariance matrix \(\widehat{\mathbf V}\):
\[
\widehat C=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat C)=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c,\qquad
SE(\widehat C)=\sqrt{\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c}.
\]
For a difference of two coefficients, the variance is the sum of their two variances minus twice their covariance. The group-only comparison makes the covariance visible. Professional minus white-collar is \(\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}-\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}=5.5071\), with \(\mathbf c=(0,1,-1)^{\mathsf T}\):

c_vec <- c(0, 1, -1)
V <- vcov(group_fit)
c(estimate = sum(c_vec * coef(group_fit)),
  SE = sqrt(drop(c_vec %*% V %*% c_vec)))

 estimate        SE 
5.5071473 0.9525437 


Both coefficients measure a group mean from the same blue-collar mean. If a sample overstates that reference mean, both coefficients fall together. Their covariance, 0.2723, is the variance of the shared mean, \(MS_W/44\). It drops out when the two coefficients are subtracted:
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat C)
=0.6587+0.7932-2(0.2723)=0.9073
=MS_W\left(\frac1{31}+\frac1{23}\right).
\]
Thus the SE is 0.9525 and, with \(t_{.975,95}=1.9853\), the pointwise 95% interval is \([3.6161,\ 7.3982]\). Omitting the covariance gives an SE of 1.2049; adding the two SEs gives 1.7022, which is not the SE of this contrast. The covariance is part of the comparison, not a correction added after it.
The same formula applies to m2 with \(\mathbf c=(0,0,0,0,1,-1)^{\mathsf T}\): the estimate is 0.0889, its SE 1.08, and its pointwise 95% interval \([-2.0561,\ 2.2338]\) (\(t_{.975,92}=1.9861\)). Sections 1.2–1.3 explain why the raw 5.5071 becomes 0.0889 when education, prestige, and the percentage of women are held fixed. This interval covers zero and leaves the adjusted comparison unresolved; it is a working-model calculation among types with thin joint support (Chapter 8). Exercise 2 practices its covariance-based variance.
The vector \(\mathbf c\) states the question. One entry set to 1 returns an ordinary coefficient; weights on type coefficients with intercept weight zero express contrasts between group means in Chapter 4’s sense. The vector changes with the reference coding, but a named comparison does not: the releveled m2 in Section 1.3 gave 0.0889 directly. Declaring a comparison before reading its result governs the calibration, not whether it is a contrast. A comparison selected after inspecting the output needs the family calibration of Chapter 4, Section 3.3, whose R calculations appear in Chapter 6, Section 2.

title: Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty
section: Adjusted Group Comparisons: The Analysis of Covariance
text:
Adjusted Group Comparisons: The Analysis of Covariance

A regression with one common slope
The occupation types differ in many ways at once. A randomized study with a baseline score lets the group question be asked more sharply. Baumann and colleagues randomly assigned 68 fourth-grade pupils in one school to three reading-instruction conditions (Baumann et al., 1992): DRA, a directed reading activity from the basal program; DRTA, a directed reading-thinking activity; and think-aloud strategy instruction. Each pupil took an error-detection test of comprehension monitoring before and after the lessons. carData::Baumann holds the 66 pupils with a recorded first posttest, 22 per group. We use the first pretest and posttest, with DRA as the reference; the investigators also analyzed further outcomes and both pretests.
The analysis of covariance adds the pretest to the group comparison as one more predictor with a single slope:
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\beta(X_{ij}-\bar X)+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad
\bar Y_j^{\,\mathrm{adj}}=\bar Y_j-\widehat\beta(\bar X_j-\bar X).
\]
Here \(Y_{ij}\) and \(X_{ij}\) are the posttest and pretest of pupil \(i\) in group \(j\). The group terms \(\mu_j\) shift the line up or down, and the pretest enters once, so every group’s line has the same slope \(\beta\). An adjusted mean is a group’s fitted mean at a stated pretest value. At the grand pretest mean \(\bar X\) it is the observed posttest mean \(\bar Y_j\) moved along the common slope by the group’s pretest departure from \(\bar X\), the second equation.
The working data reading hold these 66 pupils, all with recorded first pretests and posttests. The package’s group codes Basal, DRTA and Strat are labeled DRA, DRTA and Think-aloud, with DRA as the reference. The prediction below evaluates each group’s line at the grand pretest mean.

ancova <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group + pretest.1, data = reading)
coef(ancova)

     (Intercept)        groupDRTA groupThink-aloud        pretest.1 
      -0.5966478        3.6265538        2.0361644        0.6931872 

grand <- data.frame(group = levels(reading$group),
  pretest.1 = mean(reading$pretest.1))
predict(ancova, newdata = grand, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr       upr
1 6.188185 5.143481  7.232889
2 9.814739 8.779995 10.849482
3 8.224349 7.181274  9.267425










Figure 2: Posttest against pretest for the 66 Baumann pupils. The parallel lines are the common-slope fit over the common pretest support 6–14; each filled symbol marks a group’s observed pretest and posttest means, and its arrow follows the group’s line to the grand pretest mean 9.7879, where the open symbol marks the adjusted mean.





Read Figure 2 from each filled symbol, a group’s observed pretest and posttest means, to the open symbol on the vertical line, its adjusted mean. DRA happened to start highest, 0.7121 points above the grand pretest mean of 9.7879, so following its line to the grand mean lowers its posttest mean by \(0.6932\times0.7121\), from 6.6818 to 6.1882. Think-aloud started 0.6515 points below and rises from 7.7727 to 8.2243, while DRTA, almost at the grand mean, barely moves, from 9.7727 to 9.8147. The fit gives the common slope 0.6932 (SE 0.1015), differences from DRA of 3.6266 (SE 0.7362) for DRTA and 2.0362 (SE 0.7450) for Think-aloud, and a residual mean square of 5.894 on 62 degrees of freedom. Tested together after the pretest, the two group coefficients give \(F(2,62)=12.1689\), \(p<.0001\), a comparison of named models as in Chapter 6, Section 3.2, whose statistic Section 3.1 below develops. The adjusted means have 95% intervals \([5.1435,\ 7.2329]\), \([8.7800,\ 10.8495]\), and \([7.1813,\ 9.2674]\).
Three conditions carry that reading. The adjusted means need a common reference, here the grand pretest mean. The reference must lie inside every group’s observed pretest range, the common support: the pretests run from 4 to 16, 6 to 16, and 4 to 14, so the lines are drawn over 6 to 14, and a comparison read outside that band would rest on extrapolation. And the comparison needs a stated averaging population: for this additive model, predicting every group at the grand pretest mean gives the same values as predicting every group at each of the 66 pupils’ pretests and averaging. Because the lines are parallel, the adjusted differences, 3.6266 and 2.0362, are the same at any pretest value inside the common support; the adjusted means are not, which is why the reference value is stated.


Three analyses of a pretest–posttest study
A randomized pretest–posttest study is often analyzed in one of three ways: compare the posttest means, compare the gains (posttest minus pretest), or adjust for the pretest as above. The three are one regression that differs only in the pretest coefficient \(\gamma\):
\[
Y_i-\gamma X_i=\beta_0+\delta_{\mathrm{DRTA}}D_{\mathrm{DRTA},i}
+\delta_{\mathrm{TA}}D_{\mathrm{TA},i}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad
\gamma=0,\ 1,\ \text{or estimated}.
\]
With \(\gamma=0\) the model compares posttest means, with \(\gamma=1\) it compares gains, and with \(\gamma\) estimated it is the analysis of covariance. In R, offset() enters the pretest with its coefficient fixed at 1:

post_only <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group, data = reading)
gain <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group + offset(pretest.1), data = reading)

Under random assignment the expected pretest difference between groups is zero. Subtracting a fixed multiple of the pretest therefore preserves the average group-comparison target. Under the common-slope working model, covariance adjustment estimates that same comparison while estimating the pretest slope from the records. Random assignment covered the 68 pupils assigned, while the analyses use the 66 with a recorded first posttest, so the argument also needs a complete-record condition, for example that the two posttests went missing for reasons unrelated to what those pupils would have scored, which the design does not guarantee and the records cannot check.

The three analyses differ in precision and in how this sample’s chance pretest imbalance enters. The pretest means are 10.5000, 9.7273, and 9.1364, so DRA had a head start of 0.7727 points over DRTA, about a quarter of the pretest SD of 3.0205 across all 66 pupils. The size of that gap is what matters. A significance test of it would add nothing: random assignment already makes any baseline gap a chance gap, so the test would examine a null hypothesis known to be true. The gap accounts exactly for the spread of the estimates in Table 1: each DRTA estimate is the posttest-only difference plus \(\gamma\) times DRA’s head start, \(3.0909+\gamma(10.5-9.7273)\), which gives 3.0909, 3.8636, and 3.6266 (3.6265 from the rounded inputs).
Estimating the coefficient leaves the smallest residual SD, 2.4278 against 3.1885 and 2.5799, and the smallest standard errors, because the pretest predicts the posttest with a slope near 0.7 rather than 0 or 1. The choice belongs in the analysis plan, made before the outcomes are seen, not after comparing the three estimates.


Parallel slopes and the limits of adjustment
A common slope is a condition, not a finding. The check adds the group-by-pretest product block, which lets each group have its own slope, and compares the two named models on the same records (Chapter 6, Section 3.2; Section 3.1 below develops the general statistic):

varying_slopes <- lm(post.test.1 ~ group * pretest.1, data = reading)
anova(ancova, varying_slopes)

The product block gives \(F(2,60)=1.5054\), \(p=.2302\), with group slopes of 0.4663 (DRA), 0.6868 (DRTA), and 0.8768 (Think-aloud). These 66 records do not distinguish the two models, which is not the same as showing that the slopes are equal. When slopes do differ, an adjusted difference depends on the pretest value at which it is read; Chapter 10 develops that varying-slope model as an interaction.
What adjustment supplies depends on how the groups were formed. In groups formed by random assignment, the pretest only sharpens a comparison that the design already warrants. In observational groups, a fitted comparison at a common covariate value cannot balance what was not measured. In Section 1.2 the professional advantage fell from 5.1853 to 0.3242 at fixed education, prestige, and percentage of women, but neither number was an effect of type. A covariate measured with error can leave part of the baseline difference unadjusted (Chapter 14, Section 5.1); and a covariate recorded after the groups formed can remove part of the effect being estimated.
Lord’s paradox makes the point with intact groups that differ at baseline (Lord, 1967). The gain-score analysis asks whether the groups changed by different amounts; the covariance analysis asks whether pupils with the same pretest ended differently. The two can reach opposite conclusions from the same records, partly through the regression toward the mean of Chapter 7, Section 7.2: groups that start apart each regress toward their own mean. Neither analysis says which question is the causal one; the design does, and Chapter 14 returns to what a design supplies that adjustment cannot.

title: Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty
text:
Comparing Models and Predictors

Comparing residual sums of squares
Chapter 4 compared one common mean with group means (Sections 2.2–2.3) and additive with interaction models (Section 4.4); Chapter 6 fitted those comparisons in R (Sections 1.3 and 3.2). This section develops the general question on the occupation records: what does each mean part permit, and what restrictions distinguish them? Two models are nested when the reduced model is the fuller model with some coefficients set to zero, and both are fitted to the same records and outcome. Extra coefficients never raise the residual sum of squares; the question is whether they lower it by more than noise alone would. The extra-sum-of-squares statistic compares the two residual sums of squares:
\[
F=\frac{(RSS_{R}-RSS_{F})/q}{RSS_{F}/(n-p)}.
\]
The numerator is the drop that the \(q\) extra coefficients buy, per coefficient. The denominator is the fuller model’s residual mean square, with \(p\) its number of coefficients: the same \(s^2\) that appears in every classical standard error. When the reduced-model restrictions hold, under the Normal linear model with independent common-variance errors, the ratio has an exact central \(F\) reference with \(q\) and \(n-p\) degrees of freedom.








Figure 3: Residual sum of squares as columns are added to the occupation model on the same 98 records; each label gives the drop that the added column or block buys.





Figure 3 shows what each addition buys in the occupation models. Education buys 571.5324 of the total 1734.0792, and prestige a further 294.8931. The percentage of women then buys 236.3266 for one coefficient, while the two type columns buy only 0.4375 for two. Against the full model’s residual mean square of 6.8575, the type block’s 0.4375 over two coefficients gives \(F(2,92)=0.0319\). Section 3.2 sets this beside the women-and-type comparison in Table 2. The subtraction means something only when both models use the same rows and the same outcome, which is why every comparison in this chapter runs on the same 98 records.
The overall regression test is the special case whose reduced model is the intercept alone, with all \(p-1\) non-intercept coefficients set to zero. Chapter 8, Section 3.3, gave its formula and read it from summary(m2)$fstatistic: \(F(5,92)=32.1747\) for the full model and \(F(1,96)=47.1956\) for the education-only model on the same records. The larger value is not evidence that m0 is better, because the two statistics test different restrictions. Neither checks the mean function, and neither says how a fitted rule would predict new records (Chapter 13). The same statistic can also test any \(q\) linear restrictions on one fitted model without fitting the reduced model; Appendix A develops that form.


Testing a block of coefficients
A block test applies the preceding statistic to a declared set of coefficients jointly. Two blocks ask different questions on these same 98 records: do women and type add to education and prestige, and does type add once women is already present?

no_type <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women, data = d)
anova(m1, m2)
anova(no_type, m2)

Adding the percentage of women and the two type indicators to m1 tests three restrictions against the full model’s 92 residual degrees of freedom; dropping type from the full model tests two restrictions against the same denominator.



Table 2: Two declared adjusted block comparisons.

The first block is strongly supported: \(F(3,92)=11.5088\) against a 5% critical value of 2.7036. The second is not: \(F(2,92)=0.0319\), \(p=.9686\), against 3.0954. Joint evidence for the first block does not show that each added column contributes; the percentage of women could carry the whole block. The second result does not show that occupational type is irrelevant: once education, prestige, and the percentage of women are in the equation, the two type indicators reduce the residual sum of squares by almost nothing on these 98 records, where the types barely overlap on the other predictors.
A single anova(m2) answers a different question. It gives sequential sums of squares: each line tests a term given only the terms above it in the formula, so the answers depend on the order of the formula, and only the last line matches a block test. Section 5.2 gives the robust version of the type block.


Information criteria: AIC and BIC
A nested \(F\) test compares two models when one contains the other. Information criteria can also rank models that are not nested, using a different quantity: the maximized likelihood, penalized for the number of fitted parameters.
Chapter 8, Appendix B, built that likelihood for these models from independent Normal outcomes around the regression. Maximizing it over the coefficients reproduces least squares. Its scale estimate divides the residual sum of squares by \(n\), \(\sqrt{RSS/n}=2.5373\), where the residual SD reported by lm() divides by the residual degrees of freedom, \(\sqrt{RSS/(n-p)}=2.6187\). AIC adds \(2k\) to \(-2\log\widehat L\) and BIC adds \(k\log n\), where \(k\) counts the fitted coefficients and the residual variance, so m2 has \(k=7\), not 6. One call returns all three quantities:

c(logLik = logLik(m2), AIC = AIC(m2), BIC = BIC(m2))

   logLik       AIC       BIC 
-230.3020  474.6040  492.6988 


For m2 the call returns \(-230.3020\), 474.6040, and 492.6988. Chapter 8, Appendix B, tabulates m0, m1, and m2. The new use here compares candidates that are not nested: income on education and the percentage of women (AIC 486.3288, BIC 496.6687), and income on prestige and the percentage of women (AIC 469.3428, BIC 479.6827). Neither model contains the other, so no nested \(F\) compares them. Both have \(k=4\); the penalties cancel, and the criteria prefer prestige with women because it fits these records better.
Set m2 beside that pair: its AIC 474.6040 and BIC 492.6988 are both higher than the prestige-and-women model’s. Its three further coefficients, education and the two type indicators, do not buy enough fit to pay their penalty. Section 3.2’s type block and Section 3.4’s education comparison show why. Adjusted \(R^2\) gives the same order: .5549, .6257, and .6164 for education with women, prestige with women, and m2. A ranking is always relative to the candidates offered.
The two criteria charge differently for parameters. For the seven parameters of m2, BIC charges \(7\log 98=32.0948\) instead of AIC’s 14, because at \(n=98\) the factor \(\log n=4.585\) exceeds 2, so the criteria can disagree; a disagreement shows how strongly the extra parameters are charged, not a tie to break by preference. The criteria are comparable only among models fitted to the same records, with the same outcome on the same scale, under one likelihood convention; Section 4.2 shows a change of scale breaking the comparison. Both are calculated on the records that fitted the models, so neither is a held-out error, and both are comparative: a smaller AIC says one candidate is preferred to another, not that either describes the records well (Akaike, 1974; Schwarz, 1978). Chapter 11 develops likelihood fully.


What each predictor adds
Raw slopes use different units. The education slope, 0.1164 thousand dollars per year, looks similar to the prestige slope, 0.1406 per rating point, but a year and a point are different changes. Their predictor SDs are 2.7489 years and 17.0949 points; the percentage of women’s SD is 31.382 percentage points and income’s is 4.2281 thousand dollars. Two summaries answer different questions:
\[
\beta_j^{*}=\widehat\beta_j\frac{s_{x_j}}{s_y},\qquad
\Delta R^2_j=R^2_{\mathrm{full}}-R^2_{\mathrm{without}\ j}.
\]
A standardized coefficient, or beta weight, rescales a partial slope into outcome-SD units per predictor SD. The values are 0.0757 for education, 0.5685 for prestige, and \(-0.3971\) for women. This differs from Chapter 8’s standardization over named profiles: that operation averages fitted outcomes over a stated population, while these beta weights change the units of slopes. Their values depend on the spread of the predictors in these particular records.
A drop-one \(R^2\) asks how much of the full model’s explained variation disappears when one predictor is removed. From the full \(R^2=.6362\), the drops are .0007 for education, .0625 for prestige, and .1212 for women. Each is Section 3.2’s one-column block comparison on a different scale: the corresponding \(F(1,92)\) values are 0.1790, 15.8070, and 30.6593, each the square of its coefficient’s \(t\). Education’s near-zero drop describes the same limited unique contribution as its wide coefficient interval.
Neither summary measures importance. Restricted predictor ranges can shrink standardized coefficients. Overlapping predictor information means that the drop-one values need not sum to the joint \(R^2\); a predictor that duplicates another can contribute almost nothing uniquely while still being substantively relevant. Neither summary establishes a causal ranking or held-out value. Name the comparison before reading the number.

section: Changing a Predictor’s Form or the Outcome’s Scale
text:
Changing a Predictor’s Form or the Outcome’s Scale

Adding a squared term
In every model so far, a continuous predictor’s slope was the same at every value of that predictor. Chapter 8, Section 4.3, refitted the full model with a squared prestige term, and that refit is the worked example here. It was a check on functional form declared before it was run, not a search across candidate terms for the smallest p-value; a p-value read after such a search would not mean what it appears to mean. A squared term is one kind of polynomial term, a power of a predictor entered as an ordinary extra column, here I(prestige^2), and the model is still linear in its coefficients. What changes is the reading:
\[
E(Y\mid x,\ldots)=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\cdots,\qquad
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial x}=\beta_1+2\beta_2x,\qquad
x^{*}=-\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}.
\]
The predictor’s slope now depends on its own value, \(\beta_1+2\beta_2x\), and is zero at the turning point \(x^{*}\).

m2q <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + I(prestige^2) + women + type,
  data = d)
anova(m2, m2q)
