title: Part One: Foundations, Regression, and Generalized Linear Models
section: How the Chapters Build on Each Other
text:
How the Chapters Build on Each Other
Part One contains fourteen chapters. The first nine establish a route from questions and records to regression. Chapter 1, The Quantitative Research Journey, orients the reader in questions, evidence, design, and interpretation. Chapter 2, Data, Distributions, and Variation, develops records, distributions, and variation across repeated samples. Chapter 3, Estimates, Uncertainty, and Statistical Tests, develops estimation, intervals, and tests. Chapter 4, Group Comparisons with Analysis of Variance, develops comparisons among several groups. Chapter 5, Description and Basic Inference with R, and Chapter 6, Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R, make those foundations executable. Chapters 7–9 then develop regression from one predictor to the regression toolbox: Chapter 7, Simple Linear Regression; Chapter 8, Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions; and Chapter 9, Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty.
Chapters 10–14 extend the regression framework to conditional relationships, noncontinuous outcomes and prediction, then return to the design of a study and the limits of its claims. Interaction changes how a relationship varies across conditions; generalized linear models change the outcome model; validation asks how a fitted rule performs on new cases; and causal design asks which comparisons can support an intervention claim.








Figure 1: The foundations of Part One, from questions and records to inference, computation, and regression in Chapters 1–9.





Table 1 states the question each chapter answers. Chapters 1–9 are available on the website. Chapters 10–14 are not yet available; their rows outline the continuation of the curriculum.



Table 1: The question each chapter answers.









Chapter
The question it answers




1. The Quantitative Research Journey
How does a study turn a concern into a question, produce evidence that bears on it, and support a bounded answer?


2. Data, Distributions, and Variation
What do recorded data show about one variable, about groups and relationships, and how much would a summary change across repeated samples?


3. Estimates, Uncertainty, and Statistical Tests
What can one observed sample tell us about a target quantity, and how much uncertainty surrounds that answer?


4. Group Comparisons with Analysis of Variance
How do the means of several groups or crossed conditions differ, and which of those comparisons can a study support?


5. Description and Basic Inference with R
How are the descriptions and inferences of Chapters 2 and 3 computed, checked, and reported in R?


6. Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
How are group comparisons stated, fitted, and compared as statistical models in R, and how does repetition check what a procedure delivers?


7. Simple Linear Regression
How does an outcome’s mean change with one predictor, and how well does a fitted line describe, estimate, and predict it?


8. Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
What does a comparison on one predictor mean when the other predictors are held fixed, and how can one set of records answer several coordinated questions?


9. Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty
How can a regression’s mean part be changed or compared, and its uncertainty recalculated, when the question or the data call for it?


10. Interaction and Moderation
When does a relationship differ across the values or groups of another variable, and how is that difference estimated and reported?


11. Binary Logistic Regression
How does the probability of a yes-or-no outcome differ with predictors, and on which scale is that difference best reported?


12. Extending the GLM: Nominal, Ordinal, and Count Outcomes
How can regression represent outcomes that are unordered categories, ordered categories, or counts?


13. Prediction, Cross-Validation, and Regularization
How accurately will a fitted rule predict new cases at the moment the prediction is needed?


14. Regression Pitfalls and Causal Design
When does a regression comparison support the claim made from it, and what must a design supply for a causal claim?






Each idea has one principal home, and later chapters use it rather than teach it again. Chapter 1 previews uncertainty while reading a study; Chapter 2 develops sampling distributions and the standard error through repeated samples; Chapter 3 develops their inferential use and states the conditions they require. Chapter 2 explains the descriptive ingredients of group variation; Chapter 4 develops the full analysis-of-variance decomposition and its inferential use, comparing one common mean with group means and an additive model with a model that includes interaction. Where a later chapter needs an earlier idea, it recalls it briefly and then puts it to work in the new setting.

title: Part One: Foundations, Regression, and Generalized Linear Models
section: How to Read a Chapter and Use the Concept Reference
text:
How to Read a Chapter and Use the Concept Reference
The numbered chapters share an arrangement. A Chapter overview box opens the chapter with the route it follows and what a reader will be able to do afterwards. Numbered sections develop the material in order. A closing Reading Bridge brings the principal ideas together and connects them to the next chapter, and a selective Key terms table gives a compact reference to the concepts explained principally there. Unnumbered material follows the numbered sections: exercises for working with the ideas, appendices holding fuller derivations and specialized extensions, and the references. The arrangement keeps the main explanation distinct from fuller derivations and specialized extensions.
There are two sensible routes through the chapters. The first is the chapter sequence. The second pairs statistics with computation: Chapters 2 and 3 with Chapter 5, then Chapters 3 and 4 with Chapter 6. Either way, follow a method from its data and question through its calculation to its interpretation; a result separated from the question it answers is difficult to use.
The Part One Concept Reference is published beside this introduction. It gathers the Key terms tables of Chapters 1–14 and of Argument Chapters A and B, one table for each chapter, so a term appears with its meaning under the chapter that explains it principally. A further table lists the procedures of Chapters 3 and 4 with what each estimates and the conditions it relies on, and a closing table records the notation that several chapters share. It is a place to look something up while reading rather than a substitute for reading, because first-use explanations and worked examples stay in the chapters themselves.
Readers who would like to run R without installing anything can use the public browser practice pages that accompany Chapters 3 and 4.

title: Part One: Foundations, Regression, and Generalized Linear Models
text:
What Comes Later
Three argument chapters extend the argument-based approach. Argument Chapter A, How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument, develops the reading, evaluation, and construction of one question-level argument. Argument Chapter B, Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies, develops arguments with several statistical strands and studies with coordinated questions. Argument Chapter C concerns arguments involving latent variables or an additional measurement layer, drawing on Part Two. The argument chapters are optional, and no numbered chapter depends on them.
Argument Chapter C is reserved for that further development.
Part Two of the book turns to latent-variable modeling, where the variable of primary interest is one that no column of the data set holds. Its twelve chapters proceed from factor analysis and measurement models to structural systems, causal identification, indirect and conditional relationships, group comparisons, incomplete data, change and study planning.

title: About QMSBR
text:
Author
  Citation
  Licences
  Accessibility
  Using QMSBR in a course
QMSBR—Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral Research—is a modular collection of chapters designed to support various quantitative and statistical courses. Its modular design serves several courses at once: each course chooses its own route through one canonical set of chapters whose identities and links stay stable, so a correction to a chapter improves every route that uses it. The chapters help readers make sense of quantitative studies, following how a study turns a question into evidence and a bounded answer. They also help readers carry out analyses in which design, statistical reasoning, interpretation, and reproducible computing stay connected.
Part One covers foundations, regression, and generalized linear models. It moves from research questions, data, and variation through estimation, testing, and group comparisons to computing with R and regression, and its first four chapters can be read without running R or SPSS. Part Two covers factor analysis and structural equation modeling: how observed responses represent latent variables, and how a measurement model is developed, specified, estimated, evaluated, and extended. Part Three is reserved for multilevel and longitudinal models and is not yet available. The reading approach the chapters share is set out on The Argument-Based Approach.

title: About QMSBR
text:
Accessibility
Every chapter, part introduction, and concept reference is offered as an HTML page and a PDF. The PDFs pass automated PDF/UA-2 checks and include section headings in their tagged structure, figure descriptions and mathematical alternatives. These checks are accompanied by visual review; they do not cover every assistive technology or reading setup. The HTML page is the more flexible format: it provides a responsive layout, headings, search, descriptive link text, and selectable code, and the PDF suits printing and annotation. Figures carry alternative text, and text and link colours are chosen for readable contrast. A navigation entry for a unit that is not yet available is shown in a muted colour and marked as disabled, so it is not announced or reached as a working link.
To report an accessibility barrier, open an issue in the repository issue tracker or email jinsong.chen@live.com, naming the page and what got in the way.

title: QMSBR
text:
A modular collection for quantitative courses



QMSBR—Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral Research—is a modular collection of chapters designed to support various quantitative and statistical courses. Its modular design serves several courses at once: each course chooses its own route through one canonical set of chapters whose identities and links stay stable, so a correction to a chapter improves every route that uses it. The chapters help readers make sense of quantitative studies, following how a study turns a question into evidence and a bounded answer. They also help readers carry out analyses in which design, statistical reasoning, interpretation, and reproducible computing stay connected.
The material is organized in parts. Each part opens with a short introduction, keeps a concept reference to consult while reading, and presents its chapters in reading order. Part One covers foundations, regression, and generalized linear models; Part Two covers factor analysis and structural equation modeling. The R support pages run R in the browser, with nothing to install.
To start, read a part introduction and then its first chapter.

Browse the collections Read the argument-based approach

How to use this site
Read online, or download the PDF. Every chapter, introduction, and concept reference can be read online or downloaded as a PDF, and both are built from the same source. The web page adds a responsive layout, a table of contents, search, and selectable code; the PDF suits printing and annotation. The PDF link sits beside each page’s title in the collections above.
Keep the concept reference open while reading. Each part gathers its central concepts, symbols, and notation in a concept reference. Read a chapter for the lesson, and open the concept reference when you meet a term or a symbol and want its meaning and the chapter that explains it.
Try an analysis on the R support pages. The R support pages carry a live R session in the browser, so you can run a chapter’s analysis, change it, and see what changes without installing anything. The data sources page says where each dataset comes from and on what terms it can be reused.
Read the argument-based approach the chapters share. The chapters read a quantitative study as a question, the evidence and reasons that support an answer, and the limits of that answer. The Argument-Based Approach summarizes this reading, and Part One Chapter 1 develops it in full.

title: The Argument-Based Approach
text:
Evidence, justification, inference, and a bounded claim
  Six questions for evaluating an argument
  Where the approach comes from
  
  References
  
  Argument chapters
  
  A. How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
  B. Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
  C. Arguments involving latent variables or an additional measurement layer
A finalized quantitative study can be read as a question–answer contract. The research question declares what answer is owed. The methods, results, supplementary materials, and stated reservations provide the record from which a reader decides whether the reported answer is warranted. This page summarizes the reading approach the chapters share. Part One Chapter 1, The Quantitative Research Journey, develops it in full with worked examples and is the place to learn it.

title: The Argument-Based Approach
section: One question–answer pair, one argument, linked layers
text:
One question–answer pair, one argument, linked layers
One question–answer pair has one argument with linked layers. Pairs are counted by the substantive answers a study separately owes, not by its estimates, tests, or coefficients, so several results can contribute to one answer, and a study with several separable questions needs several arguments.
The statistical layer (STAT) concerns the recorded variables, the statistical support, the analysis, and the statistical conclusion. The substantive layer (SUB) connects that work to the people, practices, meanings, and setting named by the question. Substantive reasoning enters when a question and its measures are chosen, as well as when results are interpreted.

title: The Argument-Based Approach
section: Evidence, justification, inference, and a bounded claim
text:
Evidence, justification, inference, and a bounded claim
In each layer, Evidence and Justification support an Inference, which supports a bounded Claim: E + J → I → C. Each layer contributes all four functions.




Table 1: The four functions in the linked statistical and substantive layers.










Function
Statistical layer
Substantive layer




Evidence (E)
The observations, variables, and procedures through which the analysis data were produced or acquired
The people, setting, activities, and meaning those data represent


Justification (J)
The reasons and conditions that support the intended statistical comparison and inference
The domain reasons that support measurement meaning, implementation, explanation, and applicability


Inference (I)
The analysis connecting evidence and justification to a statistical conclusion: estimates, uncertainty, comparisons, and checks
The interpretation of that statistical inference in substantive terms, keeping its uncertainty and conditions


Bounded claim (C)
The statistical conclusion about the estimand, with its uncertainty, conditions, and scope
The question-facing answer, with its substantive scope, qualifications, and unresolved matters







Across the layers, each substantive component works on its statistical counterpart: SUB-E situates STAT-E, SUB-J augments and contextualizes STAT-J, SUB-I interprets STAT-I, and SUB-C bounds the substantive reach of STAT-C. These contributions give statistical work its meaning for the question. A software result is therefore part of the inference, not the whole of it.

title: The Argument-Based Approach
section: Six questions for evaluating an argument
text:
Six questions for evaluating an argument
Reading identifies how a study’s information supports its answer. Evaluating the argument’s quality is a separate step that asks whether that support is adequate for the question and the answer. Six evaluation questions guide it, in three groups.




Table 2: Six questions for evaluating one question-level argument.










Group
Evaluation question
What it asks




Alignment
Question alignment
Whether the question, estimand, design, evidence, analysis, and answer stay directed at the same aim


Support
Evidence integrity
Whether the observations and contextual records, their production, and their representation are trustworthy, traceable, and appropriate


Support
Justification adequacy
Whether the statistical, design, measurement, and contextual reasons warrant the proposed moves


Support
Inferential adequacy
Whether the reasoning within both layers is adequate, including estimation, uncertainty, checks, sensitivity, and interpretation


Translation
Transition fidelity
Whether the links between the layers keep meaning, uncertainty, design status, and scope


Translation
Claim calibration
Whether the strength and breadth of the reported answer match its support







Each question receives a reasoned judgment rather than a score, and the whole question–answer pair receives one conclusion: the answer is supported as stated, supported only after narrowing or revision, not supported, or not assessable from the accessible record. Chapter 1 works through these judgments on an example and also outlines how a researcher constructs one argument.

title: The Argument-Based Approach
text:
Where the approach comes from
The approach is Toulmin-informed: it keeps evidence, justified inferential steps, qualified claims, and explicit reservations from Toulmin’s account of argument (Toulmin, 2003) without treating its components as one-to-one replacements for Toulmin’s roles. LeMire’s link between statistical testing and subject-matter claims (LeMire, 2010) is a related statistical precedent, and Kane’s argument-based treatment of the interpretation and use of test scores (Kane, 2013) is a related precedent in measurement. The linked layers, the evaluation questions, and the construction workflow bring these influences together for the chapters rather than reproduce one source’s arrangement.

References


Kane, M. T. (2013). Validating the interpretations and uses of test scores. Journal of Educational Measurement, 50(1), 1–73. https://doi.org/10.1111/jedm.12000


LeMire, S. D. (2010). An argument framework for the application of null hypothesis statistical testing in support of research. Journal of Statistics Education, 18(2), 1–23. https://doi.org/10.1080/10691898.2010.11889492


Toulmin, S. E. (2003). The uses of argument (Updated). Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511840005

title: The Argument-Based Approach
text:
Argument chapters
Three argument chapters extend the approach beyond Chapter 1. They are optional enrichment: no numbered chapter in Part One or Part Two depends on them. A course can select a chapter with the statistical preparation it requires, without assuming completion of all three.


A. How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
A complete worked reading of one study as an argument: the question–answer contract; one argument with linked statistical and substantive layers, traced across a report and its related materials; the reading of a reported regression argument; evaluating a question-level argument; and a six-stage construction cycle.
Read Argument Chapter A · Download PDF



B. Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies
The approach carried from one question to several: separate questions and statistical strands; one complex argument with several strands; coordinated questions and their dependencies; evaluating answers and their coherence across questions; coordinated construction and revision; and transfer to a published experiment.
Read Argument Chapter B · Download PDF


C. Arguments involving latent variables or an additional measurement layer
A reading of how observed indicators, a measurement model, and the interpretation of a latent quantity support a substantive answer. The chapter examines measurement assumptions, identification, model checks, interpretive validity, uncertainty, and sensitivity. It distinguishes model fit and reliability from evidence for the intended interpretation and carries unresolved measurement qualifications into the answer.
This chapter is not yet available.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
This reference gathers the Key terms tables of Chapters 1–14 and of Argument Chapters A and B, followed by the procedures of Chapters 3 and 4 and the notation that several chapters share. Each table appears under its chapter’s heading and lists the concepts that chapter explains principally: each term with its common alternatives, and its meaning or the distinction that matters most. The reference is meant to be consulted while reading rather than read through: a term’s first use, its worked example, and the reasoning around it stay in the chapter that teaches it. Chapters 1–9 are available on the website; the tables for Chapters 10–14 point forward to chapter readings that are not yet available.
A few conventions govern the rows. Names that pick out the same concept share one entry, so mean and arithmetic mean appear together, and outcome, response, and dependent variable are explained as one analytical role. A more specific role, such as treatment, exposure, or confounder, carries additional design or substantive meaning that the study itself must supply. Related concepts with different meanings, such as mean and median or SD and SE, keep separate entries. A term is listed under the chapter that explains it principally rather than the chapter that first mentions it, so a brief early introduction and a later full account can coexist: Chapter 1 introduces cases and samples through its studies, while Chapter 2 develops their use in reading records and calculations. Argument Chapters A and B, How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument and Extending the Argument-Based Approach to Quantitative Studies, extend the reading of one question-level argument to several statistical strands and coordinated questions; the notation table abbreviates them as Arg. A and Arg. B.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
Chapter 1: The Quantitative Research Journey



Table 1: Key terms of Chapter 1.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Question-answer pair
What a study asks and the answer it eventually offers for that question. Each separately owed substantive answer has its own argument.


Traceable information
Specific study content through which an argument component’s function can be identified at a documentary location. Identifying that contribution precedes judging its adequacy.


Estimand
The target quantity sought for the named units, conditions, outcome, and scope. It can concern a fixed dataset, a population, a comparison, or prediction performance.


Outcome variable (response variable; dependent variable)
The variable an analysis seeks to describe, compare, or predict. These alternative names share that role in many analyses; a variable’s role depends on the question.


Predictor variable (explanatory variable; independent variable)
A variable used to represent an outcome’s relationship with other information. These analytical-role labels alone establish neither a causal effect nor statistical independence.


Sampling (recruitment; selection into a study)
How units come to enter a study, by probability selection, volunteering, or availability. It is contrasted with assignment, which concerns the conditions allocated to participating units.


Assignment (allocation)
The allocation of study conditions to participating units, by any mechanism. Actual treatment received may differ from the assigned condition.


Random sampling (probability sampling)
Selecting units from a defined population or sampling frame through a probability mechanism that gives every eligible unit a known, nonzero chance of selection, not necessarily the same chance. “Random selection” alone can describe other chance-based decisions.


Random assignment (random allocation)
Allocating study conditions to participating units through a specified probability mechanism. The assigned units may be individuals or groups; realized groups need not be identical.


Causal effect (counterfactual contrast)
The difference between the outcomes that would occur for the same units or target population under two specified conditions, only one of which is observed for each unit. The contrast may be zero; interpreting a comparison causally needs design and identification support.


Confounding
Mixing an exposure’s effect with effects of other factors that influence both exposure and outcome. Such a factor is a confounder, a specific causal role.


External validity (generalizability)
Support for extending findings to other people, settings, or conditions. The intended extension determines which similarities and differences matter.


Unit
The entity selected, assigned, measured, or analyzed in a particular operation. The units of assignment, measurement, and analysis can differ, and all are distinct from measurement units such as points or minutes.


Evidence
Observations and contextual records contributing to an answer, including information about how they were produced.


Justification
Reasons and conditions invoked to support a comparison, analytical move, or interpretation.


Inference
Reasoning and analysis connecting evidence and justification to a conclusion.


Bounded claim
The reported conclusion with its uncertainty, conditions, and scope: in the statistical layer, the conclusion about the estimand; in the substantive layer, the question-facing answer with its qualifications.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
Chapter 2: Data, Distributions, and Variation



Table 2: Key terms of Chapter 2.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Case
The entity or measurement occasion described in a dataset. Depending on the study, a case may be a student, a class, or one measurement occasion for a student.


Variable
A characteristic that can take different values across cases or occasions. A dataset records values of one or more variables for its cases.


Quantitative variable (numerical variable)
A variable expressing an amount, including continuous measurements and discrete counts or scores. Its units and scale determine what numerical differences mean.


Categorical variable
A variable whose values identify categories. Nominal categories have no intrinsic order; ordinal categories have an order; a binary variable has two categories.


Population
The collection of units a question concerns. It may be the participating students themselves or a wider collection to which the findings might extend.


Sample
A selected set of units from a larger collection. Calling a set a sample does not by itself explain how it was selected or which population it represents.


Analysis sample
The units whose data contribute to a particular analysis. Eligibility, missing measurements, and exclusions can make this set and its denominator differ across analyses.


Sampling design (sampling scheme)
The specified procedure for selecting a sample, including selection stages, grouping, and, for probability sampling, the selection probabilities.


Simple random sampling
Selection in which every possible sample of the specified size has the same probability of being chosen.


Empirical distribution (observed distribution; data distribution)
How the observed values are distributed across values or intervals, including their frequencies, center, spread, and shape. A probability model is a separate description of possible values.


Skewness and kurtosis (left or negative skew; right or positive skew; tail weight)
Skewness describes asymmetry: in a right (positive) skew the long tail points toward larger values and the mean usually lies above the median; in a left (negative) skew the long tail points toward smaller values and the mean usually lies below the median. Kurtosis describes tail weight relative to a Normal distribution with the same mean and SD, not peakedness.


Mean (arithmetic mean)
The sum of the numerical values divided by their count. Every included value contributes, so unusual values can shift the mean.


Median
The middle value after ordering the data, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even. It describes the center by position.


Quartile
A cut point dividing ordered data into quarters. The first and third quartiles mark approximately the lower and upper edges of the middle half; calculation conventions can differ.


Interquartile range (IQR)
The third quartile minus the first quartile: the width of the middle half of the ordered data, expressed in the variable’s original units.


Variance
A measure of spread based on squared deviations from the mean. The usual sample variance divides their sum by \(n - 1\) and is expressed in squared units.


Standard deviation (SD)
The square root of the variance, expressing spread around the mean in the variable’s original units. Applied to individual observations, it describes variation among their values; applied to a statistic’s sampling distribution, it is the SE.


Grand mean
The mean across all included cases. It equals the average of the group means weighted by their group counts, so larger groups contribute more.


Degrees of freedom (df)
A count reflecting freely varying information after constraints or fitted quantities are taken into account. The \(n\) deviations from their own mean sum to zero, leaving \(n - 1\) free.


Standardized value (z score)
A value minus a specified mean, divided by a specified standard deviation. It expresses distance in SD units; standardizing alone preserves the distribution’s shape.


Normal distribution (Gaussian distribution)
A symmetric, bell-shaped probability model described by a mean and standard deviation. The standard Normal has mean zero and SD one; observed data need not follow this model.


Conditional proportion
The proportion in one category among cases satisfying a stated condition. Its denominator is the count in that conditioning group, such as students in one education-intention category.


Covariance
A summary based on products of paired deviations from the two means. Its sign shows the direction of joint variation; its magnitude depends on both variables’ units and spreads.


Pearson’s correlation (Pearson’s r; product-moment correlation)
Covariance divided by the product of the two SDs. For variables with nonzero spread, it describes direction and strength of linear association on a scale from \(-1\) to 1.


Sampling distribution
The distribution of a statistic, such as a sample mean, across repeated samples generated by a stated sampling procedure or model. Repeated sample summaries in a simulation approximate this distribution.


Sampling error
The part of an estimate’s departure from the population quantity that arises from observing a sample rather than the whole population. It varies across repetitions, and its spread is the SE; coverage, nonresponse, and measurement error are separate.


Standard error (SE)
The standard deviation of a statistic’s sampling distribution under a stated sampling procedure or model. It describes spread across repeated sample summaries, distinct from individual-value SD and one sample’s difference from the population quantity.


Design effect (deff)
The factor by which a sampling design multiplies the variance of a statistic relative to simple random sampling of the same size. For a mean from equal clusters of \(m\) units it is about \(1+(m-1)\,\mathrm{ICC}\), where the intraclass correlation (ICC) is the share of outcome variance lying between clusters: units in one cluster supply overlapping information.


Data matrix
A rectangular arrangement with cases in rows and variables in columns; \(x_{ij}\) denotes case \(i\) on variable \(j\).


Binary variable (0/1 coding)
A binary variable has two possible categories; a 0/1 coding marks membership or occurrence. Its sample mean is the proportion coded 1.


Linear transformation
\(Y=a+bX\) changes the center to \(a+bE(X)\) and the SD to \(\lvert b\rvert SD(X)\); a negative \(b\) also reverses order.


Bernoulli; binomial; categorical; Poisson; lognormal; logistic
Respectively a binary outcome, a count of successes in fixed independent equal-probability trials, one category, an event count under a specified rate model, a positive variable with Normal log, and a continuous symmetric distribution used here as a preview. Logistic regression later models Bernoulli outcomes.


Density; cumulative distribution function; quantile
Density determines probability by area for a continuous variable; the CDF gives \(P(X\le x)\); a quantile is a value reaching the stated cumulative probability.


Rank correlation; point-biserial correlation
Spearman uses ranks; Kendall summarizes concordance; point-biserial is Pearson correlation with one binary variable coded 0/1. Each addresses a specified relationship.


Partial correlation
Correlation between two variables after their linear relationships with stated controls are removed by regression; it describes residual association and does not establish causal adjustment.


Parameter
A numerical characteristic of a population or probability model, such as a population mean. A parameter may be the estimand; the question determines which quantity is sought.


Statistic
A quantity calculated from sample data, such as a sample mean or proportion. The same statistic can summarize the sample or serve as an estimate for a wider target.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 3: Estimates, Uncertainty, and Statistical Tests
text:
Chapter 3: Estimates, Uncertainty, and Statistical Tests



Table 3: Key terms of Chapter 3.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Estimate
A numerical approximation to an estimand, calculated from the available data. A point estimate expresses the approximation as one value.


Estimator
The rule used to calculate an estimate from data. Its bias and precision concern how the rule behaves across the repetitions specified by the study’s procedure or model.


Bias (of an estimator)
The difference between an estimator’s expected value over the specified repetitions and the estimand. An unbiased estimator has bias zero; precision describes its spread, a separate quality.


Pooled variance (\(s_p^2\); pooled within-group variance)
A weighted average of within-group sample variances, each weighted by its degrees of freedom: \(s_p^2=\{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_0-1)s_0^2\}/(n_1+n_0-2)\) for two groups. It estimates a variance the groups are assumed to share; its square root is the pooled SD.


Confidence interval (CI)
An interval expressing uncertainty about an estimand. Under its conditions, the procedure covers that estimand at its stated rate across repetitions; the rate describes the procedure.


Critical value
The cut-point of a reference distribution, such as the Normal or t, selected by a confidence or significance level. It multiplies the SE in an interval and marks the rejection region of a test.


Coverage
The proportion of repetitions in which an interval procedure contains the estimand under its conditions. The confidence level is the procedure’s target coverage, not a probability for one realized interval.


Null hypothesis
The statistical proposition used as the reference for a test, such as equality of specified population means. The alternative hypothesis states the departure being considered.


Test statistic
A quantity calculated from data to assess departure from a null hypothesis. The test compares it with a reference distribution justified under that null and stated conditions.


p-value
Under a specified null hypothesis and conditions, the probability of a test result at least as extreme as the observed one, using the test’s stated tail rule.


Significance level (alpha)
The threshold used for rejecting a null hypothesis, chosen to control the probability of rejecting a true null under the test’s conditions. This error is called a Type I error.


One-sample z test; one-sample t test
Both compare a sample mean with a stated null mean using its SE; z uses a known process SD under its model, whereas t estimates that SD and uses the appropriate t reference. Neither choice follows an automatic sample-size cutoff.


Paired-samples t test
A one-sample t test of within-pair differences against a specified mean difference, with independent pairs under the stated model.


Equal-variance two-sample t test (pooled t test; Student’s two-sample t test)
One of the two independent-samples t tests. It compares two independent group means under the condition that the populations share one variance: its SE is \(s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_0}\), and its reference is t with \(n_1+n_0-2\) df.


Welch’s unequal-variance t test (Welch test)
The other independent-samples t test. It compares two independent group means without assuming a common variance: its SE adds the two estimated mean variances, and its approximate t reference uses Welch–Satterthwaite df. With equal group sizes its statistic equals the equal-variance statistic, and only the df can differ.


Expected count
The count a cell of a two-way table would have under a stated null pattern such as independence, given the observed margins: row total times column total, divided by the overall total.


Pearson’s chi-square statistic (\(X^2\))
The sum over cells of squared differences between observed and expected counts, each divided by its expected count, compared with a chi-square reference with \((R-1)(C-1)\) degrees of freedom under the stated model.


Multiway table (three-way table; layered two-way tables)
A table that cross-classifies three or more categorical variables: a two-way table holds two variables, a three-way table three, and a four-way table four. A three-way table is read as two-way tables within the layers of the third variable; a chi-square test of one two-way table cannot test the variables jointly, which needs a method that uses all three variables at once, such as a model for multiway tables.


Standardized mean difference
A difference in means divided by a specified SD. The chosen denominator determines the standardized quantity; the raw difference retains the outcome’s original units.


Power (statistical power)
The probability of rejecting the null under a specified alternative, design, and test. Failure to reject under that alternative is a Type II error; power is one minus its probability.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 4: Group Comparisons with Analysis of Variance
text:
Chapter 4: Group Comparisons with Analysis of Variance



Table 4: Key terms of Chapter 4.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Factor (grouping factor)
In ANOVA, a categorical variable defining groups or conditions; its categories are levels. This meaning differs from a latent factor used to model shared indicator variation.


Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
A method for studying mean differences through sources of variation. One-way ANOVA uses one grouping factor, and multi-way (factorial) ANOVA uses two or more crossed factors, as two-way and three-way ANOVA do; each factor can have several levels.


Fitted value
The value a fitted model assigns to an observed case. In a one-way group-mean model, it is that case’s group mean.


Residual
An observed outcome minus its fitted value. A residual is calculated from the fitted model; an error is the corresponding unknown departure in the population model.


Mean square (MS)
A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom. In classical ANOVA, the within-group mean square estimates the common error variance under the model’s conditions.


F statistic (F ratio)
In classical ANOVA, a ratio of the mean square for a tested source to the appropriate error mean square. Its null F reference depends on the model and both degrees of freedom.


Omnibus test
A test of one joint null hypothesis about a whole pattern, such as equality of all group means. Rejecting it does not identify which comparisons differ or how large they are.


Eta squared
The proportion of total observed variation attributed to a specified source in an ANOVA decomposition. In one-way ANOVA, it is between-group divided by total sum of squares.


Contrast (linear contrast)
A weighted combination of means whose weights sum to zero, expressing a specific comparison. The means, weights, and target population determine the quantity compared.


Familywise error rate (FWER)
The probability of at least one Type I error among a defined family of tests. Procedures such as Bonferroni allocate the error allowance across that family.


Simultaneous confidence intervals
A set of intervals calibrated so that, under their conditions, all of them cover their estimands together at the stated familywise rate; Bonferroni, Tukey, and Dunnett are different calibrations for different families.


Cell mean and marginal mean
In a two-factor layout, a cell mean is the mean of the cases sharing one level of each factor; a marginal mean averages the cell means across the levels of the other factor, with stated weights.


Main effect
A comparison across one factor’s levels averaged over the other factor’s levels, using stated weights. It remains an average when the conditional pattern differs across levels.


Interaction
A pattern in which a comparison across one factor’s levels changes with the other factor’s level. A difference of differences expresses one such comparison.


Simple effect
A comparison across one factor’s levels at a specified level of the other factor. It describes a conditional comparison within the factorial design.


Three-way interaction (higher-order interaction)
A pattern in which a two-way interaction changes across the levels of a third factor. Each added factor multiplies the cells and adds interactions, so the highest-order interaction is read first and a few comparisons are declared in advance.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 5: Description and Basic Inference with R
text:
Chapter 5: Description and Basic Inference with R



Table 5: Key terms of Chapter 5.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Script and Quarto source
A saved .R script records commands so an analysis can be rerun; a .qmd source connects prose, mathematics, executable code, tables, figures, and references, and renders to PDF, HTML, or Word.


Simulation and seed (Monte Carlo simulation)
Generating data from a declared process to see what a statistic or procedure does across repetitions. A seed makes the random draws repeatable; it does not make the process true for an actual study.


Monte Carlo standard error
The numerical uncertainty of a simulated probability or mean that comes from using finitely many repetitions; more repetitions shrink it. It is distinct from a study’s SE, which depends on the study’s sample size.


Covariance matrix
A square table of variances on the diagonal and covariances off the diagonal for a stated set of variables and observations.


Correlation matrix
A square table of pairwise correlation coefficients for a stated set of variables and observations; its diagonal is 1 for variables with positive variance.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 6: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
text:
Chapter 6: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R



Table 6: Key terms of Chapter 6.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Model formula (R formula)
Notation such as score ~ group naming an outcome and the variables that explain it for a fitting function. It does not state whether observations are independent or paired; that comes from the design.


Categorical effect scales (difference in proportions; risk ratio; odds ratio; Cramér’s V)
Four ways to state the size of an association in a table, each answering its own question: the difference in proportions gives an absolute gap, the risk ratio a relative gap, the odds ratio a ratio of odds that stays the same when rows and columns exchange roles, and Cramér’s V a unit-free strength, from 0 to 1, for a table of any size.


Objective function
A numerical criterion evaluated at candidate parameter values for fixed data; fitting seeks a stated minimum or maximum.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
Chapter 7: Simple Linear Regression



Table 7: Key terms of Chapter 7.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Simple linear regression (simple regression model; regression line)
A model in which an outcome’s mean is a straight line in one predictor, \(E(Y\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x\), with errors around the line that average zero and share one SD \(\sigma\); its three parameters are the intercept, the slope and \(\sigma\). The least-squares line estimates the model’s line: its descriptive use concerns the records fitted, and a model-based use needs a declared process.


Intercept
The fitted outcome at predictor value zero. It places the line vertically; when zero is outside the observed support, it is a mathematical anchor rather than a supported prediction. Centering the predictor moves it to a supported reference point.


Slope (regression coefficient)
The difference in fitted outcome per one-unit difference in the predictor, in outcome units per predictor unit. It compares units that differ in the predictor; it is not a change within one unit unless a design supports that reading.


Ordinary least squares (OLS)
The rule that chooses the intercept and slope minimizing the residual sum of squares. With an intercept, the fitted line passes through the mean point and the residuals sum to zero; the slope equals covariance divided by predictor variance.


Residual sum of squares (RSS)
The sum of squared residuals from a fitted line, in squared outcome units. Total squared variation about the mean splits into a regression part and RSS when the model has an intercept.


Residual standard deviation (residual standard error)
The square root of RSS divided by its residual degrees of freedom, in outcome units; with an intercept and one predictor the degrees of freedom are \(n-2\). Under the process model it estimates the error SD.


R-squared (coefficient of determination)
One minus RSS divided by total squared variation: the proportion of centered squared outcome variation accounted for by the fit in these records. In simple regression with an intercept it equals the squared correlation.


Confidence interval for a mean response (mean-response interval)
An interval for the process mean outcome at a stated predictor value, using the SE of the fitted value. It concerns an average, narrows near the predictor mean, and does not cover individual outcomes.


Prediction interval (new-case interval)
An interval for one new outcome at a stated predictor value from the same process. Its variance adds the error variance to the fitted-mean variance, so it is wider than the mean-response interval and keeps a nonzero floor as the sample grows.


Leverage
A measure of how unusual a record’s predictor value is relative to the others; it grows with distance from the predictor mean and appears in the SE of a fitted value and in influence measures.


Cook’s distance (influence)
A summary of how much the fitted values change when one record is omitted, combining its residual and its leverage. It prompts inspection of provenance and a disclosed sensitivity, not automatic deletion.


Heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance (HC3; sandwich estimator)
A coefficient covariance estimate that allows unequal error variance across predictor values under independence. It changes SEs and intervals, not the fitted coefficients, and does not repair curvature, dependence, measurement error, or confounding.


Extrapolation (predictor support)
Using a fitted line at predictor values outside the observed range or where observations are sparse. Software returns a number there; the data do not support it.


Regression toward the mean (regression to the mean)
For a simple linear prediction in standard units, \(\widehat z_y=r\,z_x\); when \(\lvert r\rvert<1\), the predicted value is nearer its mean than the predictor is to its mean. In a stable repeated-measurement model with independent occasion errors, a group selected on an extreme noisy first score is expected to be less extreme on the second. These are statements about predictions or conditional averages, not every case; a narrower spread of predictions does not imply a narrower outcome distribution (the regression paradox).


Regression fallacy
Attributing to an intervention the movement expected from selection on an extreme noisy measurement. Evaluating an intervention requires a credible no-intervention benchmark, supplied by a suitable design or untreated comparison under stated assumptions; a fitted line through treated outcomes alone does not supply it.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 8: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Chapter 8: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions



Table 8: Key terms of Chapter 8.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Multiple regression (multiple regression model; additive model)
A model in which an outcome’s mean is an intercept plus one term per predictor, \(E(Y\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}\), with errors of one common SD \(\sigma\); its \(p\) coefficients leave \(n-p\) residual df, and least squares estimates them. Each coefficient compares means at the same values of the other predictors; the additive form assumes each comparison is the same across those values.


Partial slope (conditional coefficient; adjusted coefficient)
The difference in fitted outcome per one-unit difference in one predictor, holding the model’s other predictors fixed. Its meaning depends on the conditioning set named with it; it is not an intervention effect or a claim about unmeasured differences.


Indicator variable (dummy variable) and reference category
A 0/1 variable marking membership in one category of a factor; a factor with \(J\) levels needs \(J-1\) indicators, and the omitted level is the reference. The intercept refers to the reference category; each indicator coefficient is a difference from it at the same other predictors. Releveling changes coordinates, not fitted values.


Partial regression (residualization; added-variable form)
Regressing both the outcome and one predictor on the other predictors, then relating their residuals. The residual slope equals the partial slope; the residual correlation is the partial correlation, unit-free.


Coefficient covariance matrix
The estimated variances and covariances of the fitted coefficients (vcov() in R). Any linear combination of coefficients, such as a fitted mean or a contrast, has variance \(\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c\); adding SEs or ignoring covariances is a different, incorrect calculation.


Variance inflation factor (VIF)
One divided by one minus the \(R^2\) from regressing a predictor on the other predictors. Its square root multiplies that coefficient’s SE relative to an orthogonal design, holding residual variance fixed; it describes precision, not bias, and is not a deletion rule.


Joint support (covariate hull)
Whether a combination of predictor values lies within the region where observations actually occur, not merely within each variable’s separate range. A fitted value outside joint support is extrapolation even if each coordinate is observed somewhere.


Standardization over a named distribution (model-averaged fitted value)
Averaging the model’s fitted values after setting one predictor to a chosen value for every profile in a declared set with fixed weights. Its uncertainty uses the coefficient covariance; it is not an observed group mean, a causal effect, or held-out performance.


Learning rule (learning procedure)
A fixed recipe that turns training records into a prediction equation, such as fitting a declared OLS formula. Prediction performance concerns the rule at stated training sizes, not one final fitted equation.


Cross-validation (held-out validation)
Dividing records into folds, fitting a rule on the other folds, predicting the held-out fold, and pooling the errors so that no outcome contributes to its own prediction. Resplits describe sensitivity to the partition, not new independent studies.


Mean absolute error (MAE)
The average absolute difference between held-out outcomes and their predictions, in outcome units. It is an evaluation loss chosen separately from the squared-error criterion that OLS minimizes.


Cross-question coherence
The additional evaluation question for coordinated answers: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions, estimands, methods, uncertainty, and limits of the separate answers rather than merging them into one omnibus claim?

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 9: Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty
text:
Chapter 9: Multiple Regression II: Categorical Predictors, Model Comparison, Nonlinearity, and Robust Uncertainty



Table 9: Key terms of Chapter 9.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




ANCOVA (analysis of covariance)
A regression comparing groups while including a quantitative covariate with one common slope; its adjusted group means are read at a stated covariate value within common support. The posttest-only, gain-score and ANCOVA analyses are one regression whose pretest coefficient is 0, 1 or estimated; adjustment cannot supply what random assignment supplies.


Homogeneity of regression slopes (parallel slopes)
ANCOVA’s condition that the outcome–covariate slope is the same in every group, checked by testing the group-by-covariate product block; when the slopes differ, the adjusted difference depends on the covariate value at which it is read.


Nested-model \(F\) test (extra sum of squares; block test)
Compares a reduced model with a fuller one fitted to the same records and outcome: the RSS reduction per added coefficient, divided by the fuller model’s residual mean square, referred to \(F\) with the number of restrictions and the fuller model’s residual df. It tests the added block jointly, not each coefficient separately.


Information criteria (AIC; BIC)
Penalized in-sample fit: \(-2\log\widehat L\) plus \(2k\) (AIC) or \(k\log n\) (BIC), with \(k\) counting the coefficients and the residual variance. Smaller is preferred among models fitted to the same records and outcome scale; neither is held-out error.


Standardized coefficient (beta weight)
A partial slope rescaled by the predictor and outcome SDs, in outcome-SD units per predictor SD, with the other predictors held fixed. It differs from standardization over named profiles and does not measure causal importance.


Polynomial term (quadratic term; curvature)
A power of a predictor added as a further column so that the fitted mean can curve. The predictor’s comparison then depends on its value; centering before squaring reduces collinearity without changing the fitted curve.


Log-transformed outcome (geometric-mean scale)
Fitting the logarithm of the outcome, so that a coefficient is an additive difference in expected log outcome and \(100(e^{\beta}-1)\) percent is a multiplicative difference in geometric means. A changed outcome scale is a changed question, and its criteria are not comparable with the original scale’s.


Bootstrap (case resampling; percentile interval)
Refitting the model to many resamples of the records drawn with replacement and using the spread of the refitted estimates as an SE, or their middle 95% as a percentile interval. It treats the resampled units as independent and exchangeable; it does not repair dependence, thin support, measurement error, or an observational design.


Cluster-robust standard error (school-clustered covariance)
A coefficient covariance that sums residual contributions within clusters, such as schools, before combining them, allowing dependence within clusters under an approximation that treats clusters as independent. It changes uncertainty, not the coefficient, and does not repair missing outcomes or weighting.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
Chapter 10: Interaction and Moderation



Table 10: Key terms of Chapter 10.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Product term (interaction term; multiplicative term)
A column formed by multiplying predictors, so that a fitted comparison can depend on their values. A two-way product coefficient is a difference in slopes when no higher-order product makes that difference conditional, and nonadditivity is defined on the modeled scale: a nonlinear change of outcome scale can create or remove it.


Conditional slope (simple slope; conditional effect)
The fitted difference in outcome per one-unit difference in a focal predictor evaluated at stated values or groups of the other predictors. It is a linear combination of coefficients, so its SE uses their covariance, and it describes a conditional mean, not an individual case.


Moderator (moderating variable; moderation)
The variable across whose values or groups a named focal relationship is allowed to vary. The product-term algebra is symmetric in the two predictors, so the label comes from the research question; a moderation reading describes when a relationship differs, not how an effect is transmitted.


Hierarchy principle (marginality; well-formulated model)
The rule that a model containing a product retains its component terms and all lower-order products contained in it. Omitting them imposes restrictions tied to the coded origins; a three-way product therefore retains all three two-way products as well as the three component terms.


Centering a predictor (anchoring; reparameterization)
Replacing a predictor by its difference from a chosen value, so that coefficients anchored at zero become comparisons at that value. It changes the intercept and lower-order coefficients while preserving fitted values, residuals and tests of equivalent model restrictions. The highest-order product coefficient stays unchanged under a change of origin; lower-order product coefficients can change in a higher-order model. Centering repairs no design, selection, or measurement problem.


Probe value (pick-a-point value)
A stated value of the moderator at which a conditional slope or contrast is evaluated, chosen from the measurement scale, a threshold, or a decision need rather than by an automatic mean-and-SD rule, and restricted to values the records support.


Johnson–Neyman boundary (region of significance)
A moderator value at which a pointwise interval for a conditional slope touches zero, found as a root of a quadratic whose leading coefficient decides which side is the region. A boundary outside the observed support describes the algebra and not the data, and a pointwise band is not a simultaneous band.


Interaction contrast (difference in differences within a model)
A linear combination of coefficients comparing two conditional comparisons, such as one group’s difference minus another group’s difference. Under reference coding it equals a product coefficient up to sign; its SE uses the coefficient covariance, and its causal reading depends on design, not on the algebra.


Moderated moderation (three-way interaction; higher-order interaction)
A two-way interaction that changes across a second moderator. A hierarchical three-way model retains all component and two-way terms; conditional slopes depend on both moderators, and a direct contrast tests how the named interaction differs rather than comparing separate significance decisions.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
Chapter 11: Binary Logistic Regression



Table 11: Key terms of Chapter 11.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Event and non-event (the category coded 1)
The category a binary model treats as occurring, named together with the category coded 0. Reversing the event reciprocates the odds ratios and complements fitted event probabilities; probabilities for the original event agree after relabelling.


Prevalence (event rate)
The proportion of analytic rows that are events. Coefficient precision also depends on conditional probabilities, predictor spread and overlap; the rare-outcome approximation of an odds ratio by a risk ratio depends on the risks being compared.


Generalized linear model (GLM)
A response distribution, a linear predictor and a link connecting the conditional mean to the linear predictor; changing the response distribution and link gives the models of Chapters 11 and 12.


Link function; logit link and inverse logit (logistic function)
The logit is the log of the odds and its inverse the S-shaped function bounded in \((0,1)\), equal to one half and steepest at a linear predictor of zero.


Odds and log-odds
The odds are \(\pi/(1-\pi)\) and the log-odds their logarithm; the three scales describe one quantity with null values 1 and 0, and the log-odds scale is symmetric under reversing the event.


Odds ratio (OR)
The factor \(e^{\beta_j}\) by which the odds differ between units differing by one unit in a predictor and agreeing on the others; it depends on the units, reference, event and adjustment set, is not a risk ratio unless the event is rare, and implies no constant probability difference.


Noncollapsibility (of the odds ratio)
A conditional odds ratio generally differs from the marginal one even with no confounding, so a coefficient that moves under adjustment is not by itself evidence of confounding.


Likelihood and log-likelihood
The probability or density of the observed data under a declared model, viewed as a function of its parameters with the data fixed; the log-likelihood is its logarithm. It is not a probability distribution over the parameters.


Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
Choosing parameter values that maximize the likelihood, equivalently the log-likelihood, over the stated parameter space; near the maximum, the curvature of the log-likelihood gives the large-sample SE.


Bernoulli likelihood and score equations (binary-outcome likelihood)
The probability of the observed data as a function of the parameters, maximized to estimate them; for a binary outcome it is a product of Bernoulli probabilities whose score equations have no closed form, and a model with an intercept reproduces the observed event total.


Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)
The algorithm that repeatedly solves a weighted linear regression with weights \(\widehat\pi_i(1-\widehat\pi_i)\) until the coefficients stop changing; its convergence flag and iteration count belong in the record and establish no adequacy.


Deviance and the likelihood-ratio test (\(G^2\))
For ungrouped binary data the deviance is \(-2\) times the maximized log-likelihood and carries no goodness-of-fit reading alone, while the difference between nested models on the same rows and event is referred to chi-square.


Wald test and profile-likelihood interval
The Wald statistic squares the estimate-to-SE ratio while a profile interval collects the values the log-likelihood does not reject; they diverge for rare events, small samples or near-infinite estimates.


McFadden pseudo \(R^2\)
One minus the ratio of the fitted to the intercept-only maximized log-likelihood: bounded in \([0,1]\), not a proportion of variance explained, and routinely small for useful models.


Empirical logit
The log-odds of a grouped event count with one half added to each count, plotted against a predictor to check linearity of the log-odds in that predictor as entered.


Binned residual
The mean raw residual within a bin of rows sorted by fitted probability, against a two-standard-error band; it replaces the residual-versus-fitted plot, which shows only two curved bands here.


Separation (complete; quasi-complete)
A predictor pattern separates events from non-events completely or on a boundary, so at least one coefficient has no finite ordinary maximum-likelihood estimate. Diverging coefficients, large standard errors and convergence warnings can be symptoms; no one warning or numerical pattern is required.


In-sample calibration and discrimination checks (fitted-probability checks)
Calibration asks whether fitted probabilities match observed event frequencies, discrimination whether they rank events above non-events; the two answer distinct questions, and honest evaluation of new-case performance requires held-out data.


Linear probability model (LPM)
Ordinary least squares on a 0/1 outcome, whose coefficients are probability differences but whose mean function is unbounded and whose conditional variance cannot be constant.


Averaged probability difference (average marginal comparison)
The mean, over the analytic rows with their own other predictor values, of the difference between fitted probabilities at two values of one predictor.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 12: Extending the GLM: Nominal, Ordinal, and Count Outcomes
text:
Chapter 12: Extending the GLM: Nominal, Ordinal, and Count Outcomes



Table 12: Key terms of Chapter 12.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Outcome triage
The measurement judgment, made before any model is fitted, classifying an outcome as binary, nominal, ordered, a count, a rate, a proportion of known trials, or a duration. The model follows the classification and cannot establish it.


Generalized logit model (baseline-category logit; multinomial logistic regression)
For \(K\) unordered categories, \(K-1\) log-ratio equations against one baseline, each with its own intercept and slopes. The fitted probability surface is the same whichever baseline is chosen; the coefficients are not.


Baseline outcome category
The outcome category in the denominator of every generalized-logit equation: a coordinate choice, distinct from the reference level of a categorical predictor, whose change alters every reported ratio.


Relative-risk ratio (RRR)
The exponentiated generalized-logit coefficient: the factor by which one category’s probability relative to the baseline’s differs per predictor unit. It is not a probability difference, and is incomplete unless both compared categories are named.


Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA)
The generalized logit’s assumption that the ratio of two categories’ probabilities does not depend on which other categories were available: a claim about the choice set, argued rather than settled by one test.


Cumulative probability and cumulative logit
\(\gamma_{ij}=P(Y_i\le j)\) at each of the \(K-1\) cut points, and its log-odds. A category probability is a difference of two adjacent cumulative probabilities.


Threshold (cut point; ordinal intercept)
One of the ordered constants \(\zeta_1<\cdots<\zeta_{K-1}\) placing the cut points on the logit scale. Their ordering keeps fitted probabilities nonnegative; they are not comparisons and are not read as effects.


Proportional odds (common-slope restriction; partial proportional odds)
The restriction that one slope vector governs every cut point, so a single odds ratio applies at all of them. It is imposed by the analyst, not conferred by ordering the levels, and is testable against a cut-specific alternative.


Poisson regression (log-linear count model)
A GLM with a Poisson random component and a log link, so the conditional mean is positive and differences are multiplicative on the count scale. Its conditional variance is not free: it is forced to equal the mean.


Incidence-rate ratio (IRR; rate ratio)
For an ordinary log-link count or rate model, the exponentiated coefficient gives the factor by which the expected count, or rate with an exposure, differs per predictor unit. An absolute difference also requires its baseline. In a two-process model, a count-component coefficient alone does not give the overall mean ratio.


Exposure and offset
The window over which each unit was observed, and \(\log t_i\) entered with its coefficient fixed at one so the model describes a rate. An offset is a decision about the estimand, not an estimate: no SE, no \(p\)-value, and freeing its coefficient gives a testable alternative.


Overdispersion and the dispersion statistic
Conditional variance exceeding the conditional mean, assessed by the mean squared Pearson residual \(\widehat\phi\) under a suitable mean model; the deviance ratio is a rough diagnostic and need not be near 1 for sparse counts even under a correct Poisson model. The diagnosis is conditional; a marginal ratio above one is not evidence.


Quasi-Poisson (quasi-likelihood; scaled Poisson)
The Poisson mean with variance \(\phi\mu\): identical estimates and every SE multiplied by \(\sqrt{\widehat\phi}\). No full distribution is specified, so there is no log-likelihood and no AIC or BIC.


Negative-binomial regression
A count model with variance \(\mu+\mu^2/\theta\), arising when the Poisson mean varies across units sharing predictor values. A different likelihood, not a rescaling: estimates move because large fitted means are down-weighted, and the Poisson comparison sits on the boundary \(1/\theta=0\).


Zero-inflated model
A mixture of an extra-zero component and a count component that can also generate zeros. The count-component mean differs from the overall mean; an observed zero does not identify which component generated it, and fitted extra-zero membership does not establish a substantive structural-zero mechanism.


Hurdle model (two-part count model)
A binary model for zero versus a positive count combined with a zero-truncated count distribution for positive values. The overall mean combines the probability of a positive outcome with its positive-count mean. Its binary coefficient concerns crossing zero, which differs from membership in a zero-inflated model’s extra-zero component.


Zero-truncated count distribution
A count distribution conditioned on a positive outcome: its zero probability is removed and the positive probabilities are renormalized. Its mean is the original distribution’s mean divided by its probability of a positive count, so it differs from the untruncated mean parameter.

title: Part One Concept Reference
text:
Chapter 13: Prediction, Cross-Validation, and Regularization



Table 13: Key terms of Chapter 13.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Generalization error (prediction error; risk)
Expected loss on a new unit from the stated deployment distribution. It can be defined for one fitted model conditional on its training data, or averaged over training samples for a learning rule at a stated training size; held-out observations estimate the chosen target.


Deployment moment (prediction time)
The point at which a prediction must be produced, which decides whether a predictor is available. A variable recorded later may improve measured performance but cannot be used for that earlier prediction task.


Apparent error (training error; resubstitution error)
Loss on the records used to fit the rule. Using those outcomes in fitting generally makes this loss optimistic for new-case performance; greater fitting flexibility can increase that optimism, without guaranteeing an ordering in every sample or for every loss.


Root mean squared error (RMSE)
The square root of the mean squared prediction error, in outcome units. It penalizes a large error far more than MAE does, so the choice between them states which mistakes matter.


Out-of-sample \(R^2\)
One minus the held-out squared error divided by the held-out squared error of a named constant reference fitted in the same analysis rows. It can be negative and is not the in-sample \(R^2\) of Chapter 7.


Data leakage (information leakage)
Using information unavailable at the deployment moment, or letting held-out records influence a training or selection step used to predict them. It can make performance estimates optimistic; there is no general proportional rule for the size of that optimism.


Development and test split (holdout set)
A partition in which fitting, screening and tuning use the development records, while test outcomes remain protected until the rule is fixed. Adapting the rule after seeing test results uses the test set for development; repeating an unchanged calculation does not itself do so.


Penalized regression (shrinkage; ridge; lasso; elastic net)
Fitting that adds a coefficient penalty to the loss, trading bias against variance. Ridge’s squared penalty generally shrinks coefficients without selecting exact zeros; the lasso’s absolute-value penalty can set coefficients to zero, and elastic net combines the penalties.


Tuning parameter (penalty; \(\lambda\))
A quantity that indexes a family of fits and is chosen from data the fit did not see. Choosing it is itself a data-dependent step and belongs inside the resample.


One-standard-error rule
A convention choosing the largest penalty whose observed cross-validated loss is within the estimated standard error at the minimum. It prefers a simpler fit under that empirical tolerance; it does not bound the increase in true prediction error.


Proper scoring rule (log loss; Brier score)
A score for a predicted probability that is minimized in expectation by the true probability, so that honest uncertainty is rewarded. Accuracy and a single confusion matrix are not proper scores.


Calibration
Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event rates among cases with similar predictions. It is invisible in a ranking measure such as AUC and is checked on held-out predictions.


Discrimination (AUC; concordance)
The probability that a randomly chosen event case receives a higher score than a non-event case, with half credit for tied scores. It depends on ranking and does not establish calibration of the probabilities.


Decision threshold (operating point)
The predicted probability above which an action is taken, determined by the ratio of the costs of the two errors and not by the model. Two decision-makers with different costs read the same probabilities and act differently.


Dataset shift
A difference between the distributions in the development and use settings, potentially involving predictors, outcome frequencies or their relationship. Internal resampling alone does not establish performance in a different setting.

title: Part One Concept Reference
section: Chapter 14: Regression Pitfalls and Causal Design
text:
Chapter 14: Regression Pitfalls and Causal Design



Table 14: Key terms of Chapter 14.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Directed acyclic graph (causal diagram; DAG)
A diagram whose arrows state assumed direct causes and whose directed paths cannot return to their starting point; it records assumptions that can be questioned, rather than conclusions produced by the data.


Mediator (intermediate variable)
A variable caused by the focal predictor and lying on a path to the outcome; one kind of post-treatment variable, not a synonym for every variable measured after treatment. Conditioning on it changes a total-effect comparison; a direct causal reading needs additional identification and modelling conditions.


Collider (common effect)
A variable caused by two others. A path through a collider is blocked unless the collider or a descendant is conditioned on; such conditioning can induce an association along that path.


Adjustment set
The variables conditioned on for a stated estimand under an assumed structure, justified by that structure and the timing rather than by the available columns or a coefficient’s movement.


Aggregation reversal (Simpson’s paradox; strict Simpson reversal)
A sign difference between a pooled comparison and the stratified or standardized comparisons, strict when every stratum points the opposite way to the pooled result; it arises from composition, not from a computational error.


Within-group, between-group, and pooled comparison
Three estimands from one dataset: inside a level of the grouping variable, across group summaries, and across all rows ignoring the grouping, with the pooled slope a weighted average of the other two by the within and between shares of predictor variation.


Direct standardization (standardized comparison)
Recomputing each group’s summary under one declared common distribution of a stratifying variable; a third estimand rather than a compromise between the pooled and conditional comparisons.


Range restriction (restriction of range)
Keeping only part of the observed range; restricting the predictor under a correctly specified linear model costs precision, apparent strength and support outside the window, while restricting on the outcome also moves the slope.


Missingness mechanisms (MCAR; MAR; MNAR)
MCAR means missingness is unrelated to observed and missing values; MAR means it is unrelated to missing values conditional on observed information; MNAR means dependence on missing values remains. Complete-case validity depends on the target and mechanism, and MNAR requires assumptions not identified by the observed data alone.


Attenuation from measurement error
In a single-predictor linear model, classical predictor error multiplies the population slope by reliability. With several predictors the direction can differ; a mismeasured control can leave residual confounding.


Ecological inference (ecological fallacy)
Inferring an individual-level relationship from aggregate records. Aggregate and individual relationships can differ in sign and magnitude; the aggregate relationship alone does not identify the individual comparison.


Specification sensitivity (multiverse analysis; analyst degrees of freedom)
The spread of an estimate across the defensible analyses that could have been run; a disclosure about specification, not evidence about an omitted common cause, selection or measurement shared by every version.


Pseudoreplication (dependence as a design fact)
Treating dependent observations as independent replicates, misrepresenting uncertainty. The relevant dependence, sampling and assignment structure must be represented; its effect on a standard error depends on the comparison.


Identification argument (design warrant)
The explicit reasons a comparison estimates the intended causal quantity, whether assignment or a named quasi-experimental design with its stated assumption; naming a design is not meeting its assumption.


Bounded regression claim (credible-claim template)
A concluding statement whose unit, verb, conditioning set, supported range, design and disclosed sensitivity all match the analysis that produced it.
