The model without the three-way term leaves RSS 152 on 38 df and the full model 120 on 36, so
\[
F=\frac{(152-120)/(38-36)}{120/36}=4.8,
\]
with 2 and 36 df and \(p=.0142\), the A × B × C row. The denominator is again the larger model’s within-cell mean square, 3.3333, the same value as in the two-way analysis because every cell’s residuals are \(-2\), \(-1\), 1 and 2. The design is balanced, so the order of the factors in the formula leaves every row unchanged.
The three-way row says that the feedback-by-practice pattern differs between the timings, so the averaged two-way row describes neither timing. The practice changes within each timing show the pattern itself:

cell_means <- tapply(timing_data$score, list(timing_data$feedback,
  timing_data$practice, timing_data$timing), mean)
practice_change <- cell_means[, "Spaced", ] - cell_means[, "Massed", ]
practice_change
#>                      Right after practice One week later
#> Rereading                               2              0
#> Answer feedback                         2              4
#> Explanatory feedback                    2              8

tapply() with three grouping factors returns a three-way array of cell means, one feedback-by-practice table per timing; subtracting the Massed column from the Spaced column within each table gives the practice change for every feedback condition and timing. Right after practice spacing adds 2 points under every kind of feedback; one week later it adds 0, 4 and 8. Report these two patterns separately, as Chapter 4 recommends when a higher-order interaction is present.
One three-way contrast, declared in advance, is the change in Section 3.3’s difference of differences: Answer’s practice change minus Rereading’s, one week later minus right after practice, \((4-0)-(2-2)=4\). It combines eight cell means with coefficients \(\pm1\), each mean resting on four students, so
\[
SE=\sqrt{MS_E\,(8\times1/4)}=\sqrt{3.3333\times2}=2.5820,
\]
\(\sqrt2\) times the two-way contrast’s 1.8257. With \(t_{.975;36}=2.0281\), its pointwise 95% interval is \([-1.2365,9.2365]\) and \(p=.1301\). The 2-df three-way row rejects while this one declared direction does not: as in Section 3.3, the F test asks whether both three-way directions are zero jointly, and the other direction, Explanatory’s practice change minus Answer’s, also changes by 4 points between the timings. Neither result cancels the other, and a contrast chosen after seeing the table would need a family such as Scheffé’s.

title: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
text:
The Chi-Square Test
Not every outcome is a score. When each record falls into one category, such as completed or not, the data are counts in a table, and Chapter 3, Section 6, built the chi-square test of association for such a table. This section carries out that test in R, extends it to a table with more than two rows or columns, and sets out the scales on which the size of an association is stated.

The two-by-two table
Table 9 returns to Chapter 3’s invented completion example. It contains aggregate counts for 100 records, classified by learning format and completion. These records have no linkage to either score dataset above, and the counts themselves establish neither random allocation nor representative sampling.



Table 9: Authored completion counts for two learning formats.





Format
Completed
Not completed
Total




Online
32
18
50


In person
18
32
50


Total
50
50
100






Ask whether completion probability differs by format. The event is completion, and each format’s denominator is its 50 records. The null hypothesis is that format and completion are independent in the working population model, equivalently that the two formats share one completion probability. The test treats the records as independent units; if they were clustered within classes or repeated the same people, this uncertainty model would require modification. Constructing labelled counts prevents an accidental change in the event or group direction.
The matrix counts records the four cells in the displayed row and column order, with dimnames naming the rows and columns. Its row proportions and the independence test are

counts <- matrix(c(32, 18, 18, 32), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(Format = c("Online", "In person"),
    Result = c("Completed", "Not completed")))
prop.table(counts, margin = 1)
#>            Result
#> Format      Completed Not completed
#>   Online         0.64          0.36
#>   In person      0.36          0.64
chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)
#> 
#>  Pearson's Chi-squared test
#> 
#> data:  counts
#> X-squared = 7.84, df = 1, p-value = 0.005110261

margin = 1 divides each row by its own total. Completion rates are .64 for Online and .36 for In person, a difference of .28, or 28 percentage points, in the Online-minus-In-person direction. Under independence the fitted expected count in row \(j\), column \(k\) is
\[
E_{jk}=\frac{(\text{row }j\text{ total})
(\text{column }k\text{ total})}{N}.
\]
All four expected counts here equal \(50\times50/100=25\). Pearson’s statistic accumulates the squared discrepancies relative to those expected counts:
\[
X^2=\sum_{j,k}\frac{(O_{jk}-E_{jk})^2}{E_{jk}}
=4\left(\frac{7^2}{25}\right)=7.84.
\]
For a \(J\)-by-\(K\) table the usual independence reference has \((J-1)(K-1)\) degrees of freedom. Here \(df=1\) and p .0051. The observed Pearson statistic \(X^2\) is a number calculated from the table; \(\chi^2_1\) names its approximate reference distribution under the null model.
The Pearson residuals are \((O-E)/\sqrt E\): 1.4, \(-1.4\), \(-1.4\), 1.4 in row order. Their signs locate the pattern: more Online completions and fewer Online non-completions than the independence fit predicts, with the opposite departures for In person. Squaring and adding these residuals recovers \(X^2\). They are related through the table margins, so their signs do not constitute four independent cell tests.
The approximation concerns expected counts under the fitted null model, along with independent observational units and a sampling model appropriate to the table. Looking only at observed cell counts misses part of this check. Sparse expected cells may require an alternative reference or a more careful model. In the present example all expected counts are 25, supporting the ordinary chi-squared approximation under the stated unit model.
The test asks whether the two format probabilities are equal, and it estimates their common probability under the null, .5, from the full table. It does not establish that changing format would cause completion to change without relevant design information.


Larger tables
Nothing in Section 4.1’s calculation depends on the table having two rows and two columns. For a table with \(J\) rows and \(K\) columns, each expected count keeps the margins, \(E_{jk}=(\text{row }j\text{ total})
(\text{column }k\text{ total})/N\), and the Pearson residual of each cell and the statistic are
\[
r_{jk}=\frac{O_{jk}-E_{jk}}{\sqrt{E_{jk}}},\qquad
X^2=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{jk}^2,\qquad
df=(J-1)(K-1).
\]
The df count the cells that remain free once the margins are fixed.
A real example comes from a 1977 Canadian survey of 263 women, supplied as carData::Womenlf (Fox et al., 2022). Each woman’s labour-force participation is recorded as full-time work, part-time work or not working outside the home, and her household as having children or not. Both variables are recorded as categories, so the table needs no grouping choices. Does the distribution of participation differ between women with and without children at home?

d0 <- carData::Womenlf
work <- factor(d0$partic, levels = c("fulltime", "parttime", "not.work"),
  labels = c("Full-time", "Part-time", "Not working"))
children <- factor(d0$children, levels = c("absent", "present"),
  labels = c("No children", "Children"))
work_table <- table(children, work)
work_table
#>              work
#> children      Full-time Part-time Not working
#>   No children        46         7          26
#>   Children           20        35         129
round(prop.table(work_table, margin = 1), 4)
#>              work
#> children      Full-time Part-time Not working
#>   No children    0.5823    0.0886      0.3291
#>   Children       0.1087    0.1902      0.7011

factor() puts the participation categories in the order of the question and gives both variables readable labels; d0 keeps the supplied records unchanged. The row proportions show the pattern before any test: full-time work is the most common status for women without children at home and the least common for women with children, for whom not working outside the home is most common.

work_test <- chisq.test(work_table)
work_test
#> 
#>  Pearson's Chi-squared test
#> 
#> data:  work_table
#> X-squared = 65.945261, df = 2, p-value = 4.788158e-15
round(work_test$residuals, 2)
#>              work
#> children      Full-time Part-time Not working
#>   No children      5.88     -1.58       -3.01
#>   Children        -3.85      1.04        1.97

Here \(J=2\) and \(K=3\), so \(df=(2-1)(3-1)=2\), and the test gives \(X^2(2)=65.9453\) with \(p<.0001\). Every expected count is at least 12.616, so the chi-square reference is well supported. The residuals locate the departures from independence. The largest, \(r_{11}=5.8786\), is full-time work among women without children, and the signs reverse in the second row: women with children work full time less often and stay out of paid work more often than independence predicts. The residuals are tied together by the margins, so they are not six independent tests; a follow-up comparison of two cells is a new question that belongs to a declared family, as in Section 2.
The size of the association is read from the proportions and from an effect scale such as Cramér’s V of Section 4.3:
\[
V=\sqrt{\frac{X^2}{N\min(J-1,K-1)}}=\sqrt{\frac{65.9453}{263\times1}}=.5007,
\]
a strong association on its 0-to-1 scale. The p-value alone does not describe that size: larger samples can detect more modest associations. These are survey records, and the presence of children travels with other circumstances, such as age, the husband’s income and the cost of child care, so the table describes an association, not an effect of having children. Chapter 12 returns to these records with a model for the three participation categories.


Effect scales and alternative procedures
A chi-square test says whether the table departs from no association, not how large the association is or on which scale. Table 10 sets four common scales side by side for the completion table, with \(p_1\) the Online and \(p_0\) the In-person completion proportion, and gives the question that each one answers (Agresti, 2018).



Table 10: Four effect scales for the completion table, Online versus In person.











Scale
Definition
Value
What it answers




Difference in proportions
\(p_1-p_0\)
.2800
How many percentage points more often the event occurs in one group: an absolute gap


Risk ratio
\(p_1/p_0\)
1.7778
How many times as probable the event is in one group: a relative gap, which changes when the other outcome is called the event


Odds ratio
\(\dfrac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_0/(1-p_0)}\)
3.1605
How many times as large the odds of the event are; it stays the same when rows and columns exchange roles, so a design that samples on the outcome can still estimate it


Cramér’s V
\(\sqrt{\dfrac{X^2}{N\min(J-1,K-1)}}\)
.2800
How strong the association is, from 0 to 1, for a table of any size; it carries no direction and names no cell comparison






The same counts give a gap of 28 percentage points, a risk ratio of 1.7778 and an odds ratio of 3.1605. The odds ratio lies farther from 1 than the risk ratio because completion is common: Online’s completion odds are \(32/18=1.7778\) and In person’s are \(18/32=.5625\), so an odds ratio is not read as a risk ratio. Calling non-completion the event changes the risk ratio to \(.36/.64=.5625\) and the odds ratio to its reciprocal, .3164, so the event and the direction are named beside every scale. The balanced margins make Cramér’s V (Cramér, 1946) and the absolute difference in proportions coincide here; with other margins they generally differ.
For a larger table the first three scales compare one chosen pair of rows on one chosen event, such as full-time work among women without and with children at home, while Cramér’s V summarizes the whole table, as Section 4.2 computed for the participation table.
Other procedures change one part of the analysis while keeping the same table, and each answers its own question. The two-proportion interface gives a large-sample interval for the difference in proportions. For the Online-minus-In-person difference, .28, the uncorrected two-proportion procedure gives the approximate pointwise 95% interval [.0918, .4682], under independent binomial sampling within the two groups. It describes uncertainty about that difference, rather than about Online’s probability alone. A continuity correction changes the calibration of the Pearson statistic. Fisher’s exact test (Fisher, 1935) conditions on the table margins and uses an exact reference, which matters when expected counts are small. These procedures answer different uncertainty questions for the same counts. Keep the event, comparison and reference model explicit when choosing among them.

title: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
text:
Numerical Optimization
The fitted means of Sections 1 and 3 were chosen by a criterion: least squares, which makes the sum of squared deviations as small as possible. Numerical optimization searches over candidate values to find the minimum or maximum of a stated function. We begin with a function whose best value can also be found exactly, then return to least squares.

Finding the peak of a parabola
Figure 5 shows the parabola \(y=15+10x-2x^2\). Its peak lies at \(x=2.5\), where \(y=27.5\). How can such a point be found systematically? Finding the maximum or minimum of a function is an optimization problem. For this smooth curve, calculus gives the answer exactly: the slope of the curve, \(10-4x\), is positive to the left of 2.5, zero there and negative to the right, so the curve rises to its peak and then falls. A numerical search finds the same point without that algebra, which matters when a criterion has no convenient formula.

parabola <- function(x) 15 + 10 * x - 2 * x^2
peak <- optimize(parabola, interval = c(-2, 5), maximum = TRUE)
c(x = peak$maximum, y = peak$objective)
#>    x    y 
#>  2.5 27.5

parabola() returns the height of the curve at any \(x\). optimize() searches one argument over the stated interval; maximum = TRUE asks for the largest value, where the default looks for the smallest. It returns the location of the optimum, maximum, and the function’s value there, objective: here 2.5 and 27.5.








Figure 5: The parabola \(y=15+10x-2x^2\) over the search interval from \(-2\) to 5, with its peak at \(x=2.5\), \(y=27.5\).





The same search applies to any criterion that can be evaluated at a candidate value. Fitting a model reverses the roles of data and parameters: the observations stay fixed, the candidate parameter value changes, and the criterion scores each candidate.


Least squares for one center
The fitted means in Section 1 were chosen by a rule: minimize the sum of squared deviations from the observations. We can inspect this rule with the ten Silence scores, 8, 9, 9, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15 and 16. These observations stay fixed. What changes is the proposed center, denoted by \(c\).
An objective function assigns a numerical criterion to each candidate parameter value for fixed data. For a center fitted by least squares, the objective is
\[
Q(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{10}(y_i-c)^2
     =(8-c)^2+(9-c)^2+\cdots+(16-c)^2.
\]
At \(c=12\), the deviations are the Silence residuals of Section 1, and their squares sum to 66 squared score points. At either 11 or 13, they sum to 76. The sample mean minimizes this criterion; here it is 12 points. A numerical search lets us reproduce the minimizing value without writing it into the fitting instruction.

silence <- subset(sound_data, sound == "Silence")$score
loss <- function(center) sum((silence - center)^2)
mean_fit <- optimize(loss, interval = range(silence))
c(center = mean_fit$minimum, squared_loss = mean_fit$objective)
#>       center squared_loss 
#>           12           66

The function loss() evaluates the squared-loss criterion at a proposed center. optimize() searches over \([8,16]\), which contains the sample mean. This smooth bowl has one minimum to locate. Changing the candidate center changes the criterion value while keeping all ten scores fixed.
The two returned quantities have different meanings. minimum is the parameter location, 12 points; objective is the function value there, 66 squared points. The latter is a sum of squared deviations, Silence’s contribution to \(SS_W\) in Section 1, rather than an SE or an estimate of the mean. The search interval also belongs to the fitting instruction: excluding the best center would restrict which answer the search could return. Numerical accuracy concerns how closely the search locates that answer; statistical uncertainty concerns what an estimate would do across the repetitions justified by the study.
Figure 6 draws this objective for many candidate centers. The horizontal axis gives a proposed center in score points, and the vertical axis gives its squared loss. Each point on the curve answers a fitting question for the same ten observations. The bottom of the bowl is the best center according to this criterion.

curve(sapply(x, loss), from = 8, to = 16,
  xlab = "Candidate center", ylab = "Squared loss")









Figure 6: The search interval changes the permitted answer, while the data and squared-loss curve stay fixed.





Predict, then explain. Suppose the search is restricted to \([13,16]\). Which center can it return, and have the scores changed? The right panel retains the same curve but permits only centers at least 13. Loss rises through that interval, so the exact constrained minimum is its left endpoint, 13, with loss 76. The unrestricted mean 12 is excluded. The objective and the permitted parameter values jointly determine the answer, even though the observations stay fixed.
A more accurate numerical search can locate the permitted minimum more closely. It cannot make ten students into a larger sample or make their mean more representative of a population. These least-squares identities are arithmetic; an uncertainty statement for the fitted mean adds a model or design and its conditions.

title: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
text:
Simulation and Planning
The preceding analyses started with observed data and produced estimates, intervals and tests. We can also begin with a declared generating model, create data from it, and examine what an analysis does over repeated studies. Here the questions concern an omnibus ANOVA procedure and the sample size for a specified comparison.

One generated study and its repetition
Imagine three independent groups whose outcomes follow Normal distributions, each with standard deviation \(\sqrt{10/3}=1.8257\) points. First set all three population means to 8, so that the equal-means null hypothesis is true; later the unequal means 6, 8 and 10 describe an alternative. These values borrow the scale of the feedback study in Section 3, whose Massed cells have means 6, 8 and 10 with four students each and whose factorial fit has residual mean square \(10/3\). They define a hypothetical world in which we know the truth; the constructed scores do not establish that this generating model describes real students.
Begin with four observations per group and analyse one generated study.

set.seed(60630)
n_per_group <- 4
sim_group <- factor(rep(1:3, each = n_per_group))
sim_score <- rnorm(3 * n_per_group,
  mean = rep(c(8, 8, 8), each = n_per_group), sd = sqrt(10 / 3))
anova(lm(sim_score ~ sim_group))

Sum Sq
Mean Sq
F value
Pr(>F)




sim_group

1.036520926
0.3934504588


Residuals

The twelve outcomes are drawn from populations with the stipulated common mean and SD. The seed fixes the illustrated draw. Fitting one mean per group and comparing it with a common mean gives 2 group degrees of freedom and \(12-3=9\) error degrees of freedom. For these generated data, \(SS_B=7.5977\) and \(SS_W=32.9851\), giving \(F=1.0365\) and \(p=.3935\). Applying the rule \(p<.05\) therefore does not reject the equal-means null in this study. Although the three generating means are identical, the three sample means vary, so the between-group sum of squares is positive. The estimated error variance, \(MS_W=3.665\), also varies around the generating variance \(10/3\).








Figure 7: One study contributes one p-value to the repeated results. The shaded first bin contains p-values below .05; the panels use different count scales.





The loops below repeat the one-study calculation 2,000 times under each generating model, starting again from seed 60630, and the result table first_p records one p-value and generating-model label per simulated study. Its graphical comparison is

set.seed(60630)
B <- 2000
null_mean <- rep(c(8, 8, 8), each = 4)
alternative_mean <- rep(c(6, 8, 10), each = 4)
null_p <- numeric(B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  sim_score <- rnorm(12, mean = null_mean, sd = sqrt(10 / 3))
  null_p[b] <- anova(lm(sim_score ~ sim_group))[1, "Pr(>F)"]
}
alternative_p <- numeric(B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  sim_score <- rnorm(12, mean = alternative_mean, sd = sqrt(10 / 3))
  alternative_p[b] <- anova(lm(sim_score ~ sim_group))[1, "Pr(>F)"]
}
models <- c("Equal means: 8, 8, 8", "Unequal means: 6, 8, 10")
first_p <- data.frame(p = c(null_p, alternative_p),
  model = rep(models, each = B))
ggplot(first_p, aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .05, boundary = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, scales = "free_y")

One generated study cannot describe a procedure’s long-run behaviour. Repeating the same calculation many times gives a collection of p-values to compare with .05. In Figure 7, the dashed line marks the .3935 from the study we just followed. That study contributes one p-value to the left-hand distribution; each additional study supplies another. The shaded first bin counts rejections. With equal generating means, 112 of the 2,000 studies reject, giving .056. With means 6, 8 and 10, 1,309 reject, giving .6545. The latter fraction estimates power for this alternative. The vertical scales differ, so compare the fractions of studies in the first bin, not the bars’ physical heights.
Table 11 reports 2,000 studies for each of four conditions. The null conditions use means \((8,8,8)\); the alternative conditions use \((6,8,10)\). Each condition retains independent Normal observations and the same common SD. To reproduce the results, restart at seed 60630 for the repeated studies, then generate 2,000 studies under each condition in this order: null and alternative at four students per group, then null and alternative at twelve. The doubled-SD null and alternative at four per group, discussed below, follow those four blocks without resetting the seed. The preceding one-study illustration is separate from this restart.



Table 11: Operating characteristics in the declared generating models, \(B=2000\) studies per condition.












Students per group
Null rejection rate
MCSE
Power at means 6/8/10
MCSE




4
.056
0.0051
.6545
0.0106


12
.050
0.0049
.9990
0.0007






The null rejection rate estimates the Type I error probability: how often this .05 omnibus procedure rejects when all three population means are equal. Both estimated rates are close to .05. The power column estimates the probability of rejecting that same null under the specified unequal means. It rises from .6545 with four students per group to .9990 with 12. This is power against the particular means 6, 8 and 10, with the stated spread and independence; a smaller separation would give different power.
Each rate is itself an estimate based on finitely many repetitions. If \(\widehat q\) is a simulated rejection proportion from \(B\) independent studies, its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is
\[
MCSE(\widehat q)=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat q(1-\widehat q)}{B}}.
\]
For the estimated power .6545, it is \(\sqrt{.6545(1-.6545)/2000}=0.0106\), and the table’s MCSE columns apply the same formula to each rate. This value describes the numerical uncertainty from using 2,000 simulations: a fresh set of 2,000 simulated studies can give a somewhat different power estimate. The MCSE is distinct from a student outcome’s SD or the SE of a group mean or contrast within one study. A rate very close to one, such as .999, also deserves care: only two of the 2,000 studies failed to reject, so its tiny plug-in MCSE rests on very few non-rejections.
Increasing study size \(n\) changes the information within a study, its error degrees of freedom and its ability to detect the specified difference. Increasing the number of repetitions \(B\) makes the simulated rate more precise; it leaves the study being simulated unchanged. Simulation describes a procedure under the declared model; agreement with its expected behaviour does not establish that the model fits a particular real study.
Change the spread, keeping the comparison. Before running another set of studies, predict what happens if the common SD doubles from 1.8257 to 3.6515 points, while the population means, four students per group, independence, Normality and .05 test rule stay the same. Under the null, both the between-group and within-group variation rise together; the F reference remains appropriate. Under the alternative, the mean differences are smaller relative to the noise, so we expect less power. The final two blocks in the sequence specified above give a null rejection rate of .0525, with MCSE 0.005, and power .2165, with MCSE 0.0092. Compare the latter with .6545 under the original SD. More repetitions would estimate this lower power more precisely; they would not restore the information lost through greater within-group variation. The change preserves the equal-variance condition. It compares two hypothetical population spreads rather than establishing which one describes real students.


Planning power and precision
The omnibus simulation asks whether some population group means differ. A future study may instead be planned to estimate or detect one particular difference. Consider a future balanced one-factor study of the three feedback conditions, with a declared two-comparison Bonferroni family: Answer feedback versus Rereading, and Explanatory feedback versus Rereading. The family has the same form as Section 2’s two comparisons with Silence. Keep it, with family significance level .05, even when calculating power for just one of its comparisons.
Suppose the comparison of interest has a population difference of \(\delta=2\) points. Plan equal group sizes \(n\), independent Normal outcomes and common SD \(\sigma=\sqrt{10/3}\), the square root of the factorial fit’s residual mean square in Section 3. The planning SE for a difference of two group means is \(\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\). All three groups contribute to the pooled error variance, so its degrees of freedom are \(3(n-1)\), even though the contrast compares only two of the means.
Bonferroni assigns two-sided significance level \(.05/2=.025\) to each comparison. Dividing that amount between its two tails puts .0125 in each tail. The rejection cutoffs are therefore \(-c\) and \(c\), where
\[
c=t_{1-.05/(2\times2),\,3(n-1)}=t_{.9875,\,3(n-1)}.
\]
Under the zero-difference null, the test statistic has the central \(t\) distribution already used for the comparison. Under a specified nonzero difference, its distribution moves towards that difference. The noncentral \(t\) distribution describes this statistic when its numerator has a nonzero mean and its denominator still estimates the common spread. Its noncentrality parameter expresses the population difference in planning SE units:
\[
\lambda=\frac{\delta}{\sigma\sqrt{2/n}}.
\]
For this alternative, power is the area beyond the same two rejection cutoffs: \(P(T<-c)+P(T>c)\) for a noncentral \(t\) variable with \(3(n-1)\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality \(\lambda\). These are probabilities over future studies, rather than a p-value from observed data. Both tails belong to the two-sided procedure, even when the planning difference is positive.

error_df <- 3 * (17 - 1)
critical <- qt(1 - .05 / 4, df = error_df)
ncp <- 2 / sqrt((10 / 3) * 2 / 17)
pt(-critical, df = error_df, ncp = ncp) +
  pt(critical, df = error_df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE)

At \(n=17\), the planning SE is 0.6262, the error degrees of freedom are 48, the critical value is 2.3139, and \(\lambda=3.1937\). Summing the two tail areas gives power .8073. Checking successive integer sizes gives 17 students per group, 51 in total, as the first size reaching .8 power; 16 gives .7793. Tested alone at two-sided .05, the same comparison would need only 14 per group (power .8068), against 17 inside the family: that is the power price of the family guarantee.
This is the power of one specified comparison within the declared family. It is neither the probability that both comparisons reject nor the power of the omnibus F test. For example, with 12 students per group the specified two-point comparison has power .6328, whereas the omnibus simulation in Table 11 gives estimated power .9990 against the complete pattern \((6,8,10)\). The hypotheses and rejection rules differ, so these numbers answer different questions.
A precision target concerns the interval’s width rather than its probability of excluding zero. Suppose the aim is a simultaneous interval whose planned half-width is no more than one point. The family and degrees of freedom stay the same, giving
\[
\text{planned half-width}
=t_{.9875,\,3(n-1)}\,\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}.
\]
This calculation substitutes the planning SD \(\sigma\) for the error SD that the future study will estimate. The planned half-width is 1.0078 points at 34 per group and 0.9929 at 35, so 35 per group, or 105 students in total, is the first size meeting this target. The realised interval uses the observed \(\sqrt{MS_W}\) and therefore has a random width. Choosing 35 does not guarantee that its half-width will be at most one in every study. Figure 8 shows why a power target and an interval-width target can select quite different sample sizes.








Figure 8: Power and planned interval width impose different sample-size targets.





Finally, distinguish the desired number of available outcomes from the number recruited. If outcomes are expected to be available for 90% of recruits, the 17-per-group power target needs \(\lceil17/.9\rceil=19\) recruits per group, 57 in total, with an expected 17.1 available outcomes per group under that retention assumption. It is an average allowance, not a guarantee of 17 outcomes in every group or a correction for bias from systematically missing outcomes.
A two-group power calculation declares a different study, with different error degrees of freedom, and cannot silently replace this three-group calculation. Choose a planning difference from the substantive question and relevant prior evidence. Selecting statistically significant results can favour exaggerated estimates; an observed difference from such a selection is not automatically a suitable planning alternative.

title: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
text:
Reading Bridge
Each section used one framework, which later chapters carry further:

A model for the records, with parameters to read: the group means and indicators (Section 1), two-way and three-way models (Section 3), the independence model for a table (Section 4) and declared generating model (Section 6.1).
A fitting criterion: least squares for means (Sections 1.2 and 5.2), found by a numerical search that first located the peak of a parabola (Section 5.1).
A comparison of named models on the same records: one mean against three (Section 1.3), additive and full models and the sequence behind a two-way table (Section 3.2), the three-way model against all two-way interactions (Section 3.4), and each simulated omnibus test (Section 6.1).
A comparison family and an effect scale: pointwise, Bonferroni, Tukey and Scheffé intervals (Sections 2 and 3.3), and four categorical scales for two-by-two and larger tables (Section 4.3).
Behaviour under repetition: rejection rates, power and planned width under stated generating models (Section 6).

When reading a study, identify the question, analysed records, model, estimate and uncertainty procedure before judging their adequacy. Keep a comparison’s direction, history and family beside its interval; a table’s event and effect scale beside its estimate; and generating assumptions and the specified procedure beside any simulation or planning result.
Chapter 7 carries the framework from group means to a line: squared loss for an intercept and slope, the normal equations and projection, and uncertainty for slope and fitted mean. Chapter 8 carries it to several predictors, named controls and the overall F as a comparison of models. Chapter 9 generalizes indicators to factors with several levels, gives the fuller nested-model F with block tests, and develops analysis of covariance in Section 2, using Section 3.2’s comparison for parallel slopes. Chapter 11 introduces likelihood with binary regression, and its Appendix A develops maximum likelihood estimation, exact boundary estimates, multiple-parameter fitting, starting values and convergence checks.

Key terms and notation
The following concepts connect the chapter’s models, fitting criteria and comparisons.



Table 12: Selected concepts introduced or developed here.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Model formula (R formula)
Notation such as score ~ group naming an outcome and the variables that explain it for a fitting function. It does not state whether observations are independent or paired; that comes from the design.


Categorical effect scales (difference in proportions; risk ratio; odds ratio; Cramér’s V)
Four ways to state the size of an association in a table, each answering its own question: the difference in proportions gives an absolute gap, the risk ratio a relative gap, the odds ratio a ratio of odds that stays the same when rows and columns exchange roles, and Cramér’s V a unit-free strength, from 0 to 1, for a table of any size.


Objective function
A numerical criterion evaluated at candidate parameter values for fixed data; fitting seeks a stated minimum or maximum.






The notation follows the local question. \(C=\sum_jc_j\mu_j\) is a contrast, and Type II error probability \(\beta\) differs from a model coefficient such as \(\beta_x\). Observed Pearson \(X^2\) differs from the reference distribution \(\chi^2\), and \(\Delta p=p_1-p_0\) is a difference in proportions. Section 6.1 distinguishes study size \(n\) from repetitions \(B\), and an estimator’s SE from finite-simulation MCSE.


Further reading
For the linear-model basis of ANOVA, contrasts and nested-model comparisons, see Kutner et al. (2005). Tukey (1953) develops simultaneous comparison ideas, and Agresti (2018) develops the chi-square test and the effect scales for two-way tables. Cohen (1988) discusses power and the dependence of a planning result on its chosen effect and procedure, and Çetinkaya-Rundel & Hardin (2024) develops the simulation-based treatment of operating characteristics used in Section 6. R’s documentation gives the arguments and returned components for aov, lm, TukeyHSD, oneway.test, chisq.test and optimize (R Core Team, 2025). The plotting chapters of Wickham et al. (2023) develop the data, mapping and layer vocabulary behind the chapter’s figures.

title: Group Comparisons and Statistical Modelling with R
text:
Exercises
The chapter’s printed output, tables and figures supply the values each exercise reads, with a calculator for the few calculations that the reasoning needs. State the records, working conditions and comparison direction in each interpretation.


Exercise 1: Read the one-way fit from its output
For the thirty background-sound scores, anova(one_fit) reports sums of squares 80 and 178 on 2 and 27 df, \(F=6.0674\) and \(p=.0067\), and coef(indicator_fit) returns 12, \(-2\) and \(-4\) with Silence as the reference level.

Say what each sum of squares measures in these scores, and why Instrumental music, whose mean equals the grand mean of 10, adds nothing to the between-group sum of squares although its ten scores vary.
Explain what the within-group df, 27, count, and why \(F\) divides by the residual mean square, 6.5926, rather than by the variance of all thirty scores, \(258/29=8.8966\).
State the equal-means null, and interpret \(p=.0067\) under the working model, including what the result leaves unanswered about particular pairs of conditions.
Predict the three coefficients if Instrumental music were made the reference level, and say which parts of the ANOVA output would change.





Exercise 2: Keep the comparison and its family together
Instrumental music minus Silence is \(-2\) points with SE 1.1483 on 27 df. Its 95% interval is \([-4.3561, 0.3561]\) when the comparison stands alone, \([-4.7253, 0.7253]\) inside the declared family of the two comparisons with Silence (Bonferroni) and \([-4.8470, 0.8470]\) inside the family of all three pairs (Tukey).

The estimate and SE are the same in all three intervals. Explain why the limits differ, naming the family that each interval protects.
Explain why the SE uses 27 residual df, although the comparison involves only the twenty students in two conditions.
An analyst reports Music with lyrics minus Silence, \(-4\) points, because it is the largest of the three observed differences. Say which family its interval should come from, and why.
The omnibus F rejected equal means, yet all three intervals above include zero. Explain why these results are compatible, and why an interval that includes zero does not show that the two means are equal.





Exercise 3: Read interaction as a change in comparison
In the 24-student feedback-by-practice study, the Massed and Spaced cell means are 6 and 6 for Rereading, 8 and 12 for Answer feedback and 10 and 18 for Explanatory feedback, and the full two-way model gives the interaction test \(F(2,18)=9.6\), \(p=.0015\).

Give the three Spaced-minus-Massed changes, and say what the nonparallel lines of the interaction plot show and what they cannot show without a model.
The practice margins are 8 and 12. Explain why the 4-point practice main effect needs the interaction beside it when a reader asks how spaced practice works.
The study plan declared one difference of differences in advance: Answer feedback’s change minus Rereading’s change, 4 points with SE 1.8257 and pointwise 95% interval \([0.1643, 7.8357]\). Had the same contrast been picked after inspecting the plot, its Scheffé interval over the two-dimensional interaction family, \([-0.8680, 8.8680]\), would apply. Explain how that interval can include zero while the interaction F test rejects, and why the declared history warrants the pointwise interval.
Answer feedback’s simple practice effect is also 4 points, with SE 1.291. Explain why its SE is smaller and why the interaction family’s guarantee does not cover it.





Exercise 4: Name the two models behind an interaction test
The interaction test for the 24 feedback/practice scores compares two models fitted to the same students: the additive model, with residual sum of squares 124 on 20 df, and the full factorial model, with 60 on 18 df.

Name the two models and say what the larger one adds.
The comparison gives \(F=9.6\) on 2 and 18 df. Explain why its denominator comes from the full model rather than the additive model.
After the two Explanatory-Spaced students scoring 19 and 20 are removed, the sequential sums of squares for feedback and practice change with the order of the formula, yet the comparison of the additive and full models gives \(F(2,16)=5.7426\) in either order. Explain why.
Say what a nonsignificant result of this comparison would and would not show about additivity.





Exercise 5: Preserve the event, denominator and expected counts
In the invented table, Online has 32 completions and 18 non-completions; In person has 18 completions and 32 non-completions. Pearson’s test gives \(X^2=7.84\) on 1 df and \(p=.0051\). For Section 4.2’s participation table of 263 women, it gives \(X^2=65.9453\) on 2 df, with Cramér’s \(V=.5007\).

State the null hypothesis and the denominator of each completion proportion, .64 and .36, for the two-by-two test.
Calculate the expected count of Online completions under independence, and explain why the chi-squared approximation is checked against expected rather than observed counts.
The difference in proportions is .28, the risk ratio 1.7778 and the odds ratio 3.1605. Explain why the odds ratio lies farther from 1 than the risk ratio here. Cramér’s V also equals .28; explain why their equality here does not make the measures interchangeable in general.
Explain why the participation table has 2 df, why its p-value alone does not describe the size of the association, and what design information a claim that children at home reduce full-time work would additionally need.





Exercise 6: Distinguish study size, repetitions and planning targets
In the chapter’s simulation, each condition repeats 2,000 generated studies of three Normal groups with common SD \(\sqrt{10/3}\) and applies the .05 omnibus ANOVA. With equal means \((8,8,8)\) the rejection rates are .056 at four students per group and .050 at twelve; with means 6, 8 and 10 the estimated power is .6545 at four and .9990 at twelve.

Say what the rejection rates under equal means estimate, and explain why the power rises from four to twelve students per group while those rates stay near .05.
The Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) of the power estimate .6545 with \(B=2000\) is 0.0106. Say what it measures, and why it differs from the SE of a contrast within one simulated study.
Predict what quadrupling \(B\) to 8,000 would do to this MCSE and to the power that the simulation estimates.
For the declared two-comparison family, 17 students per group first reach power .8 for a 2-point comparison, and 35 per group first reach a planned simultaneous half-width of at most one point. Say what each target controls, and why a realised interval can have a different width from its planning value.





Exercise 7: Distinguish an estimate from its fitting criterion
Keep the ten Silence scores of Section 5.2 fixed. Minimizing their squared loss with optimize() over \([8,16]\) returns minimum 12 and objective 66; at a center of 11 or 13 the loss is 76.

Say which returned value is the parameter estimate and which is the criterion value, and why 66 is neither an SE nor a variance of the mean.
For the parabola of Section 5.1, the slope of \(y=15+10x-2x^2\) is \(10-4x\). Use its sign to explain why the maximum lies at \(x=2.5\), and say which argument of optimize() asks for a maximum.
Before calculating, predict how the best center and the minimum loss would change if every Silence score appeared twice, 20 records in all. Then compare your prediction with the result: the center stays 12 and the minimum loss is 132.
Restricted to \([13,16]\), the exact constrained optimum is the endpoint 13, with loss 76; a default optimize() search returns about 13.0001 and 76.0015. Explain why a more accurate search cannot return 12, and why neither result says how precisely the center estimates a population mean.





Exercise 8: Write a qualified result paragraph
Choose the one-way comparisons, the declared interaction contrast or the two-group count comparison from this chapter. Write a short paragraph giving the question, data and denominator, estimate, interval and its family or pointwise status, working conditions and scope. Identify one tempting claim that the numerical result does not establish, and explain the missing support.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
NoteChapter overview



One set of records can owe several answers, and multiple regression is the model behind most of them. This chapter first writes the multiple regression model, says what a partial slope compares, and draws a simulated process with two predictors. It then fits the model to the 98 occupations of Chapter 7 that have a recorded type, attaches uncertainty to the education slope and checks the model, computes a fitted profile and an average over named profiles, and compares two prediction rules on held-out occupations. It closes with a short report that owes three answers, a marginal description, a conditional association and a prediction comparison, and reads and evaluates them. By the end you will be able to write, fit and read an additive multiple regression in R, keep changes of records, comparison, coefficient coordinates and uncertainty calculation apart, judge a held-out comparison, and evaluate coordinated answers without merging them.
A report on occupational income may ask whether education and income move together, whether that relationship remains when other characteristics of the occupations are held constant, and whether those characteristics help predict income. The questions inform one another, but answering one does not answer the other two.
We use a retrospective teaching study written for this chapter. Its records are the Prestige data distributed with the carData package (Fox et al., 2022; Fox & Weisberg, 2019), whose documentation describes the data; the analyses and the short report are ours.
A simple regression models an outcome with one predictor, \(Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i\). Multiple regression keeps that form and adds one term for each further predictor.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Model Formulation and Interpretation

The population and observation forms
With several predictors, the model for an outcome is
\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}+\varepsilon,
\]
\[
E(\varepsilon\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=\sigma^2;
\]
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{i,p-1}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
The part \(\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}\) is the mean of \(Y\) among units that share those predictor values, and the error \(\varepsilon\) collects everything else. The model has \(p\) coefficients, counting the intercept. \(\beta_0\), the intercept, is the mean when every predictor is zero; it anchors the equation and describes real units only if that combination is plausible within the data. \(\beta_j\), a partial slope, is the difference in the mean of \(Y\) for a one-unit difference in \(x_j\), holding the other predictors fixed. \(\sigma\) is the typical spread of outcomes around the mean at fixed predictor values. The conditions apply at every combination of predictor values: the errors average zero and share one variance \(\sigma^2\); they are independent of one another, which comes from how the data arose; and for the exact \(t\) reference they are Normal. The intervals used here require independent errors, the classical SE also needs the common variance, and the exact \(t\) also needs Normal errors; the HC3 covariance of Section 3.3 relaxes the common variance under its own large-sample conditions.
Under the Normal-error model, \(Y_i\) at its fixed predictor values is Normal with mean \(\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\beta_jx_{ij}\) and SD \(\sigma\). Estimating \(p\) coefficients leaves \(n-p\) residual degrees of freedom. A factor with \(J\) categories contributes \(J-1\) indicator columns, as Section 2.3 explains using the occupation records.


What a partial slope compares
Take two predictors, \(x\) and \(z\). The model mean is \(\mu(x,z)=\beta_0+\beta_Xx+\beta_Zz\). Comparing two means a unit apart in \(x\) at the same \(z\) gives
\[
\mu(x+1,z)-\mu(x,z)=\beta_X(x+1)-\beta_Xx=\beta_X.
\]
All the shared terms cancel. Holding constant names this comparison of model means; it does not mean that \(x\) was changed experimentally, that two observed units match on everything else, or that unmeasured differences have been controlled. A partial slope’s meaning belongs to its named conditioning set. The same predictor can have a different coefficient when a different set is held fixed. The additive form also makes its comparison the same at every value of the other predictors; Chapter 10 asks when that comparison itself varies.
Partial correlation holds variables fixed another way, by residualizing: it removes their fitted linear parts from two variables before correlating what remains. A fitted equation with several predictors holds the others fixed directly, because two of its fitted means that differ in one predictor share every other term; Section 3.1 shows that the two routes give the same slope. Chapter 9, Section 2, applies the same idea to adjusted group means in the analysis of covariance.


Simulating and graphing a two-predictor model
A known process makes the comparison concrete. Suppose
\[
Y=50+2X+5Z+\varepsilon,
\qquad E(\varepsilon\mid X,Z)=0,
\]
with finite variances and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)/\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.65\). The conditional \(X\) coefficient is 2, and the marginal linear slope is
\[
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
=2+5\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
=2+5(0.65)=5.25.
\]
Generate independent standard Normal values \(X\) and \(U\), let \(Z=.65X+\sqrt{1-.65^2}U\), and add independent Normal errors with SD 6. Both predictors then have variance one and correlation .65. Figure 1 draws one generated sample of 250 cases from this process, with the process’s own mean lines rather than fitted ones. Each solid line holds \(Z\) at one value and rises 2 for each unit of \(X\). The dashed marginal line rises 5.25, because higher \(X\) comes with higher \(Z\) (the darker points sit toward the upper right) and the marginal line carries that association along.








Figure 1: One generated sample from the known process, with its marginal line and three lines at fixed \(Z\).





With these generated columns named x, z and y in sim, the following calls estimate the marginal and conditional equations. The short examples throughout this chapter show the statistical operation on the data just described.

coef(lm(y ~ x, data = sim))
coef(lm(y ~ x + z, data = sim))

In this sample the fitted \(X\) coefficient is 3.0259 (SE 0.5325), the \(Z\) coefficient 4.3991 (SE 0.5282), and the marginal slope 5.9971 (SE 0.4466). Each lies within two SEs of its programmed value, 2, 5, and 5.25 respectively. A single sample estimates the process rather than reproducing its parameters exactly.
Mapping x and y to position and z to colour draws the points in Figure 1. The fitted slopes and the known process lines answer related but distinct questions.

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(sim, aes(x, y, colour = z)) + geom_point()

The two slopes answer different questions: one holds \(Z\) fixed, the other includes how \(Z\) moves with \(X\), and neither alone says what would happen if someone intervened on \(X\). Calling 5.25 “biased” requires naming the target it is used for; as the marginal linear slope it is correct. Appendix A gives the derivation and the repeated samples.

section: Estimating the Model on the Occupation Records
text:
Estimating the Model on the Occupation Records

The records and the working model
A row is an occupation, not a worker. Income is the occupation’s average annual income in 1971 Canadian dollars, divided here by 1,000; education is average years of education; women is the percentage of women; prestige is a rating from a mid-1960s survey, earlier than the 1971 income and education; and type is blue-collar (bc), professional/managerial/technical (prof), or white-collar (wc). These historical occupational averages are not current individual earnings.
Chapter 7 used all 102 occupations. The full variable set leaves 98 complete records, because athletes, newsboys, babysitters, and farmers have no recorded type; the three types keep 44, 31, and 23 records. We keep the source row order, which also makes the validation split of Section 6 reproducible. The original 102 records are d0; dat holds the 98 complete records, with income_k in thousand dollars and type levels ordered bc, prof, wc.

c(original = nrow(d0), retained = nrow(dat))
table(dat$type)

We refit the education-only model on these same 98 records before any adjusted comparison, so that the move from 102 to 98, a change in which records are described, is never presented as an adjustment effect. Complete records make the computations comparable; they do not make the omitted occupations irrelevant or the 98 a probability sample of Canadian occupations.
The working occupation model is
\[
\mathrm{income}_k=\beta_0+\beta_Ee+\beta_Pp+\beta_Ww
+\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}+\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}}
+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(e\) is education, \(p\) prestige, \(w\) percentage of women, and each indicator \(D\) is 1 for its named type. Blue-collar, with both indicators zero, is the reference type. There are six coefficients. The conditional question concerns \(\beta_E\), comparing education at the same prestige, women and type. Least squares describes the recorded occupations whether or not that stochastic model holds; Section 3 applies its conditions to attach uncertainty.
A best linear projection, summarizing a curved relationship over a stated predictor distribution, is a different declared target, not a rescue adopted after curvature appears. Chapter 9, Appendix A, develops it.


Least squares and the fits on the same rows
Least squares chooses the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares smallest. Its residual SD, \(s_e=\sqrt{RSS/(n-p)}\), describes the typical residual size; the full model below gives 2.6187 thousand dollars on 92 df. \(R^2\) is the share of centered outcome variation accounted for in these records; Appendix B introduces its adjusted version.

m0 <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = dat)
m_w <- lm(income_k ~ education + women, data = dat)
m1 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige, data = dat)
m2 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type, data = dat)
coef(m_w)

(Intercept)   education       women 
-1.19760964  0.92922682 -0.06536432 

coef(m2)

(Intercept)   education    prestige       women    typeprof 
  0.4205235   0.1164336   0.1406054  -0.0535047   0.3241934 
     typewc 
  0.2353306 





Table 1: The model sequence separates sample composition from conditioning.











Records and predictors
Education slope
In-sample \(R^2\)
Role here

0.8988
.3336

Same 98, education and women

Holds women fixed; the slope barely moves


Same 98, education and prestige
\(-0.2179\)

The conditional answer about \(\beta_E\)






The education-and-women fit gives a concrete reading: two occupations one year apart in education, with the same percentage of women, differ in fitted income by 0.9292 thousand dollars (education SE 0.1044). At the same education, one percentage point more women corresponds to 0.0654 thousand dollars lower fitted income (SE 0.0091). Its \(R^2\) is .5641. These are comparisons of occupations, not effects of changing an individual’s education or occupation.
Why does adding prestige reverse the education slope while adding women barely changes it? Education correlates .8665 with prestige and .0619 with women. Correlation alone is only part of the explanation: how far the education slope moves depends on the added predictor’s coefficient and its slope on education. For least-squares fits on the same rows, the sample omitted-variable identity is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{marginal slope}&=\text{slope with }Z\\
&\quad+(\text{coefficient of }Z)(\text{slope of }Z\text{ on education}),\\
0.8830&=-0.2179+0.2043(5.3884)\qquad(Z=\text{prestige}),\\
0.8830&=0.9292+(-0.0654)(0.7069)\qquad(Z=\text{women}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Appendix A derives the identity; the displayed numbers are rounded. The carried parts are 1.1009 for prestige and \(-0.0462\) for women. Figure 2 shows the corresponding fitted lines beside the marginal line, extending the known-process display to real records.








Figure 2: Fitted income against education at three held values of prestige (a) or of the percentage of women (b), each line drawn over the education observed near its held value, with the dashed marginal education-only line.





In panel (a), each solid line falls 0.2179 per education year at fixed prestige. The higher-prestige lines sit over higher education, so the rising marginal line crosses them. In panel (b), the solid lines rise 0.9292 per year, nearly the marginal slope, because women hardly tracks education. Each line uses the education range among records within 7.5 points of its held value, a display choice that respects nearby observations; Section 4.2 checks support more fully.
For example, the first panel’s line at prestige 50 combines the fitted intercept with \(50\widehat\beta_P\); its slope is \(\widehat\beta_E\). The nearby points keep the comparison close to observed education values.

near <- dat[abs(dat$prestige - 50) <= 7.5, ]
ggplot(near, aes(education, income_k)) + geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(m1)[1] + 50*coef(m1)["prestige"],
              slope = coef(m1)["education"])

The sequence of slopes names different comparisons; it is not a true effect being explained away. Adding predictors on the same rows cannot increase the smallest achievable RSS, so training \(R^2\) cannot fall. The separate gains need not add up: women adds .2345, prestige adds .1701, and the full model adds .3066 over education alone. These gains concern training fit, not held-out prediction.


Indicators and a fitted profile
A three-level factor needs two indicators. With blue-collar as reference, \(D_{\mathrm{prof}}\) and \(D_{\mathrm{wc}}\) identify the other types; the full occupation fit is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\mathrm{income}}_k
={}&0.4205+0.1164e+0.1406p-0.0535w\\
&+0.3242D_{\mathrm{prof}}+0.2353D_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtract two fitted means one education year apart at the same prestige, percentage of women and type. Every term except education cancels:
\[
\widehat m(e+1,p,w,t)-\widehat m(e,p,w,t)=\widehat\beta_E=0.1164.
\]
Thus two such occupations differ by about 116 dollars in fitted income. At the same values of all the other predictors, a prestige point compares about 141 dollars more, and a percentage point more women compares about 54 dollars less. Each sentence names what is held fixed.
For a white-collar profile with education 11, prestige 45, and women 50, \(D_{\mathrm{prof}}=0\) and \(D_{\mathrm{wc}}=1\), and the unrounded fitted coefficients give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat m_*
={}&\widehat\beta_0+11\widehat\beta_E+45\widehat\beta_P
+50\widehat\beta_W+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}\\
\approx{}&5.5886,
\end{aligned}
\]
a fitted mean of about 5,589 dollars on the historical income scale, not a guarantee for any occupation or worker.
The intercept refers to zero education, prestige, and women in the reference type; it anchors the fitted surface and need not describe a plausible occupation. Nor is one type coefficient “the effect of occupational type”. When a factor stands alone, each coefficient is a difference between group means; here each type coefficient compares fitted means at the same education, prestige, and women. Appendix A gives the group-mean and releveling calculations, and Chapter 9 develops contrasts, block tests, and the analysis-of-variance identity.
The substitution uses six multipliers, one for each coefficient. Table 2 puts them in coefficient order for three actual occupations and for the declared profile. The first multiplier is 1 because every fitted value includes the intercept. A professional record selects the professional coefficient, a white-collar record the white-collar coefficient, and a blue-collar record selects neither.

This gives a concrete meaning to the vector notation. Write the multipliers as the column vector \(\mathbf x_i=(1,e_i,p_i,w_i,D_{\mathrm{prof},i},D_{\mathrm{wc},i})^{\mathsf T}\) and the corresponding coefficients as \(\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_E,\beta_P,\beta_W,
\delta_{\mathrm{prof}},\delta_{\mathrm{wc}})^{\mathsf T}\). A vector is an ordered collection of numbers; the superscript \(\mathsf T\) denotes the transpose, which turns a column into a row. The product \(\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\) adds the six multiplier–coefficient products, exactly as the scalar equation does.
Stacking the 98 observed rows gives the \(98\times6\) design matrix \(\mathbf X\). Stacking the outcomes and errors gives the compact model \(\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon\). The design matrix stores predictors and indicators, not income. Distinct coefficients require that no column be an exact linear combination of the others, the full-column-rank condition. Near collinearity affects precision, as Section 4.2 explains. The profile is a new row for prediction, not an extra record used to fit the model. model.matrix() recovers the observed multiplier rows; multiplying row by the fitted coefficients recovers the profile mean.

rows <- c("nursing.aides", "gov.administrators", "medical.technicians")
model.matrix(m2)[rows, ]
row <- c(1, 11, 45, 50, 0, 1)
sum(row * coef(m2))

Section 5 uses this notation to carry coefficient uncertainty to the profile; Chapter 9, Appendix A, develops the matrix mathematics. Section 4.2 checks whether the three continuous values of that white-collar profile occur together, using a weighted combination of observed records.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Inference for the Partial Slope
Apply Section 1.1’s model to the occupation records: incomes vary independently around the linear mean of Section 2.1 at the recorded predictor rows, with a common error SD \(\sigma\). The residual SD 2.6187 estimates it on 92 df. The repetition imagined for the classical intervals is new incomes at the same 98 predictor rows; the historical records do not establish that model or a probability sample.

The partial slope from residuals
The partial slope can be recovered by removing the fitted parts of the other predictors from both variables. Regress education on prestige, percentage of women, and type and keep the residuals \(r_{E,i}\); do the same for income to obtain \(r_{Y,i}\). Both auxiliary fits include an intercept and use exactly the 98 rows of the full fit. Then
\[
b_E=\frac{\sum_i r_{E,i}r_{Y,i}}{\sum_i r_{E,i}^2}
    =r_{EY\cdot Z}\frac{s_{r_Y}}{s_{r_E}},
\]
where \(Z\) denotes the control columns and \(r_{EY\cdot Z}\), the correlation of the two residual vectors, is the partial correlation. The numerator is the linear co-variation left after the controls and the denominator the education variation left; the ratio of residual SDs turns the unit-free correlation into thousand dollars per education year.

r_E <- residuals(lm(education ~ prestige + women + type, data = dat))
r_Y <- residuals(lm(income_k ~ prestige + women + type, data = dat))
sum(r_E * r_Y) / sum(r_E^2)

The uncertainty must count the fitted controls. Prestige and women supply one column each and type two, so with education and the intercept the model estimates \(p=6\) coefficients from \(n=98\) rows, leaving \(n-p=92\) residual degrees of freedom. Using the residual variance \(s_e^2=RSS/(n-p)\) of Section 2.2,
\[
SE(b_E)=\sqrt{\frac{s_e^2}
                         {\sum_i r_{E,i}^2}},
\qquad
t_E=r_{EY\cdot Z}\sqrt{\frac{n-p}{1-r_{EY\cdot Z}^2}}.
\]
The slope identity is algebraic; the SE and the \(t_{92}\) reference for \(H_0:\beta_E=0\) rest on the classical model of Section 1.1. In Table 3 the first row is the full model’s education row, which these formulas reproduce, and the second is a fresh fit of residual income on residual education.



Table 3: The residual slope reproduces the full-model coefficient; only the full model’s df gives its uncertainty.

Both rows share the slope 0.1164 and the partial correlation .0441. The fresh fit counts \(98-2=96\) df, as if fitting the four control columns had cost nothing, so its SE is smaller by the factor \(\sqrt{92/96}\). Use m2, or the formulas with \(n-p=92\), for uncertainty.
Only the education variation left after the controls informs this coefficient: its residual SD is 0.9661 years, against 2.7489 before residualizing. The added-variable display below shows what remains.








Figure 3: Marginal and residualized income–education comparisons in the same 98 occupations.





Figure 3 sets the two comparisons side by side. The marginal line rises 0.8830 per year; after the fitted linear parts of prestige, women, and type are removed from both variables, the residual line rises only 0.1164, with wide scatter around it. Residualizing removes those fitted linear components, not every substantive difference between occupations. The residualized panel can be drawn directly from these two residual vectors and the full model’s slope.

ggplot(data.frame(r_E, r_Y), aes(r_E, r_Y)) + geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = coef(m2)["education"])



Two covariance matrices
Covariance now has two meanings. cov() describes how recorded variables spread and move together; vcov() estimates the covariance of the fitted coefficients. Table 4 compares them on the same 98 rows.



Table 4: Two covariance matrices from the same 98 records answer different questions.

cov(dat[c("income_k", "education", "prestige", "women")])

The education entries differ by a factor of about 100 because they measure different things: the spread of education across occupations and the squared uncertainty of one fitted coefficient. The matrices are not interchangeable; Section 5 uses the coefficient covariance in \(\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf x_*\).


Interval and tests
With 92 residual degrees of freedom, the classical 95% interval for education is
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_E\pm t_{.975,92}SE(b_E)
&=0.1164\pm1.9861(0.2752)\\
&\approx[-0.4302,\ 0.6631].
\end{aligned}
\]
Under the classical assumptions the interval is compatible with negative and positive conditional slopes, including differences of several hundred dollars per year of education. With no margin of practical equivalence declared, the direction and the practically relevant size remain unresolved; the interval does not show that the slope is zero or that adjustment has removed an effect of education.

confint(m2, "education")

               2.5 %    97.5 %
education -0.4301895 0.6630567

hc3_covariance <- sandwich::vcovHC(m2, type = "HC3")
hc3_se <- sqrt(hc3_covariance["education", "education"])
coef(m2)["education"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, 92) * hc3_se

[1] -0.6429122  0.8757794


HC3 keeps the coefficient and replaces its covariance estimate, giving SE 0.3823 and, with the same \(t_{92}\) convention, the approximate interval \([-0.6429,0.8758]\). It allows unequal error variances among independent observations under large-sample conditions and is not an exact small-sample guarantee. Neither interval allows for unmodeled dependence, selection, measurement error, or a wrong mean form.
The matching test addresses \(H_0:\beta_E=0\) in the stated full model, not “education has no effect”. Its classical \(t=0.423\) and \(p=.6732\) do not prove the null, and the test does not decide which of the three questions deserves an answer.
The overall \(F\) test compares the full regression with a one-mean model on the same rows, setting all \(p-1\) non-intercept coefficients to zero. This extends Chapter 4’s comparison of named mean models. Under the same Normal-error conditions as the coefficient tests, its statistic is
\[
F_{\mathrm{overall}}=
\frac{RegSS/(p-1)}{RSS/(n-p)},
\qquad RegSS=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2.
\]

summary(m2)$fstatistic

  value   numdf   dendf 
32.1747  5.0000 92.0000 


The full model gives \(F(5,92)=32.1747\), \(p<.0001\); the education-only model on the same 98 records gives \(F(1,96)=47.1956\). For education alone the statistic is the square of its slope’s \(t=6.8699\). Each tests its stated joint restriction; the full-model test does not identify which coefficient differs from zero. Neither verifies the mean function or shows how well the fitted rule will predict a held-out outcome. Chapter 9 develops the general nested comparison behind this statistic, its matrix form, and the contrasts, block tests, and adjusted group means that a factor with several levels invites.
Not every change to a model changes the scientific estimand. In a randomized study, well-specified covariate adjustment can estimate the same declared average assignment effect more precisely; releveling a factor changes the coefficient coordinates but not the fitted values; and a different uncertainty estimator changes the interval but not the coefficient.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Checking the Model
What would these plots look like if the working model described the data well? A fit produces numbers even when its mean or uncertainty model is unsuitable. Checking asks which part of the interpretation the evidence supports; no single graph passes or fails the model.

Residuals, leverage, and influence
A residual is an observed deviation from a fitted value, not the unobserved error. Leverage measures how unusual a record’s combination of predictor values is; a high-leverage record pulls the fit toward itself, so its residual tends to be smaller. A standardized residual therefore divides each residual by its own estimated SD, which combines the common residual scale with the record’s leverage, and an externally studentized residual does the same with the scale estimated with that record left out. Influence, measured by Cook’s distance, combines leverage with the size of the residual (Cook, 1977). This call lists the five occupations with the largest Cook’s distance.

sort(cooks.distance(m2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]

Figure 4 shows four views. If the linear mean described the records well, the residuals in panel (a) would scatter evenly around zero with a flat smooth; here the smooth drifts downward and the scatter widens at high fitted income. With constant spread, the smooth in panel (b) would stay level; it rises. Panel (c) follows the Normal reference line in the middle but departs in both tails, most strongly on the right, where a few occupations earn far more than the model predicts; on the left, ministers earn far less. The two largest positive residuals, general managers and physicians in the printed list, also have the largest Cook’s distances, drawn as the biggest circles in panel (d).








Figure 4: Four complementary diagnostic views for the full additive model.





The first panel compares fitted means with observed deviations. A horizontal reference at zero makes systematic departures visible.

check <- data.frame(fit = fitted(m2), resid = residuals(m2))
ggplot(check, aes(fit, resid)) + geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)

These features challenge the linear mean form and the constant-variance description, and the heavy tails matter for exact small-sample Normal-theory inference, although OLS can still be calculated. A large residual, high leverage, and high influence are different features, and none alone shows that a record is invalid. No residual graph can establish that occupations are independent draws from a wider population.


Joint support and collinearity
Joint support concerns combinations of predictor values. First, Table 5 asks a coarser question: how far does each variable extend within each recorded type?

Do the three values of Section 2.3’s white-collar profile, education 11, prestige 45 and women 50, occur together in the records? Separate ranges cannot say. A convex combination of records is a weighted average whose weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and a joint-support witness is a convex combination of observed records that returns the profile. The witness places the profile inside the joint covariate hull of the white-collar records on all three continuous predictors. It does not show that many occupations lie near the profile, that one matches it exactly, or that a causal comparison is supported.
Section 2.2’s adjusted-versus-marginal figure restricts its lines to nearby records. Its education ranges are plotting neighborhoods, not a formal guarantee of support for the full-model profile.
Collinearity means that a predictor is strongly linearly related to the other predictors, so they largely predict it, and it costs precision. The auxiliary \(R^2\) from regressing education on the other predictors, .8765, measures how strongly: they account for most of education’s variation, and education’s variance inflation factor is
\[
VIF_E=\frac{1}{1-R^2_{E\mid P,W,T}}\approx8.0968,
\qquad \sqrt{VIF_E}\approx2.8455.
\]
Figure 5 draws the SE multiplier \(\sqrt{VIF}\) against the auxiliary \(R^2\) for the three continuous predictors. The curve rises slowly at first, so women (auxiliary \(R^2\) .2312, multiplier 1.1405) loses little precision, and it climbs steeply beyond about .8, where prestige (.8066, multiplier 2.2738) and education sit.








Figure 5: The SE multiplier grows steeply as the other predictors account for more of a predictor’s variation.






r2 <- summary(lm(education ~ prestige + women + type, data = dat))$r.squared
c(VIF = 1/(1 - r2), SE_multiplier = sqrt(1/(1 - r2)))

Under the classical model, holding the residual variance and education’s total variation fixed, education’s SE is 2.8455 times what it would be in an orthogonal design, where education is uncorrelated with the other predictors. This compares two variance formulas: deleting a predictor would change the comparison and can change the residual variance, so a VIF is not a deletion rule, and near collinearity does not by itself bias the coefficient under the maintained zero-conditional-mean model.


Sensitivity to curvature and to one record
A regression is linear in its coefficients: a squared predictor can enter a linear model even though its mean curve bends. Its form is a changed specification to assess, not a transformation selected automatically by a significant test.
A component-plus-residual plot adds the fitted prestige term back to each residual, \(e_i+\widehat\beta_P P_i\). In Figure 6 the smooth bends upward at high prestige, away from the straight fitted component. That motivates a declared form sensitivity; it does not show that any one curve is the true process.








Figure 6: The prestige component plus residual in the full additive model.





The refit adds a squared prestige term to m2. The two fits are nested: they share the outcome and the 98 rows, and the smaller fit’s predictors are a subset of the larger fit’s. The comparison of named mean models applies here with continuous predictors. Its null hypothesis is that the squared-prestige coefficient is zero, so that m2’s mean function suffices; the statistic sets the residual sum of squares that the added term removes against the larger fit’s residual variance, on 1 and \(98-7=91\) degrees of freedom. A small p-value says the term removes more variation than the error scale would ordinarily produce under that null. It does not make the enlarged equation the correct mean function, and it is not a rule for choosing a model; Chapter 9 develops the general comparison.
