title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Fitted and Standardized Quantities
The fitted model also gives quantities for particular profiles: a fitted mean with its two intervals, and an average over a named set of profiles. These are teaching extensions of the model, not further answers the study owes; Pair 2 remains about \(\beta_E\).

A fitted mean and its two intervals
For a complete input row, predict() returns two intervals: interval = "confidence" concerns the model’s mean at that profile, and interval = "prediction" concerns one new outcome at the same profile. Both use the full fitted model and its classical assumptions.

wc_type <- factor("wc", levels = levels(dat$type))
profile <- data.frame(education = 11, prestige = 45, women = 50,
                      type = wc_type)
predict(m2, newdata = profile, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 5.588634 4.486469 6.690799

predict(m2, newdata = profile, interval = "prediction")

       fit       lwr      upr
1 5.588634 0.2722037 10.90506


Where do these intervals come from? Use the Section 2.3 profile vector \(\mathbf x_*=(1,11,45,50,0,1)^{\mathsf T}\). With \(\widehat{\mathbf V}\), the coefficient covariance of Section 3.2, the fitted mean and its estimated classical variance are
\[
\widehat m_*=\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat m_*)=\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf x_*,
\quad \widehat{\mathbf V}=\operatorname{vcov}(m2).
\]
The variance includes the coefficient variances and their covariances: two terms \(a\widehat\beta_j+b\widehat\beta_k\) contribute \(a^2\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\beta_j)+
b^2\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\beta_k)+
2ab\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\widehat\beta_j,\widehat\beta_k)\). Adding coefficient SEs, or ignoring the covariances, is a different calculation, and the square root comes only after the variance is complete. Here the fitted mean is 5.5886, its variance 0.308, and its SE 0.5549 thousand dollars, giving the fitted-mean interval \([4.4865,6.6908]\) that predict() printed.

V2 <- vcov(m2)
sqrt(drop(row %*% V2 %*% row))

One new outcome adds its own error variance, \(s^2=6.8575\), so its SE is \(\sqrt{s^2+\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf x_*}\approx2.6768\) and its interval \([0.2722,10.9051]\). Figure 7 draws both intervals across the white-collar education range at prestige 45 and women 50. The dark fitted-mean band is narrowest near education 11.2, about 2.2 thousand dollars wide, and widens toward the edges of the records, to about 3.1 at 9.17 years. The light band for one new occupation stays between about 10.6 and 10.9 wide along the whole range, because the new occupation’s error variance, 6.8575, dominates a fitted-mean variance of about 0.3.








Figure 7: Two 95% intervals for a white-collar profile at prestige 45 and women 50, across the white-collar education range.





Both intervals rest on the independent, Normal, common-variance model, which the checks of Section 4 qualify rather than confirm; replacing \(\widehat{\mathbf V}\) with HC3 alone does not estimate a new outcome’s conditional error distribution. Neither interval says how accurately a learning rule predicts held-out records; that is Pair 3’s question.


Standardizing over the observed profiles
A standardized fitted value averages over a named set of profiles rather than using one. Here the target is the mean fitted income if all 98 observed combinations of education, prestige and percentage of women were evaluated as white-collar. Each combination receives the same weight, so the target keeps their joint distribution rather than selecting one typical occupation.

white_profiles <- dat
white_profiles$type <- factor("wc", levels = levels(dat$type))
mean(predict(m2, newdata = white_profiles))

[1] 7.016406


The result, 7.0164, is an average of model predictions after a specified change of profile, not the observed white-collar group mean. Every one of the 98 profiles receives weight \(1/98\). For its uncertainty, use Section 5.1’s coefficient-covariance formula with the average of these 98 design rows replacing the single profile row \(\mathbf x_*\). This gives SE 0.6177 and classical interval \([5.7896,8.2432]\), treating the profiles and weights as fixed. The predictions share fitted coefficients; averaging their interval endpoints would ignore that joint uncertainty. Repeating the operation for each type gives Table 8, which sets the results beside the observed mean income of each type.

The observed means differ sharply: professional occupations average 10.5595 thousand dollars, about twice the other two types, but they also have more education, higher prestige, and different percentages of women. The standardized estimates give every type the same 98 profiles, so they differ only by the type coefficients, 0.3242 for professional and 0.2353 for white-collar relative to blue-collar.
Because m2 is linear and additive in the continuous predictors, its average fitted value equals its fitted value at their means (education averages 10.7951 years); with squared terms, interactions, or a nonlinear response function, the prediction at the means need not equal the mean prediction. Any other fixed weighting used for all three types, whether another named set of profiles or unequal weights on these 98, would move the three standardized levels but leave their differences at the type coefficients.
Relabelling every profile professional or white-collar creates some combinations the records do not support, and averaging does not remove that problem; the white-collar profile of Section 5.1 is a different, locally supported quantity. Standardization alone neither identifies a causal effect nor validates out-of-sample performance.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
The Held-Out Prediction Question

Learning rules and the loss
A learning rule says how training records become a prediction equation. Our two rules are fixed: education-only OLS, and the full additive OLS equation with education, prestige, women, and type. OLS fits by minimizing squared training errors; we separately choose the mean absolute error (MAE) to evaluate the predictions in income units.
A prediction opportunity here is a hypothetical same-source occupation whose predictors are all available before its income is used, not a forecast from information that arrives later. The records cannot show that this exchangeability holds for other countries, periods, individual workers, or types absent from the dictionary.
For held-out outcomes \(y_i\) and predictions \(\widehat y_i^{(-)}\) fitted without those outcomes,
\[
MAE=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
       \sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}\left|y_i-\widehat y_i^{(-)}\right|.
\]
A smaller MAE means a smaller average absolute error on the evaluated cases, not a better prediction for every case.


Shared ten-fold validation
In shared ten-fold cross-validation the 98 records are divided into ten folds, and each fold takes a turn as the held-out set: both rules are fitted to the other records and predict the held-out cases (Figure 8), and the 98 case-level errors are then pooled. Table 9 records the protocol.








Figure 8: Shared held-out cases let two fixed learning rules face the same prediction task.








Table 9: The internal-validation protocol was fixed before this teaching comparison.










Decision
Frozen teaching protocol
Why it matters




Candidates
Education-only and the declared full additive OLS rule
No search for the best-looking model after validation


Folds
Shared balanced random ten-fold assignment, seed 80806
Both rules face the same held-out cases


Summary
Pool absolute errors over all 98 held-out cases
Each case receives equal weight; folds of different size do not


Sensitivity
200 new resplits of the same records, seed 80807
Describes sensitivity to splitting, not new independent studies






This is a retrospective reanalysis of familiar data, so “fixed before this comparison” is not a claim of historical preregistration. It means that the candidates were not revised after the primary errors were seen. The sensitivity refits of Section 4 are not added to the candidate set. The 98 complete rows, unit conversion and type dictionary stay fixed. Every training set must contain all types and have full column rank. One fold illustrates the protocol: fold 9 holds the first source record, government administrators, with eight other occupations. train contains the other 89 records and held these nine cases. Both rules use the same training records and predict the same held-out records.

fold_simple <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = train)
fold_full <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type,
                data = train)
pred <- predict(fold_full, newdata = held)

Both fits exclude government administrators’ outcome. Every training set in this comparison contains all three types and has full column rank, so both specified rules are estimable. Chapter 13 develops the validation protocol further.
No held-out outcome is used to estimate a coefficient. Learned preprocessing, such as scaling, imputation, or variable selection, would also have to be fitted on training records only; a fixed unit conversion such as dollars to thousands is not learned.


Held-out errors and resplits
For government administrators, observed income is 12.351 thousand dollars. The full-rule prediction is 11.5948, giving
\[
|12.351-11.5948|=0.7562,
\]
and the education-only prediction is 8.9461, giving \(|12.351-8.9461|=3.4049\). This record favors the full rule, but one record is not the comparison; Table 10 pools all 98 errors.
For the nine cases in the illustrated fold, the MAE formula becomes one average of absolute prediction errors:

mean(abs(held$income_k - pred))

The table uses the errors from all ten folds, so every one of the 98 records contributes once.



Table 10: Case-weighted absolute errors from the frozen shared-fold comparison.









Learning rule
Held-out MAE (thousand dollars)




Education-only OLS
2.4031


Full additive OLS
1.5412


Difference: full minus education-only
\(-0.8619\)






The full rule’s average held-out absolute error is about 862 dollars lower. Because the two errors are subtracted for each same case before averaging, differences in difficulty between cases cannot favor either rule through different test sets. The same predictions give the root mean squared error, which weights large errors more heavily: 3.5051 for education-only and 2.7111 for the full rule, the same preference here, although the two losses need not agree in other data.
Eight fits use 88 training records and two use 89; the pooled errors describe the learning rules at those training sizes, not the one equation fitted to all 98. Chapter 13, Section 2, develops the full protocol and the training-size mixture.
The 200 resplits give differences from \(-0.914\) to \(-0.741\), all favoring the full rule; this is sensitivity to splitting the same records, not a confidence interval from independent studies. New-sample uncertainty is not quantified, so the advantage remains provisional.
The comparison supports lower internal held-out error for the full rule in these records under this protocol. It does not isolate the predictive contribution of education, because the rules differ by prestige, women, and type together, and it does not establish external transport, individual earnings prediction, or a causal education effect.

section: Reading and Evaluating the Three Answers
text:
Reading and Evaluating the Three Answers

The study report



Table 11: Three separately owed answers in the occupation teaching study.










Pair and role
Question
Estimand and owed answer




1. Contextual description
How does income vary linearly with education across the 98 retained occupations?
The finite-record marginal least-squares slope; a descriptive answer for these records


2. Primary conditional association
How does income differ with education at the same prestige, percentage of women, and type, within support?
The linear conditional-mean coefficient \(\beta_E\) under the declared working model; fitted \(b_E\) is its estimate from the 98 retained records


3. Secondary prediction analysis
Does the full additive learning rule predict eligible same-source occupation records with lower expected absolute error than the education-only rule?
Difference in expected absolute error of the two learning procedures at the declared training sizes; an internal validation answer






Each row is a question–answer pair with one argument with linked layers. The three are not statistical strands of one argument: the report owes separate conclusions about marginal association, conditional association, and prediction. Estimands become strands only when one integrated conclusion needs them all, and printing several coefficients creates neither extra questions nor extra strands.
The report below gathers the analyses of Sections 1–6. It is our teaching record, not a statement by the source investigators.

R0 – Common record and declared scope. We analyzed the 98 complete occupation records described in Section 2. Income was scaled to thousand 1971 Canadian dollars. Education and income were historical occupational averages; prestige came from an earlier rating survey. We retained the same rows for all three questions and make no claim of verified probability sampling or randomized education.
R1 – Marginal answer. Across these records the education-only least-squares slope was 0.883 thousand dollars per year. This is a descriptive linear summary: occupations with more education tended to have higher average income. It is not an individual or causal effect.
R2 – Conditional answer. The intended estimand was the linear conditional-mean education coefficient \(\beta_E\), comparing education at the same prestige, percentage of women, and occupational type. Its fitted estimate was \(b_E=0.1164\), with a classical 95% interval [\(-0.4302\), 0.6631] under the independent linear conditional-mean working model with common variance. HC3 gave [\(-0.6429\), 0.8758]. Influence, functional-form, and support checks limit that model’s interpretation. The direction and practically relevant magnitude remain unresolved under these calculations; the result does not establish no conditional relationship.
R3 – Prediction answer. The two fixed OLS learning rules were compared with the shared ten-fold protocol in Section 6. The full rule had MAE 1.5412 versus 2.4031 for education-only, difference \(-0.8619\). The examined resplits all favored the full rule. This is internal evidence about learning procedures trained on 88/89 eligible records under the stated same-source exchangeability assumptions. Lower expected error is a provisional conclusion because new-sample uncertainty is not quantified; this is not external validation of a final 98-record equation.
R4 – Synthesis. Education has a positive marginal linear association with income in these historical records. Its conditional association is imprecisely resolved by the specified additive model, while the full learning rule predicts the held-out records more accurately than the education-only rule. These conclusions answer different questions and do not establish that changing education would change income.



Functions and traces in the report
Reading starts by locating what each passage does. The labels use STAT for the statistical layer and SUB for the substantive layer; E, J, I and C mean evidence, justification, inference and bounded claim. Thus STAT-E identifies the data supporting a statistical answer, while SUB-E identifies their substantive meaning and context. One passage can serve several functions: R0 identifies the records and supplies their historical context. A passage serves justification only when it offers a reason connecting evidence to an inference; “we used R” offers none. Table 12 records each function and where its shared or pair-specific content appears.



Table 12: Reading the linked-layer functions without three duplicate maps.










Function
Shared or pair-specific content
Trace in this teaching record




STAT-E
Named 98 rows, variables, exclusions, and computations’ inputs
R0; the row audit and import code in Section 2


SUB-E
Occupations rather than workers; historical dollars, education, ratings, and types
R0; variable/source descriptions


STAT-J
Pair 1: fixed-record least-squares definition. Pair 2: declared stochastic model and uncertainty conditions. Pair 3: held-out fitting, fixed rules, loss, and exchangeability
R1–R3; model declaration; validation protocol and code


SUB-J
Reasons connecting those measurements and comparisons to historical occupational income, with limits on individual, current, and causal interpretations
R0–R3; unit/time explanations and prediction-opportunity definition


STAT-I
Pair 1’s 0.8830 slope; Pair 2’s 0.1164 estimate, intervals, coefficient test and checks; Pair 3’s case-level errors, MAEs, and split sensitivity
Section 3 through Section 6; R1–R3


STAT-C
Descriptive positive marginal slope; unresolved conditional slope under the model; smaller internal error for the full rule under the protocol
R1, R2, and R3 respectively


SUB-I
Interpret years, income units, conditioning, and prediction errors in the named historical occupation setting
Worked substitutions and error calculation; R1–R3


SUB-C
Each question-facing answer with its own limits; none supplies a causal or individual-earnings answer
R1–R3; their distinctions preserved in R4






The substantive layer also augments and contextualizes the statistical justification (SUB-J), interprets the inference (SUB-I), and bounds the substantive answer (SUB-C).
Read gaps and conflicts beside the statements they concern. R2 states the independence assumption, for example, but nothing in the record shows that independence holds under the original selection of occupations; a stated assumption and evidence for it are different information. The unit conversion, by contrast, makes reading 0.883 thousand dollars as about 883 dollars traceable. This record contains no conflicting source, though a real study may contain incompatible descriptions to record and investigate. Locating a reason and identifying missing support prepare the separate judgment of its adequacy.
Professional knowledge helps identify a trace’s function but does not license adding an unreported design feature. An invalid reason such as “all rows are in the same dataset, therefore they are independent” is still stated J, whose adequacy is judged separately: reading records the reason actually offered, not a repaired one.


Evaluating each answer
Evaluation now judges the quality of the reasoning just identified. Chapter 1’s six questions apply to each argument (Table 13); they are not six scores to total.



Table 13: Apply the six questions before evaluating the study-level synthesis.









Quality-evaluation question
Application to these arguments




Question alignment
R1 matches its finite-record slope. R2 names \(\beta_E\), its fitted estimate, the conditioning set, and the model extension. R3 names the learning procedure, loss, and training sizes rather than substituting a coefficient test.


Evidence integrity
The 102-to-98 accounting and common rows are explicit. Missing type still limits what is represented. CV excludes held-out outcomes from fitting; source selection is not repaired by that procedure.


Justification adequacy
Least squares is sufficient for the declared finite description. Pair 2’s model conditions and Pair 3’s same-source exchangeability remain assumptions with incomplete empirical support. Statistical computation alone cannot establish them.


Inferential adequacy
The slope, intervals, error arithmetic, and comparisons are reproducible. Neither zero-crossing nor a large p-value proves absence; repeated folds are not independent replication. Substantive reasoning must retain those distinctions.


Transition fidelity
Occupation-level average income remains occupation-level average income; partial adjustment is not a causal intervention, and model fit is not held-out performance.


Claim calibration
R1 remains finite and historical; R2 reports unresolved magnitude/direction rather than no relationship; R3 remains internal and procedure-specific. No claim extends to individual workers or modern populations.






Chapter 1 distinguishes judgments about a reason from the conclusion about a whole question–answer pair. Here the finite description is supported as stated; the explicitly unresolved conditional answer is also supported as stated, under its disclosed model limits. A correctly reported inconclusive answer need not establish a stronger claim to be supported. The prediction comparison is supported as a qualified internal result, while external superiority of the final all-record equation is not assessable from the accessible record. Argument Chapter B, Section 4, develops the full judgment account and its alternatives.


Is the synthesis coherent?
Coordinated questions add one evaluation question, Cross-question coherence: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions, estimands, methods, analytic statuses, uncertainty, and limits of the separate answers? We introduce it here; Argument Chapter B develops it further but is not needed to apply it.
R4 reports a positive marginal slope, an unresolved conditional slope, and better internal prediction. Predict and explain: can an interval that includes zero for the education coefficient coexist with a lower held-out MAE for the full rule? Identify the question each result answers before reading this alternative synthesis:

Once the other predictors were controlled, education had no effect; nevertheless, the significant full regression proves it will predict workers’ incomes accurately.

The results can coexist: the interval concerns one conditional coefficient, whereas the rules differ by prestige, women and type together. Better predictions from the full rule do not isolate education’s contribution. R4 retains these distinct answers.
Reading first identifies the inference and claim the alternative offers. Evaluation then finds three failures: “no effect” substitutes a causal null for the conditional-association answer, an omnibus significance test is not held-out validation, and occupations have become workers. The corrected synthesis is R4, not a fourth overarching argument that erases the separate conclusions.
These records were collected for earlier purposes, not prospectively for our three teaching questions. Chapter 1’s repair-versus-new-cycle rule applies: correcting an error under the same target is a repair; choosing a causal target after seeing an association is a revised or new cycle whose timing must be stated. Argument Chapter B, Section 5, develops the full coordinated construction workflow.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Reading Bridge
Start with a model naming its outcome, predictors, coefficients and error variation. The known process showed partial slopes at fixed other predictors before the occupation records supplied estimates. Multiple regression adds conditional comparisons without conferring automatic causal control. Subtracting fitted means showed what a coefficient compares; residualizing connected it to covariance; residual, influence, support, and precision checks each bounded the answer differently; a fitted profile and a standardized average extended the conditional model; and held-out errors answered a separately owed question. The occupation study owed three answers, a finite-record marginal description, a working-model conditional interval with unresolved magnitude, and a qualified internal prediction comparison, and its shared records made the questions coordinated without making their justifications identical. Chapter 9 develops extensions of this model (factors with several levels and their contrasts, nested model comparison and information criteria, changed predictor and outcome forms, and robust, clustered, and bootstrap uncertainty) and transfers the reading to Project STAR, where a randomized design supplies a different warrant. Chapter 10 then extends the interaction reasoning of Chapters 4 and 6 to regression.

Key terms
Use this short reference to revisit the concepts introduced here. The Part One Concept Reference gives the broader reference and the principal home of each concept; the simple-regression, interval, ANOVA, and reading vocabulary used in this chapter is explained in Chapters 1–4 and 7.



Table 14: Selected concepts for multiple regression across coordinated questions.









Term and common alternatives
Meaning




Multiple regression (multiple regression model; additive model)
A model in which an outcome’s mean is an intercept plus one term per predictor, \(E(Y\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}\), with errors of one common SD \(\sigma\); its \(p\) coefficients leave \(n-p\) residual df, and least squares estimates them. Each coefficient compares means at the same values of the other predictors; the additive form assumes each comparison is the same across those values.


Partial slope (conditional coefficient; adjusted coefficient)
The difference in fitted outcome per one-unit difference in one predictor, holding the model’s other predictors fixed. Its meaning depends on the conditioning set named with it; it is not an intervention effect or a claim about unmeasured differences.


Indicator variable (dummy variable) and reference category
A 0/1 variable marking membership in one category of a factor; a factor with \(J\) levels needs \(J-1\) indicators, and the omitted level is the reference. The intercept refers to the reference category; each indicator coefficient is a difference from it at the same other predictors. Releveling changes coordinates, not fitted values.


Partial regression (residualization; added-variable form)
Regressing both the outcome and one predictor on the other predictors, then relating their residuals. The residual slope equals the partial slope; the residual correlation is the partial correlation, unit-free.


Coefficient covariance matrix
The estimated variances and covariances of the fitted coefficients (vcov() in R). Any linear combination of coefficients, such as a fitted mean or a contrast, has variance \(\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c\); adding SEs or ignoring covariances is a different, incorrect calculation.


Variance inflation factor (VIF)
One divided by one minus the \(R^2\) from regressing a predictor on the other predictors. Its square root multiplies that coefficient’s SE relative to an orthogonal design, holding residual variance fixed; it describes precision, not bias, and is not a deletion rule.


Joint support (covariate hull)
Whether a combination of predictor values lies within the region where observations actually occur, not merely within each variable’s separate range. A fitted value outside joint support is extrapolation even if each coordinate is observed somewhere.


Standardization over a named distribution (model-averaged fitted value)
Averaging the model’s fitted values after setting one predictor to a chosen value for every profile in a declared set with fixed weights. Its uncertainty uses the coefficient covariance; it is not an observed group mean, a causal effect, or held-out performance.


Learning rule (learning procedure)
A fixed recipe that turns training records into a prediction equation, such as fitting a declared OLS formula. Prediction performance concerns the rule at stated training sizes, not one final fitted equation.


Cross-validation (held-out validation)
Dividing records into folds, fitting a rule on the other folds, predicting the held-out fold, and pooling the errors so that no outcome contributes to its own prediction. Resplits describe sensitivity to the partition, not new independent studies.


Mean absolute error (MAE)
The average absolute difference between held-out outcomes and their predictions, in outcome units. It is an evaluation loss chosen separately from the squared-error criterion that OLS minimizes.


Cross-question coherence
The additional evaluation question for coordinated answers: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions, estimands, methods, uncertainty, and limits of the separate answers rather than merging them into one omnibus claim?








Further reading

The OpenIntro multiple-predictor tutorial offers concrete equations and indicator interpretations; this chapter borrows its equation-first device but not its stepwise selection.
The ISLR regression lab connects fitting, coefficients, checks, and predictions, and the ISLR cross-validation lab develops the train, predict, and check sequence (James et al., 2021).
The carData documentation (Fox et al., 2022; Fox & Weisberg, 2019) supplies the Prestige variable meanings and provenance; the three questions and the R0–R4 report are this chapter’s own.
Fox (Fox, 2016) and Kutner and colleagues (Kutner et al., 2005) develop the linear-model algebra behind partial slopes, indicators, and diagnostics, and Argument Chapter B develops coordination and its auxiliary construction workflow in greater detail.

title: Multiple Regression I: Conditioning, Checks, and Coordinated Questions
text:
Exercises
Use the supplied numbers; rounding within 0.02 thousand dollars is acceptable unless a different precision is requested. These prompts do not require Argument Chapter B or the appendices.


Exercise 1: Keep the three answers distinct (Foundational)
A report promises: (a) a description of education and income across 98 occupations, (b) an education comparison at the same prestige, women, and type, and (c) a comparison of two prediction rules on held-out records.

Explain why these are three question–answer pairs rather than three statistical strands serving one integrated answer.
For each, name its estimand in plain language and one kind of output that could contribute to its answer.
Does sharing the same 98 records establish the same justification for all three? Give one concrete reason.




Exercise 2: Name what changes (Foundational)
Classify each change as primarily changing the records, the comparison, the coefficient coordinates, or the uncertainty calculation. State whether it necessarily creates a new scientific question.

Refit education-only regression after excluding four missing-type records.
Add prestige, women, and type to the education-only association equation.
Change the reference category from blue-collar to white-collar.
Keep the fitted equation but replace classical SEs with HC3 SEs.

Finally, explain why appropriately specified adjustment in a randomized study need not change its declared average assignment-effect estimand.



Exercise 3: Interpret a fitted comparison (Foundational)
Use this rounded hypothetical equation, with income in thousand dollars:
\[
\widehat y=1+0.20e+0.10p-0.04w+0.30D_{\mathrm{prof}}
           +0.15D_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\]

Two white-collar profiles share prestige \(p=40\) and women \(w=50\); one has education \(e=12\) and the other \(e=10\). Which terms cancel when their fitted means are subtracted? Give the modeled difference and interpret it in dollars.
What does the coefficient 0.15 compare, and at which values of the other predictors?
What must be checked before calling the education comparison in part 1 supported by the observed data?
Why is the modeled difference not an estimate of the effect of giving a worker two more years of education?

Calculate the MAE of each rule.
Explain why the average of the four paired differences, full minus education-only, equals the difference between the two MAEs, and why it matters that both rules predict the same four occupations.
Does the better average rule have to be better for every occupation? Point to the table.
Explain why this comparison is neither a coefficient interval nor validation of a model subsequently fitted to all available records.




Exercise 5: Locate a reason before judging it (Integrative)
An accessible report states:

We retained the same 98 occupations for both equations. This makes the observations independent. The full equation has higher training \(R^2\), so we conclude it predicts new occupations more accurately.

The report provides import code and fitted-model output, but no validation split, held-out predictions, or study-specific evidence about dependence.

Identify the reasons offered, the inference, and the claim.
Record the documentary status of the independence reason and the held-out prediction evidence separately. Do not rewrite “stated” as “not located” merely because a reason is wrong.
Apply Justification adequacy, Inferential adequacy, and Claim calibration.
Give a whole-pair evaluation conclusion for the prediction answer and name the additional work it would require.




Exercise 6: Evaluate the study-level synthesis (Integrative)
Use the occupation study’s reported results: marginal slope 0.883; fitted conditional estimate \(b_E=0.1164\) of \(\beta_E\), with classical interval [\(-0.4302\), 0.6631]; and held-out MAEs 2.4031 for education-only versus 1.5412 for the full rule.
A summary says:

Education does not matter after adjustment, but the model proves that increasing workers’ education raises income and predicts earnings well in other countries.


Predict whether the conditional interval’s including zero conflicts with the full rule’s lower held-out MAE. Explain which question each result answers, then identify the claims actually offered in the summary before evaluating them.
Identify which separate answer obligation is being replaced or exceeded by each clause.
Apply Cross-question coherence and write a corrected three-sentence synthesis that retains the three reported answers and their limits.
If the authors now want a causal effect of education, is that a repair of their existing uncertainty calculation or a new/revised question-level cycle? Explain.

section: Appendix A: Omitted Variables and Group Means
text:
Appendix A: Omitted Variables and Group Means
This appendix develops the mathematics behind Section 1. Its occupation calculations use the same 98-row object dat, the models m0, m1, and m2 of the main text, and the type codes bc, prof, and wc; they introduce no other sample. Chapter 9 develops contrasts, block tests, adjusted means, the matrix form, and the Project STAR transfer.

Why the marginal slope includes another association
Suppose a population process is
\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_X X+\beta_Z Z+\varepsilon,
\qquad E(\varepsilon\mid X,Z)=0,
\]
with finite variances and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\). The marginal least-squares slope is a covariance divided by a variance. Substituting the outcome equation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
&=\frac{\beta_X\operatorname{Var}(X)
+\beta_Z\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)
+\operatorname{Cov}(X,\varepsilon)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\\
&=\beta_X+\beta_Z
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
The zero-error-covariance condition removes the final term. The sample counterpart holds exactly for least-squares fits on the same rows, as Section 2.2’s prestige and women calculations show. The discrepancy therefore involves both the association between \(X\) and \(Z\) and \(Z\)’s coefficient in the outcome model; neither ingredient alone determines its size. If the target is the conditional coefficient, omitting \(Z\) creates bias relative to that target. If the target is the marginal slope, that marginal quantity is not a biased version of an unstated conditional target. The two coefficients name different comparisons, and neither supplies a causal warrant for observational variables.


Repeated samples from the known process
Let independent standard Normal variables \(X\) and \(U\) generate \(Z=.65X+\sqrt{1-.65^2}U\), so that both predictors have variance one and correlation .65. Independently generate a Normal error with SD 6, and set
\[
Y=50+2X+5Z+\varepsilon.
\tag{2}\]
This is the process of Section 1: the marginal slope is \(2+5(.65)=5.25\) and the conditional \(X\) slope is 2. The sample in Figure 1 has 250 observations and uses seed 82108. Its marginal slope is 5.9971 and its conditional slope 3.0259: within two SEs of their targets, as Section 1.3 reads from the generated sample.
A separate repeated-study design, with its own stated sample size, shows the sampling variation: 1,000 samples of 150 observations each, with seed 82109. Each sample fits the marginal and conditional equations to new observations from the same process. The density curves summarize their estimated slopes.

That is a result of this specified process, not a general promise that adjustment always lowers precision: prognostic covariates and their relations to the focal predictor both matter. A simulation shows the consequences of its assumptions; it cannot certify the observational occupation study.


Fitted group means from indicators
Start with a model containing only the three-level type factor. With blue-collar as reference,
\[
\widehat y_g=\widehat\beta_0+
\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}+
\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\]
The fitted means are \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{bc}}=\widehat\beta_0\), \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{prof}}=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}\), and \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{wc}}=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}\). OLS minimizes squared deviations separately within each group, so these equal the observed group means; the hats distinguish fitted summaries from hypothetical population means.

The group-only coefficients are \(\widehat\beta_0=5.3741\), \(\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}=5.1853\) and \(\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}=-0.3218\); each fitted mean combines them as the indicator columns direct and equals the observed mean income of its type. section: Appendix B: Formulas Behind the Checks and Criteria
text:
Appendix B: Formulas Behind the Checks and Criteria
This appendix gives the formulas and fuller tables behind Sections 3 and 4, on the same dat, m0, m1, and m2. None of these refinements supplies a missing design, measurement, independence, or transport warrant.

Cook’s distance
With \(p\) coefficient columns including the intercept, leverage is \(h_{ii}=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf x_i\). Cook’s distance can be calculated as
\[
D_i=\frac{e_i^2}{p s^2}\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}
=\frac{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(-i)})^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X
(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(-i)})}{p s^2}.
\]
The second expression measures the change in all coefficients when record \(i\) is deleted, in the design matrix’s metric rather than as an unweighted sum of squared coefficients with incompatible units.

Refitting without it moves education from 0.1164 to 0.4372, and the type coefficients move as well. The comparison records a diagnostic perturbation of the fit, not a new research question for each coefficient that moved or evidence that the reduced sample is preferable.


The HC3 covariance
For independent observations, the HC3 covariance estimator is
\[
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{HC3}}=(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\left\{\sum_i \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\frac{e_i^2}{(1-h_{ii})^2}\right\}
(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}.
\]
The outer factors are the familiar design component. The middle component lets each record carry its own residual scale, inflated for leverage (Long & Ervin, 2000; Zeileis, 2004). The OLS coefficients do not change; only their covariance does, as Table 18 shows for all six coefficients; vcovHC() evaluates this covariance calculation.

Education’s HC3 SE is 0.3823 rather than 0.2752, and with \(t_{92}\) as an approximate reference the interval is \([-0.6429,0.8758]\); this is not an exact finite-sample HC3 coverage result. Women’s HC3 SE is smaller than its classical counterpart: robust covariance need not widen every interval.
For a maintained linear conditional mean, HC3 addresses unequal variance among independent observations. For a random-design best-linear-projection target, a suitable sandwich covariance can support large-sample projection inference without making the mean exactly linear. Neither use repairs measurement error, dependence, selection, causal identification, or absent joint support.


VIF and generalized VIF
For a single predictor column, the classical conditional variance of its coefficient can be written
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_j\mid\mathbf X)=
\frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_i(X_{ij}-\bar X_j)^2}
\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.
\]
Here \(R_j^2\) comes from regressing that predictor on the remaining columns, including the intercept. The variance inflation factor is \(VIF_j=1/(1-R_j^2)\), and its square root is an SE multiplier, holding the residual variance and the focal predictor’s variation fixed (Kutner et al., 2005). Education gives \(R_j^2=.8765\), VIF 8.0968, and SE multiplier 2.8455 (Section 4.2), from the auxiliary regression or car::vif(m2). The education–prestige correlation is .8665, but the VIF uses all the other columns, not just that pair.
The two-column type term has a generalized VIF. Its raw GVIF is 7.7001; the dimension-adjusted value \(GVIF^{1/(2\,df)}=1.6658\) is on a scale comparable to the square root of a one-column VIF (Fox & Weisberg, 2019), whereas the raw two-column GVIF is not comparable with an ordinary one-column VIF.
Exact collinearity makes the design rank-deficient. Near collinearity leaves the coefficients estimable but possibly imprecise, and under the maintained zero-conditional-mean model it does not by itself bias OLS. A cutoff of 5 or 10 neither establishes the model’s assumptions nor justifies removing a variable the question requires. Measurement problems need their own evidence: the familiar attenuation story requires classical error assumptions and is not a rule for every coefficient in a multiple-predictor model.


The Normal likelihood, AIC, and BIC
Chapter 6, Section 5, searched over candidate values of a fitting criterion while the data stayed fixed. The likelihood is another such criterion: it scores each candidate set of parameter values by how probable, or for a continuous response how dense, the observed data are under the model. Here the response is continuous and the parameters are several coefficients plus an error scale. For a declared independent Normal linear model, the likelihood is the joint density of the observed outcomes at their fixed predictor values, viewed as a function of those parameters; it is not a probability assigned to a parameter, nor the probability of the exact observed vector. The log-likelihood adds the log densities of the independent records.
Write the predictor row for record \(i\) as \(\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\) and let \(\sigma>0\) be the error SD. Before fitting, the log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma)=-n\log\sigma-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y_i-\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta)^2.
\]
At any fixed positive scale only the last term changes with the coefficients, so maximizing over \(\boldsymbol\beta\) minimizes the residual sum of squares: the Normal maximum-likelihood coefficients equal the OLS coefficients. This connects Chapter 7’s squared-loss criterion to this particular distributional model, although least squares did not need the model to calculate a minimizing line.
Maximizing over the scale gives \(\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{ML}}=\sqrt{RSS/n}\), whereas the residual SD used for classical coefficient uncertainty is \(s=\sqrt{RSS/(n-p)}\), with \(p\) counting the regression coefficients. The two serve different purposes, and the ML scale, not the residual SD, belongs in the fitted likelihood. At the fitted coefficients and ML scale,
\[
\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{ML}})
=-\frac n2\left\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(RSS/n)\right\}.
\]
R’s logLik() returns this maximized value for an lm() fit: the Normal log densities of the 98 outcomes at their fitted means and the ML scale add to the same number. Two information criteria combine it with a penalty for the number of parameters:
\[
AIC=-2\log\widehat L+2k,\qquad
BIC=-2\log\widehat L+k\log n.
\]
Here \(k\) counts the regression coefficients and the estimated residual variance, so the full occupation model has \(k=7\). Smaller values are preferred under each criterion; neither is a held-out MAE (Akaike, 1974; Schwarz, 1978). For m2 the ML scale is 2.5373 and the residual SD 2.6187; the maximized log-likelihood is \(-230.302\), so its AIC is 474.6040 and its BIC 492.6988.
Table 19 compares the three declared models on the same 98 rows, response scale, and likelihood convention. Its adjusted \(R^2\), \(1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-p)\), charges each added coefficient a small penalty: it rises only when the added terms’ nested-model \(F\) statistic exceeds 1. Like \(R^2\), AIC and BIC, it is computed from the fit to the same 98 rows, so it is an in-sample summary, not a held-out measure. Chapter 11 develops likelihood fitting further for binomial outcomes; this local Normal-model calculation does not need it.

No residual graph establishes independence: the occupations share one historical labour market, and clustered or repeated records would need dependence-aware uncertainty, which HC3 alone does not supply. title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
text:
A published study asks a question and offers an answer. Between them are observations, the circumstances in which they arose, reasons for trusting a comparison, analytical work, and an interpretation. Much of that support lies outside the sentence reporting the main result. A protocol may explain allocation, an instrument may reveal what an outcome measures, and a supplement may show what changed when an unusual observation was omitted. Learning to connect those records is part of understanding quantitative research.
The invented feedback study will provide a complete example. Its reported assignment effect is 2.5 points, with a 95% interval from 1 to 4 points. Reading those numbers alone cannot tell us whether the study compared students or classes, what the score represents, or why the comparison could support an effect of assignment. The following sections make these connections explicit, then give less structured cases in which you must decide which connection matters.
crumbs: A. How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument

title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
section: From a Research Question to a Traceable Argument
text:
From a Research Question to a Traceable Argument

Start with what the study asks and answers
Consider two extracts from the invented study. Their labels are illustrative locations in the teaching record, not quotations from an actual publication.

Paper, aim: We examined whether assigning explanatory rather than usual feedback changes average delayed achievement for the 480 eligible students in 24 participating classes.
Protocol, allocation: Twelve classes were randomly assigned to each format across the full pool of 24 classes. The comparison uses equally weighted class means and an uncertainty procedure reflecting class assignment.

The aim can be restated as a question: What is the average effect of assigning explanatory rather than usual feedback on delayed achievement for these eligible students? This is a reader’s formulation of the stated aim. It names a causal comparison, an outcome and a scope. An aim such as “improve education” would need these details before it could identify a quantitative question.
The estimand is the target quantity, here the student-average assignment effect for the eligible cohort. The estimate is the reported 2.5-point result. The reported answer is the study’s conclusion about that question. It can be cautious or overstated; the reader first identifies the answer that was actually given. Replacing it with a more defensible statement is an evaluation and revision, not a discovery about what the original sentence said.
A question-answer pair gives an argument its task. Evidence and methods are relevant through their contribution to this task. A well-computed coefficient can still concern the wrong outcome, follow-up time or unit. Conversely, a carefully supported answer can remain inconclusive. A research argument need not end with a positive result to succeed.


Four functions in two linked layers
An argument component names a function of information. Evidence supplies observations and their production record; Justification supplies invoked reasons and conditions; Inference connects those contributions through analysis and reasoning; a bounded Claim states the conclusion with its limits. The statistical and substantive layers are coordinated parts of one argument. The statistical layer follows the numerical target and analysis; the substantive layer keeps their meaning connected to the people, practices and question.



Table 1: Four component functions and their linked meanings.











Component
Statistical function
Substantive function
Connection




Evidence (E)
STAT-E: information about the observations, variables, and procedures through which the analysis data were produced or acquired
SUB-E: information about the people, setting, activities, and substantive meaning represented by those data
SUB-E situates STAT-E


Justification (J)
STAT-J: reasons and conditions invoked to support the intended statistical comparison and inference
SUB-J: domain-based reasons supporting measurement meaning, implementation, explanation, and applicability
SUB-J augments and contextualizes STAT-J


Inference (I)
STAT-I: the analytical reasoning and work connecting evidence and justification to statistical conclusions, including estimates, uncertainty, comparisons, and checks
SUB-I: interpretation of that statistical inference in substantive terms, retaining the relevant uncertainty and conditions
SUB-I interprets STAT-I


Bounded claim (C)
STAT-C: the reported statistical conclusion about the estimand, with uncertainty, conditions, and scope
SUB-C: the reported question-facing answer, with its substantive scope, qualifications, and unresolved matters
SUB-C bounds the substantive reach of STAT-C






In the feedback study, class assignments and assessment records contribute Evidence. The reason that random allocation supports the assigned-group comparison contributes Justification. Computing the mean contrast, its interval and influence checks contributes Inference. Saying that assignment increased average assessed performance in these classes contributes a bounded Claim. These functions are not section headings: Methods can contain both a procedure and its rationale, and Results can contain both a calculation and a conclusion.








Figure 1: Four functions in two linked layers. Evidence plus Justification support Inference, which supports a bounded Claim; vertical links identify the substantive contribution.





The score’s content situates the statistical measurement. Reasons why the assessment represents the taught objectives augment its interpretation. Reading the interval in course terms interprets the numerical result. Limiting the answer to assessed performance in these classes bounds its substantive reach. Numerical statements can do substantive work: “one application task” is a domain interpretation of two score points. The layers are not numbers versus words, and substantive reasoning starts when the question and measures are chosen, not only after calculations finish.


Connect a function to an inspectable location
Traceable information is specific study content through which a component’s function can be identified. A documentary location is where that content can be inspected: a paragraph, table, protocol item, codebook entry or analysis file. “Research design” names a topic. “Twelve classes were randomly assigned to each format across the full class pool” identifies a particular procedure.
The useful connection is question-answer pair → component function → specific information → documentary location. You can follow it in either direction. Starting from Evidence, look for how groups arose; starting from an allocation paragraph, identify its contribution to evidence production. Keep enough of the location for another reader to find the same information.
Professional knowledge helps recognize the contribution. Knowing what a confidence interval concerns helps identify which estimate’s uncertainty is reported. Recognizing a reason does not certify its quality. “Our software estimates causal effects” is still a reason the authors offered, although running software cannot supply a causal design. Reading records the offered reason; evaluation judges it.
When information remains unclear, explain the particular gap. “The article reports 480 scores but the participant-flow table reports 460; neither explains the difference” is more informative than an overall label. A missing account in accessible materials does not establish that the action never occurred. Do not fill the gap with a procedure you would have preferred. These habits make a reading useful without turning every paper into a compulsory checklist.

title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
section: Tracing Information Through E, J, I, and C in Both Layers
text:
Tracing Information Through E, J, I, and C in Both Layers
The following tables collect fifteen recurring information types: four for Evidence, four for Justification, five for Inference and two for Claim. They are reference aids, not an exhaustive list to memorize. The information in an actual reading is the particular study’s account. Return to a row when a statistical term or an unfamiliar analysis makes its function difficult to see.

Statistical Evidence: observations and their production
STAT-E includes observations and the record of their production. Table 2 distinguishes the structure of the records, measurement, selection and implementation, and the observations actually analyzed.
An observed variable is a characteristic recorded for study units. In the feedback-format example, each student has an assessment score and a recorded feedback format. The score is numerical, so a mean and a measure of variation can help describe it. Practice format is categorical, so counts or percentages show how students are distributed across the categories. The recorded values contribute to STAT-E; calculations that summarize them contribute to STAT-I.
A variable’s role concerns how it enters a particular analysis. An outcome (or dependent variable) is what the analysis describes, explains, or predicts. If the question asks how assessment scores differ between formats, score is the outcome and feedback format identifies the comparison groups. A predictor, such as a prior assessment score, can help model the outcome. Papers may use “independent variable” for a predictor or an experimentally manipulated condition. Identify the role from the question and analysis, then follow the design and justification to understand whether the relationship receives a causal interpretation. The same variable can serve a different role in another analysis.



Table 2: Statistical Evidence: Traceable Information











Traceable information
What to identify
Common cases
Likely documentary location




Data structure, units, and variable roles
What a record represents; repeated or grouped observations; outcome and predictor roles.
Students are recorded within classes; assessment score is the outcome and assigned format is the grouping variable.
Data description; Measures; dictionary


Measurement scales, instruments, and procedures
The response scale, instrument, scoring, and administration actually reported.
Responses use ordered categories; an assessment is scored from 0 to 40 and administered two weeks after instruction.
Measures; instrument; scoring guide; Procedures


Design and implementation information
Whom the study concerns; sample selection or recruitment; assignment or exposure; comparison structure and timing.
Classes are recruited from schools and randomly assigned to formats; another study observes existing exposures without assigning them.
Participants; Design; Procedures; protocol


Analysis sample, exclusions, and missing data
Which units and observations entered each analysis, their counts, and reported omissions or exclusions.
Some recruited participants lack follow-up scores; an analysis uses the records meeting a stated inclusion rule.
Participant flow; Results; data-processing record






Note. Identify both the number entering the study and the number included in each analysis. A participant may contribute several observations, so distinguish participant counts from observation counts.
Measurement information is classified by its use. The instrument, scoring, and administration record contribute to STAT-E. Reasons for using those measurements in a statistical procedure belong in STAT-J. What the scores mean substantively belongs in SUB-E, while reasons supporting that meaning belong in SUB-J. To identify Justification, look for the reasons given for using or interpreting the instrument.


Statistical Justification: invoked reasons and conditions
STAT-J identifies the reasons and conditions the study invokes for its statistical reasoning. Table 3 separates support from the design, sample-size planning, method choice, and assumptions.



Table 3: Statistical Justification: Traceable Information











Traceable information
What to identify
Common cases
Likely documentary location




Design-based support for inference
How sampling, assignment, or comparison design is invoked to support the intended inference.
Probability sampling is invoked for population inference; random assignment is invoked to support an assigned-group comparison.
Design rationale; sampling plan; protocol


Sample-size, power, and precision rationale
Why the amount of evidence was planned in relation to an inferential goal.
Planned sample size aims at a stated confidence-interval width or power for a specified effect.
Sample-size calculation; protocol; planning supplement


Rationale for selecting statistical methods and models
Reasons connecting the chosen procedure to the estimand, measurement scale, or data structure.
Welch’s method is chosen because it allows unequal group variances; within-class dependence is allowed because students share classes.
Statistical Analysis; analysis plan


Statistical assumptions invoked
Conditions the study relies on for its comparison, model, or uncertainty calculation.
Independence between observations is assumed for a standard-error calculation; a model assumes a linear relationship.
Statistical Analysis; assumptions statement; technical supplement






Note. Alongside the named plan or method, identify the reasons invoked for its use. Evaluate those reasons’ adequacy separately.
Sampling and assignment are distinct parts of study design. Sampling concerns which units enter a study; assignment concerns which conditions they receive. Random sampling provides a basis for population inference under the sampling design, contributing to generalizability or external validity. Random assignment supports a causal comparison of assigned conditions, contributing to internal validity. Both forms of support depend on the relevant implementation and analysis conditions. A study may use either form of randomization or both. To trace assignment, look for the allocation procedure used to form the groups. A protocol documents the planned procedure; implementation records document what was carried out.
A procedure and its rationale do different work. “Students were randomly assigned” records a production procedure in STAT-E. “Random assignment provides the basis for estimating the effect of assignment from the comparison” identifies the reason invoked in STAT-J. Locate this connection in an explicit rationale or by following the documented links among design, estimand, and analysis.
Likewise, “100 participants were analyzed” records the analysis sample. “The sample size was planned to achieve the desired precision” supplies a planning rationale. Precision concerns estimation uncertainty; power concerns the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis under a specified alternative and procedure. The reader identifies the stated goal before considering whether the planning was adequate.
A statistical model represents selected relationships or variation mathematically. When a study invokes an assumption as a condition supporting inference, that contribution belongs in STAT-J. The specification actually fitted, and the reported analytical checks, contribute to STAT-I. A passage can describe the fitted model and invoke its assumptions as support; identify what each contribution does. “We used SPSS” helps identify the software used for computation. Look for the method-selection rationale to identify the reasons for the analytical choice.


Statistical Inference: analytical work and its consequences
STAT-I is often the most demanding component to understand, both technically and in its statistical reasoning, especially in large-scale, complex studies. It traces the central statistical information of the argument: how evidence, analyzed under the study’s stated conditions and justification, supports a statistical conclusion. Understanding this transition requires reasoning about variation, uncertainty, models, and alternative analyses. Some of these ideas challenge everyday intuition, so learning to follow the reasoning is as important as learning the procedures. Much of the statistical reasoning developed in later chapters therefore relates directly to STAT-I. Its contribution becomes clear through its connections with evidence production, justification, substantive interpretation, and the bounded answer.
STAT-I connects the estimand with the analysis performed, its results, uncertainty, and relevant checks. Model building specifies the statistical relationships to be estimated. Diagnostics examine how the fitted model and estimation procedure behave; sensitivity analysis examines how results change under alternative analytical choices. A statistical hypothesis expresses a proposition to be examined, such as a zero mean difference. Table 4 connects these activities to their traceable information and reported results.



Table 4: Statistical Inference: Traceable Information











Traceable information
What to identify
Common cases
Likely documentary location




Describing data and relationships
How observations and associations are summarized.
Means and standard deviations describe scores; a correlation describes a linear association between two numerical variables.
Descriptive tables; Results; figures


Model building and estimation
Model specification in equations, diagrams, or syntax; connection to declared estimands; estimation procedure, computational implementation, and point estimates.
A regression equation specifies score differences by feedback format; software estimates its coefficients and the declared contrast.
Statistical Analysis; model diagram; Results; syntax or code


Model diagnostics, modification, and sensitivity analysis
Fit and computational checks; model or analysis changes; sensitivity to choices or priors; independent assessment of model structure; predictive validation.
Residuals suggest curvature; another prior changes estimates; new observations assess a prespecified structure or a fitted prediction rule.
Diagnostic figures; analytical supplement; validation results; code


Statistical uncertainty and interval estimates
The reported uncertainty for an estimate or prediction, including its procedure and stated level.
A standard error and confidence interval accompany a mean difference; a prediction interval accompanies a new-case prediction.
Results; interval tables; figures


Statistical hypotheses, testing, and comparison
Hypotheses or restrictions examined; tests and comparison criteria; competing models where relevant; test statistics, p-values, or other comparison results.
A test examines a zero mean difference or equal coefficients; competing models are compared by a test or predictive performance.
Hypothesis statement; Statistical Analysis; Results; model-comparison table






Note. Some descriptive questions are answered by summaries alone. For analyses and modifications, record whether they were prospectively specified, exploratory, or revised when known. “Primary” describes priority. Separately describe when and how the analysis was specified or changed, and whether relevant outcomes had already been examined.
Connect a calculation to the question it addresses. A group mean difference may estimate the declared contrast between feedback formats. For a question about how two numerical variables vary together, a correlation summarizes their linear association. Regression describes an outcome in relation to one or more predictors; the coefficients address particular relationships in the fitted model. The reported calculation and its role in answering the question belong together when you read STAT-I.
Follow model building through to the estimates. An equation or a statistical path diagram might represent assessment score as an outcome related to feedback format and prior score. Identify how the model represents the declared estimand, which could be a coefficient or a contrast calculated from several coefficients. Then follow the estimation procedure to its point estimates. Computational information may appear in R scripts, software syntax, menu settings, or a Methods description; each can help identify what was implemented.
Specifying the model and fitting it contribute to STAT-I. Reasons for choosing that specification or estimation method contribute to STAT-J. Likewise, a diagram expressing the fitted statistical relationships helps trace STAT-I, while a diagram explaining a substantive mechanism may contribute to SUB-J. The diagram’s contribution depends on what it represents in this study.
Distinguish variation in the observations from estimation uncertainty. Students’ assessment scores vary, and a standard deviation describes that variation. An estimated mean difference also has uncertainty: its standard error describes how the estimate would vary under the specified sampling, assignment, or model conditions. A confidence interval concerns the mean difference. For example, an interval from 1 to 5 points expresses uncertainty about the difference between means, rather than the range of individual students’ scores.
A p-value addresses a null hypothesis under the test’s assumptions; it is not the probability that the null is true. These concepts receive fuller statistical treatment later. For now, identify what each output concerns and follow the reported uncertainty into the substantive interpretation and the study’s conclusions.
Follow the checks, changes, and their consequences. Diagnostics can examine model fit, unusual observations, or whether the estimation algorithm reached a stable solution. A modification changes the model or analysis, for example by adding a curved relationship after examining residuals. Record what changed, why the study says it changed, and the result. A stated reason for the change may also contribute to STAT-J.
Sensitivity analysis asks how estimates or conclusions change under alternative choices or assumptions. In a Bayesian analysis, a prior distribution expresses information or assumptions about model parameters before incorporating the current data. Repeating an analysis with alternative priors can show how sensitive its findings are to those choices. The prior used is part of the model specification; reasons invoked for choosing it can contribute to STAT-J.
Independent observations can assess a model’s structure as well as its predictions. For example, researchers might retain the prespecified predictors and straight-line form of a regression, re-estimate its coefficients in a new sample, and examine whether that structure adequately describes the new data. Predictive validation instead assesses an already fitted rule on observations not used to develop it, keeping that rule fixed for the assessment. Identify what was held fixed, what was re-estimated, and whether the reported assessment concerns structure or prediction.
Checks, modifications, and sensitivity analyses can inform one another. During reading, identify the study’s reported checks and assessments; quality evaluation then considers whether they provide adequate support.
Distinguish specifying a restriction from examining it. A model constraint restricts the values parameters may take, for example by setting a coefficient to zero or requiring two coefficients to be equal. Using such a constraint to specify a model belongs with model building. Examining the restriction through a test or comparison belongs with statistical hypotheses, testing, and comparison. Some constraints instead serve to define a model’s scale or make its parameters estimable; identify the role of each constraint from the study’s account.
Model comparisons can also use criteria other than hypothesis tests, such as prediction error on held-out observations. Record which models were compared, by what criterion, and with what result. The same analysis may contribute both predictive validation and a comparison; identify these connected uses without treating them as separate analyses.


Statistical Claim: the conclusion and its scope
STAT-C records the statistical proposition the study concludes, together with its stated qualifications. Table 5 uses familiar ideas from the analysis in the different function of stating an answer.



Table 5: Statistical Claim: Traceable Information











Traceable information
What to identify
Common cases
Likely documentary location




Reported statistical conclusion
What is concluded about direction, magnitude, or pattern, including a testing conclusion when reported.
The study concludes that mean scores are higher in one group; it describes an association as negative.
Results summary; Abstract; Discussion


Remaining uncertainty and scope of the conclusion
What remains unresolved and which units, comparisons, conditions, or periods the conclusion covers.
Whether an effect reaches a stated size remains unresolved; the conclusion is restricted to participating units.
Results interpretation; limitations; Conclusion






Connect analytical outputs to the statistical conclusion. A calculated mean difference with its interval contributes to STAT-I. “The comparison indicates a positive mean difference for the participating students” states a conclusion in STAT-C. A reported claim of statistical significance may be part of C; the p-value producing that claim remains an analytical result in I. Include a significance claim when the study makes one, and record the answer with its reported bounds. Keep any reader-proposed revisions separate. “We investigated whether the groups differ” identifies the question; look for the reported finding to identify its answer.


Following substantive meaning across the linked layers
The substantive layer builds on the statistical layer and connects it to the people, measures, practices, and settings named by the question. Its information is more domain-dependent and can be directly documented: look for what an assessment covers or what an intervention involved. Table 6 retains four component rows; the cases illustrate different possible studies.



Table 6: Substantive Components: Traceable Information












Component
Traceable information
What to identify
Common cases
Likely documentary location




SUB-E
People and setting, measure meanings, and implemented practices
What the recorded units, scores, conditions, or exposures represent in the substantive domain.
A course assessment covers application tasks; guided practice consists of worked examples and feedback.
Participants; Measures; instrument; intervention description


SUB-J
Theory, mechanisms, and reasons supporting interpretation
Reasons invoked about measurement, implementation, comparability, alternatives, practical benchmarks, or applicability elsewhere.
Assessment coverage supports the score interpretation; an importance benchmark is linked to expected benefits and effort.
Introduction; measurement rationale; protocol; Discussion


SUB-I
Contextual interpretation of statistical inference and uncertainty
How findings and uncertainty relate to substantive meanings, expectations, benchmarks, or proposed explanations.
An interval spans gains below and above a practical benchmark; the reported pattern is related to a proposed mechanism.
Results interpretation; Discussion


SUB-C
Question-facing answer, scope, and qualifications
The reported answer to the substantive question or answerable aim, with its stated limits and unresolved matters.
A practice improved delayed course performance in the studied setting, while the importance of the gain remains unresolved.
Abstract; Discussion; Conclusion






Note. A numerical statement can perform a substantive function when it expresses domain meaning. Identify the interpretation during reading and assess its support during quality evaluation.
Identify what a measure means and the reasons offered for that meaning. A description of an assessment’s application tasks tells you what the assessment covers, contributing to SUB-E. An explanation that these tasks cover the course objectives offers a reason for interpreting the score as course performance, contributing to SUB-J. Follow the instrument name to its description and the reasons given for interpreting its scores.
The same distinction helps with theory and mechanisms. A paper might describe a theory in its Introduction and later invoke one of its predictions to explain why feedback could improve performance. Identify the particular connection offered as substantive support. This makes the theory’s role in SUB-J visible, beyond simply recording that the paper mentions it. Apply the same reasoning to implementation, alternative explanations, and applicability elsewhere.
SUB-I retains the statistical uncertainty. When interpreting an interval against a practical benchmark, retain its full range and the possibilities it leaves open. Distinguish a pattern described as consistent with a proposed mechanism from evidence establishing that mechanism. SUB-C then states the study’s question-facing answer and its qualifications. Readers identify these interpretations and claims; quality evaluation asks whether the support warrants them.
A condition may be invoked even though the study has not checked it, and a check may later be invoked as support for another inference. Identify the use made of the information. Assuming independent classrooms is Justification for an uncertainty calculation. Examining dependence indicators and reporting the result is Inference. Using that result as a reason for a subsequent comparison gives it an additional justificatory role.
For missing outcomes, the number absent is Evidence; the assumption used to analyze incomplete records is Justification; imputation or a sensitivity analysis and its results are Inference. A method’s name alone does not settle what missingness mechanism would make its use defensible (Little & Rubin, 2019). Sensitivity analysis can make the conclusion’s dependence on an unverifiable assumption visible (National Research Council, 2010). It need not remove that dependence.
