title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
section: Reading One Argument Across a Paper and Its Related Materials
text:
Reading One Argument Across a Paper and Its Related Materials

The complete feedback packet
The following invented packet expands the same supplied feedback result. It adds documentary detail without generating a second experiment. The estimate and interval are stipulated teaching results; no set of student records is claimed to reproduce them. The class allocation is across the whole pool, not one class of each format forced within every school.

F1 – Abstract. We asked whether assignment to explanatory feedback changes average delayed achievement for eligible students in participating classes. Assignment increased average assessed course-topic performance under these conditions; the practical size remains uncertain.
F2 – Methods. Twelve schools contributed two classes each, with 20 eligible students per class. Before a six-week program, 12 of the 24 classes were randomly assigned to explanatory feedback and 12 to usual feedback across the full class pool. All 480 students supplied the common 0–40 assessment two weeks after the program and were analyzed by class assignment.
F3 – Protocol. Random allocation supplies the basis for the assignment comparison. Equally weighted class means give students equal weight because all classes have 20 eligible students. The uncertainty procedure reflects assignment of classes. The inference assumes implementation of allocation, a common outcome definition, complete follow-up and no influence of one class’s assignment on another class’s outcomes.
F4 – Assessment and implementation supplement. Both formats used the same topics and scheduled time. Explanatory feedback added explanations of errors; usual feedback supplied correctness feedback. Delivery logs documented the activities and separate materials. The assessment blueprint linked tasks to taught topics, and scorers worked without knowledge of format. The curriculum team judged two points, full credit on one application task, worth considering against the additional preparation.
F5 – Results and analytical supplement. The estimated student-average assignment effect was 2.5 points, approximate 95% CI [1, 4], with uncertainty reflecting class assignment. Checks confirmed score ranges, allocation, denominators and complete outcomes. Recalculating the contrast with each school omitted in turn left its point estimate positive. These are influence checks; the full eligible cohort remains the basis of the primary answer.
F6 – Discussion. Assignment improved average assessed performance on the taught topics in these classes and conditions. The compatible magnitudes include gains below and above the local two-point benchmark. Broader learning, durable effects beyond this follow-up and effects for every individual remain unresolved.

The claim in F1 is brief. F5 supplies its uncertainty, and F6 explains its scope. Reading these together preserves what the abstract alone leaves implicit. The protocol’s conditions also matter: the words “random assignment” cannot substitute for the allocation actually used or a matching uncertainty procedure.


Follow the comparison through both layers



Table 7: The result and the information needed to interpret it.










Quantity or feature
Supplied result
Meaning in the argument




Eligible students / assigned classes
480 / 24
Students define the target; classes receive assignment


Explanatory-minus-usual estimate
2.5 points
Estimated student-average assignment effect


Approximate 95% interval
[1, 4] points
Uncertainty reflecting class assignment


Local importance benchmark
2 points
One application task, considered against preparation effort


Assessment occasion
Two weeks after a six-week program
Delayed course-topic performance at the specified follow-up






The distinction between students and classes connects several components. The recorded score belongs to a student; allocation belongs to a class; the estimand weights students equally; and equal class sizes make equally weighted class means compatible with that target. Treating all 480 rows as independently assigned would change the inferential justification. The number of records in a file does not determine the number of independent assignments.



Table 8: A completed reading of the feedback argument.










Function
Particular contribution
Location




STAT-E
Class allocation, eligible records, scoring occasion and complete analysis sample
F2, with implementation in F4


STAT-J
Allocation rationale, equal-size weighting and conditions of the class-based uncertainty procedure
F3


STAT-I
Estimated contrast and interval; coding, denominator and influence checks
F5


STAT-C
Positive eligible-cohort average assignment-effect conclusion, with uncertainty
F1, F5–F6


SUB-E
Students, course topics, feedback activities and delayed assessment
F2 and F4


SUB-J
Blueprint, common conditions, delivery records and the local benchmark’s rationale
F4


SUB-I
Interval read against the application-task benchmark at this follow-up
F5–F6


SUB-C
Bounded answer about assessed course-topic performance, with broader claims unresolved
F6






One document can contribute to several functions, but locating it twice does not create two independent pieces of evidence. The blueprint’s description of tasks helps situate the outcome; its alignment with course objectives is also invoked as a reason for interpreting it. The statistical result supports a mean effect; it does not show that every student’s score increased by 2.5.






NotePredict, then explain: keep the numbers, change the design



Suppose the same reported estimate and interval appear in a different study where teachers selected their preferred feedback format. Before reading on, predict which part of the argument would change first and whether the same causal answer would remain warranted.


The allocation account changes Evidence and removes the random-assignment reason in Justification. Selection could be related to prior achievement, teacher resources or other causes of outcomes. The numerical table can remain the same while its causal warrant changes. Its interval also needs a stated uncertainty justification for the new design; copying the numbers does not carry the old calibration with them. A descriptive difference remains reportable, but it answers a different question from an assignment effect.


A missing explanation and a conflicting count
Two variants of the packet show why identification and judgment remain distinct. In the first, F3 is omitted from the paper but available in its protocol. The rationale is accessible: state that the protocol explains weighting and assignment-based uncertainty. Publication outside the article does not by itself weaken the reason, although readers need a way to find it.
In the second variant, F2 says all 480 students were analyzed, while a supplied flow table says 460 completed follow-up. The discrepancy is unresolved; the packet gives no reconciliation. State both accounts and their locations. Do not silently choose the number that makes the result easier to interpret. The target still concerns 480 eligible students, while the actual analysis membership and handling of missing outcomes need clarification. This may limit Evidence integrity and the ability to judge the whole answer.
The task is specific: which students are absent from which calculation, why, and how were their outcomes handled? Neither “the report has a supplement” nor “missing data were handled statistically” answers it. A useful reading identifies what further information could resolve the question.


A shorter transfer: predicting recorded student outcomes
The real data of Realinho and colleagues contain 4,424 students from the Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre, Portugal (Realinho et al., 2021; Realinho et al., 2022). Outcomes were recorded at the normal degree duration. Dropout can include changing course or institution; Enrolled means still enrolled at that endpoint; Graduate means completed. The binary teaching analysis compares recorded Dropout with the other categories combined, while preserving all three labels in the data.
The question is whether admission grade and age at enrollment improve prediction of that recorded outcome for held-out students from the same source. Both predictors are available at enrollment. Semester results would be too late for this intended prediction time. The teaching analysis uses a fixed, stratified approximately 70% training split and fits a logistic rule; this is a simplified analysis, not a reproduction of the source authors’ classifiers.



Table 9: Counts supporting the prediction comparison.





Records
Dropout
Enrolled
Graduate
Total




Full release
1,421
794
2,209
4,424


Training
994
562
1,540
3,096


Held out
427
232
669
1,328






The fitted rule assigns a probability to each held-out student’s recorded Dropout status. Average squared probability error is 0.2000, against 0.2182 for assigning everyone the training-data dropout proportion; lower is better. These errors compare probability predictions, rather than count correct alerts. At a probability cutoff of 0.5, the fitted rule flags 73 of the 427 held-out Dropout records, or 17.096%. A better average probability score therefore coexists with missing most eventual Dropout records at this threshold.
Outcome definitions, predictors, split and denominators are Evidence. Their availability at the intended time and separation of fitting from assessment supply reasons in Justification. The fit, probabilities, error comparison and threshold calculation are Inference. The reported Claim is that this simple rule improves average probability prediction on the internal held-out records, while this cutoff identifies only a small fraction of recorded Dropout.
In substantive terms, an alert is about this administrative outcome, not necessarily departure from higher education. The released data have no cohort-year field for an independent later-cohort assessment. Predicting well within this split neither establishes performance for a future cohort nor shows that an intervention prompted by an alert would help. Those are separately owed questions with different evidence requirements.


Focused passages from three other settings
Working from home. Bloom and colleagues’ experiment randomly assigned eligible volunteer employees, 131 to home work and 118 to office work (Appendix Table A.2, p. 214). The nine-month arrangement and four home-working days per week are described on p. 169. Table II, column 4, p. 187 reports a weekly log-call analysis for 134 order takers, using employee and week effects and uncertainty clustered by employee; the authors interpret the result on p. 188 as about 13% more weekly calls (Bloom et al., 2015). These are the paper’s rounded reporting choices. The 134 analysis employees are not a contradictory count of all 249 assigned employees: follow the outcome and employee group for the selected analysis. Allocation documents production; its invoked causal reason belongs to Justification; a regression and its reported comparison belong to Inference. The author’s materials allow a reader to inspect the underlying reports. Repeated weekly outcomes also explain why counting weeks as independent employees would be a mistake.
Confidence and belonging. In an invented study, three 0–100 confidence indicators ask about explaining, applying and checking learning tasks; three belonging indicators concern acceptance, inclusion and participation. The questions, scoring and administration supply measurement records. Their content situates the scores in a substantive domain. Reasons why these items represent the intended constructs provide substantive Justification. A scoring rule alone cannot establish that interpretation. Reading these contributions requires no factor analysis in this chapter.
Language progress. An invented student scores 58, 65, 68 and 76 at equally spaced occasions; another scores 62, 63, 67 and 68. Their average gains per interval are 6 and 2, but successive observed gains are 7, 3, 8 and 1, 4, 1. A constant average is not a constant observed trajectory. Student and occasion identifiers document the repeated structure. A reason for modeling within-student dependence is distinct from the data layout. A missing assessment is also different from a student who was never observed or eligible for this study.


Follow the organization and the reporting
Two auxiliary tasks help when a reading becomes difficult. Identifying organization asks which result belongs to which question, what information is shared, and which results support rather than replace the focal answer. The feedback influence checks support the one assignment-effect argument; each omitted-school calculation does not create a new substantive question. A separate question about preparation burden would need its own stated answer unless it had been defined as a strand required for one integrated decision.
Following reporting connects an abstract’s conclusion to a Results table’s interval and a Discussion’s scope. F1, F5 and F6 form that chain. The task adds no new component: it follows how the existing contributions are expressed and located. A concise abstract and a qualified Discussion need to be read together, but the fuller passage does not excuse a plainly contradictory headline. Argument B develops these tasks when several answers depend on one another. Here they organize a reading without adding another taxonomy.


Read a reported regression argument
The following teaching report concerns 102 historical occupation records from carData::Prestige (Fox et al., 2022). It is written for this tutorial. R1–R4 are locations within the teaching report, not quotations from the dataset’s authors. A slope describes how fitted occupation-average income changes with education; \(R^2\) describes the fraction of recorded income variation accounted for by the line, and residual SD describes remaining vertical scatter in income units. These local reminders support the reading; no regression calculation is required.






NoteTeaching report: an occupation-level description




R1 – Question and evidence. We described the education–income relationship in the 102 carData::Prestige occupation records. Income was expressed in thousand 1971 Canadian dollars. All records had both modeled measurements. Each occupation was weighted equally; the observed education range was 6.38–15.97 years.
R2 – Offered reasons. The upward scatterplot motivated a straight-line summary. OLS was chosen because it minimizes squared vertical discrepancies. The aim was a summary of these records, not a constant causal effect or an individual-level comparison. The source documentation identifies the measurements as historical occupational averages. No probability-sampling justification was available in the record consulted.
R3 – Analysis and interpretation. The fitted slope was 0.8988 thousand dollars per education year, with \(R^2=.3336\) and residual SD 3.4834 thousand dollars. The residual pattern and a curved-fit sensitivity qualified the line as an incomplete description. The fit and sensitivities were exploratory. The descriptive result itself was not assigned sampling uncertainty.
R4 – Reported answer. Across these 102 recorded occupations, higher average education accompanied higher average income overall. The least-squares line summarized that pattern by about 899 additional 1971 dollars of fitted occupation-average income per education year over the observed range. It did not describe every occupation closely or establish an individual or causal return to education.






Table 10: Reading one regression argument with linked statistical and substantive layers.










Function
Content read in this report
Where the information is found




STAT-E
Records, measurements, scaling, and complete sample
R1


STAT-J
Reasons for OLS as a descriptive, noncausal summary
R2


STAT-I
Slope, fit, sensitivity, and exploratory status
R3


STAT-C
Positive but incomplete description over recorded support
R4


SUB-E
Historical occupation averages, not individual measurements
R1 and the dataset documentation


SUB-J
Measurement meanings supporting an occupation-level reading
R2 and the dataset documentation


SUB-I
Meaning of about 899 dollars per education year
R3–R4


SUB-C

R4






R4 names the 102 recorded occupations and the descriptive line. It does not claim a population slope, so the reader attaches no confidence interval to that answer. The fitted slope is one statistical strand; fit summaries and checks support its interpretation rather than supply separately owed substantive answers.
Now replace R2’s reason with “We used R, so our slope is an unbiased causal effect.” The offered reason is identifiable STAT-J content even though it is inadequate. Reading records it as given. The next section judges whether it supports the claim. A reader does not silently supply random assignment or replace the report’s question with a better one.

title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
section: Evaluating the Quality of the Question-Level Argument
text:
Evaluating the Quality of the Question-Level Argument

Six questions, with reasons rather than scores
Evaluation depends on the argument that has been read. Its six questions focus attention on a particular weakness or strength; they are not six new components and their judgments are not a total quality score. Some questions overlap in the consequence they reveal. Name where a problem first arises, then explain what it changes later in the argument.



Table 11: Six questions for evaluating one question-level argument.










Group
Evaluation question
What to consider




Alignment
Question alignment
Whether the question, estimand, design, evidence, analysis, and answer remain directed at the same aim


Support
Evidence integrity
Whether the observations and contextual records, their production, and their representation are trustworthy, traceable, and appropriate


Support
Justification adequacy
Whether the statistical, design, measurement, and contextual reasons warrant the proposed moves


Support
Inferential adequacy
Whether reasoning within both layers is adequate, including estimation, uncertainty, checks, sensitivity, and substantive interpretation


Translation
Transition fidelity
Whether the links between layers retain meaning, uncertainty, design status, and scope


Translation
Claim calibration
Whether the reported answer’s strength and breadth match its support






A local judgment is adequate for this purpose, needs revision, insufficient information to judge, or not applicable. Accompany it with a reason: “the complete cohort supports the stated denominator” is informative; “Evidence integrity: adequate” alone does not show what was inspected.
The whole question-answer pair can be supported as stated, supported only after narrowing or revision, not supported, or not assessable from the accessible record. These outcomes distinguish a warranted answer from an unwarranted one and an unresolved documentary gap from a demonstrated failure. An inconclusive answer can be supported as stated. A study need not discover a benefit to provide a defensible answer to its question.


Evaluate the feedback claim and its variants
The baseline feedback answer retains the eligible cohort, assigned classes, assessment meaning and follow-up. Its interval is above zero but crosses the two-point benchmark. Within the supplied conditions, the positive average assignment-effect conclusion is supported as stated, with practical size uncertain. That judgment is about this bounded answer, not a certificate that the study has answered every educational question.



Table 12: Applying evaluation to the supplied feedback answer.









Evaluation question
Application to the feedback packet




Question alignment
The answer remains about the eligible-cohort assignment effect at the stated occasion


Evidence integrity
Allocation, common scoring, denominators and complete follow-up are documented


Justification adequacy
The class-assignment comparison and equal-size weighting address the target, under the stated implementation and no-between-class-influence conditions


Inferential adequacy
The stated uncertainty reflects assignment; checks inform the calculation without establishing every assumption


Transition fidelity
Two score points retain their course-specific meaning; a cohort-average effect does not become each student’s gain


Claim calibration
A positive delayed-assessment conclusion retains an unresolved practical magnitude and limited reach






Now consider “the format produces substantial, lasting improvements in all forms of learning for every student.” The result has not changed. Transition fidelity needs revision because an assessment of taught topics has become all learning and an average has become every individual. Claim calibration needs revision because the two-week follow-up has become indefinitely lasting and practical importance has been settled despite the interval crossing the benchmark. Narrowing that overstatement back to the declared cohort-average question preserves a supported answer. Claiming an individual response instead would introduce a different estimand requiring different evidence.
For the conflicting-count variant, Evidence integrity is unresolved. If the missing outcomes could change the comparison and their handling is unknown, the whole answer may be not assessable from the accessible record. This differs from a documented coding error that demonstrably changes the result: then the calculation and answer need revision. Different concerns call for different remedies, not a common penalty score.






NotePredict, then explain: the estimate stays the same



A separate invented study reports the same 2.5-point estimate but an interval from \(-1\) to 6 points. Its local benchmark is still two points. What changes in the conclusion about direction and importance, and what stays unchanged?


The point estimate stays positive, but the interval now includes a negative effect, zero and gains both below and above the benchmark. The study cannot settle direction or practical size at the stated level. Reporting that uncertainty can be a supported answer. “No effect” would discard compatible positive and negative values; “2.5 points proves a meaningful benefit” would discard the uncertainty. The interval concerns an average effect, not the range of individual student effects.


Evaluate the prediction promise
The student prediction comparison supports a limited promise: lower average squared probability error than the training-prevalence rule on this internal held-out set. Evidence integrity concerns the outcome coding and disjoint fit and assessment records. Justification adequacy concerns predictor availability at enrollment and an assessment population relevant to the intended use. Inferential adequacy concerns the specified error measure and any uncertainty or stability needed for a stronger comparative claim.
The 0.5 cutoff identifies 73 of 427 Dropout records. Claim calibration therefore requires a distinction between improved probability predictions and useful screening. A threshold could be changed, but deciding its value requires the consequences of missed cases and false alerts. An appropriate future evaluation would preserve the chosen rule and threshold before measuring performance in the new setting. Trying thresholds on the same assessment set and reporting only the best would spend that set on selection.
A future-cohort promise remains unassessed because the released record does not permit a later-cohort split. A causal claim that acting on alerts prevents dropout is also unassessed by this prediction analysis. More elaborate software cannot replace the missing time information or evidence about intervention consequences. The way forward is to identify the additional question and obtain evidence suited to it, rather than make the same error score carry it.


Evaluate the regression answer already read



Table 13: Evaluating the regression argument already read.









Quality-evaluation question
Application to the reported descriptive argument




Question alignment
Does the answer remain about the 102 occupations and the declared straight-line summary?


Evidence integrity
Are the source, aggregate unit, scaling, exclusions, and unusual records traceable?


Justification adequacy
Are the offered reasons adequate for a descriptive line, rather than stretched into random sampling or causal identification?


Inferential adequacy
Do the calculation and substantive reasoning support the reported pattern while retaining curvature and scatter?


Transition fidelity
Does the interpretation preserve occupation-level measurements, units, and exploratory status?


Claim calibration
Does the answer retain historical scope, supported range, and the limits of a linear summary?






R4 is supported as stated: it reports a checkable summary of named records and retains their unit and historical scope. Missing information about national sampling does not invalidate arithmetic on those named records. It would matter for a proposed national generalization. No fit summary establishes that the line describes every occupation closely; R3 acknowledges substantial scatter and a curved-fit sensitivity.
A model-based extension is a separate commitment. An interval for a process slope needs an appropriate mean model and uncertainty assumptions. The residual pattern and curvature qualify that extension. Changing only the covariance estimator might address a variance condition; it cannot make a straight conditional-mean relationship true or provide random sampling.
The news claim “another year of education increases income by about 900 dollars” is not supported by these records (Robinson, 1950). It moves from occupation averages to individuals and from description to causation. Replacing it with R4 changes the question-answer pair, not merely the tone of the conclusion. A causal comparison needs a design or identification argument. In Project STAR, for example, the within-school random assignment supplies a reason for causal comparison; the fact that a binary-regression slope equals a group-mean difference does not itself supply that reason (Finn & Achilles, 1990; Mosteller, 1995).

title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
section: From a Reading to a Documented Construction Cycle
text:
From a Reading to a Documented Construction Cycle

Six stages organize the work
A finished article is organized for communication. Its polished order does not prove when researchers made their decisions. A construction workflow describes how an argument is produced, whereas the component map describes how its support functions. A Methods paragraph may report a plan, a later repair or a post-inspection choice; dated records help distinguish them.
The six-stage cycle has two phases. Understand and plan develops a question and a coherent way to answer it. Produce and complete obtains the question-specific evidence, analyzes it and completes a bounded answer. Substantive reasons belong in both phases: measurement meaning and practical benchmarks should not be invented after the preferred result appears.



Table 14: A six-stage construction cycle for the feedback question.









Phase and stage
Feedback construction example




Understand and plan: 1. Review the problem, setting, and relevant literature
Review what feedback activities could support learning and what earlier assessments measured


2. Frame the question and, where useful, a candidate answer
Ask about the eligible-cohort average assignment effect on delayed course-topic performance


3. Align design, measurement, estimand, evidence-production or acquisition plan, and inferential plan
Commit to class allocation, equal student weighting, a common delayed assessment, complete follow-up and matching uncertainty; document the two-point rationale


Produce and complete: 4. Produce or acquire, and document, empirical and contextual evidence
Preserve allocation, delivery, scoring, follow-up and analysis-membership records


5. Estimate, check, and analyse
Estimate the contrast and interval; check coding, denominators and influential schools


6. Contextualize, interpret, and complete the bounded answer
Interpret the interval against its course benchmark and retain scope and unresolved practical size














Figure 2: The six-stage cycle has one forward handoff between planning and production. Iteration stays within each phase; changing anchored commitments starts a revised or additional cycle.







Read the decision history, not just the final order
The following chronology is an invented extension of the feedback protocol. It teaches how timing contributes to interpretation; it adds no new results.



Table 15: A decision history distinguishes refinement, repair and a new question.










Decision time
Documented action
What the record allows a reader to conclude




Before recruitment
The team specifies the eligible-cohort question, assessment occasion and two-point benchmark
These commitments precede relevant outcomes


During planning
A pilot reveals ambiguous delivery instructions; the team clarifies them and realigns the plan
A refinement within Phase 1, before production for this question


At production
The allocation list, class membership and scoring records are preserved
The plan can be compared with implementation


During analysis
A duplicated score entry is found; the original record is checked and the affected calculation corrected
A Phase 2 repair, retaining the original estimand and commitments


After inspecting outcomes
The team adds a question about baseline-score subgroups
An additional exploratory question and cycle, not a retrospectively planned primary question


At completion
The original answer retains the 2.5-point estimate and [1, 4] interval with practical size uncertain
Normal completion can preserve an unresolved practical judgment






The Phase 1 anchor records the question and mode, estimand, design, measurement, evidence-production or acquisition plan, inferential plan and, where relevant, a stopping rule. The one-way handoff makes changes to those commitments visible. It is a convention for documenting research, not a claim that investigators can never learn from outcomes and redesign a study.
For existing data, Stage 4 can mean obtaining or designating the records for this question, rather than the first time anyone has opened the original file. A decision is prospective with respect to relevant evidence only if its timing supports that claim. Calling a later reanalysis “Phase 1” does not erase prior outcome access. Conversely, a documented revision before relevant outcome access need not be called exploratory merely because it is a revision.


Completion, repair and a revised question
Three endings make the record honest. Normal completion answers the planned question, possibly inconclusively or against an expectation. Phase 2 repair corrects work while retaining its anchored question and commitments. An additional or revised cycle makes a changed question, estimand or inferential commitment explicit and gives the earlier cycle a visible outcome. If the intended delayed assessment was administered immediately, the original delayed-performance question is not answerable as planned. The immediate scores can support another question with its own scope.
Changing a score-coding error is a repair; replacing the planned outcome after seeing a disappointing result is a revised question and must preserve that timing. A prespecified sensitivity can be run within the planned cycle. A new sensitivity motivated by a surprising diagnostic can also be documented as such; it does not acquire prospective status by being sensible. If it changes a prior inferential commitment, record a revised cycle rather than overwrite the original.
A new cycle can reuse literature, records, measures and code. Reuse saves work, but does not transfer a causal warrant, population scope or prospective status automatically. For the occupation report, planning would declare historical occupation units, a finite-record slope and checks. Completion would preserve the records, estimate and examine the line, and report the bounded description. Changing to an individual causal return would require a different question and evidence, rather than a different coefficient label.
Researchers can use the six evaluation questions during construction to judge what a stage produces. The questions do not become workflow stages. Reading identifies support; evaluation judges its adequacy; construction documents how support is developed. Keeping these tasks distinct makes room for judgment without requiring a ritual sequence every time a paper is opened.

title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
text:
Summary and Reading Bridge
A useful reading connects the question and reported answer to particular information at inspectable locations. Procedures, invoked reasons, analysis and conclusions can appear in the same paragraph while doing different work. The substantive layer follows what those contributions mean for the study’s people, measures and setting. An inadequate offered reason is still part of the argument to be read; its adequacy is a separate judgment.
The feedback packet showed how allocation, weighting, assessment meaning and uncertainty support one bounded answer. The student example distinguished an internal probability comparison from a useful alert or future-cohort promise. The occupation report separated a finite-record description from individual causal claims. In each case, changing one fact can change the support even when the numerical output stays the same.
This approach is a teaching synthesis, informed by Toulmin’s warrants and qualifications (Toulmin, 2003), LeMire’s connection between statistical testing and substantive reasoning (LeMire, 2010), and Kane’s argument-based account of interpretations and uses (Kane, 2013). Work on estimands (Lundberg et al., 2021) and quantitative reporting (Appelbaum et al., 2018) develops the link between a target and the inspectable record. These sources complement statistical method knowledge; the component labels cannot replace that knowledge.
Argument B extends the reading to several statistical strands required for one answer and to separate questions whose support depends on one another. Each argument chapter supplies its own local recap and cases. Courses can select one without requiring a running case carried through every chapter.

Key terms
The Part One Concept Reference brings the shared terms together. This table selects the terms developed in this argument chapter.



Table 16: Selected terms introduced in Argument Chapter A.











Concept group
Term and common alternatives
Meaning or essential distinction
Main explanation




Argument-based reading
Argument component
One of the four functions, evidence, justification, inference, and bounded claim, that a piece of study information performs in the statistical or the substantive layer. A reader identifies the function before judging its adequacy.
Arg. A, Sec. 2


Argument-based reading
Documentary location
The place in a report or its related materials, such as Methods, a protocol, a codebook, or an analytical supplement, where the traceable information for a component is found.
Arg. A, Sec. 1


Argument-based reading
Evaluation question
One of the six questions on alignment, support, and translation used to judge the quality of a question-level argument after it has been read. Each receives a reasoned judgment, not a score.
Arg. A, Sec. 4

title: How to Read a Quantitative Study as an Argument
text:
Exercises
Each prompt supplies its own record. Explain the consequential connection; a complete component map is needed only when the question asks for one.


Exercise 1: Find the question and the reported answer (Foundational)
An invented abstract states: “We examined whether assigning weekly planning messages rather than usual course messages changes the average final-assessment score for 100 consenting students in one course. The planning group averaged 78 and the usual group 73 on a 100-point assessment. We conclude that planning messages improve achievement for every university student.” The excerpt gives no allocation procedure or interval.

Formulate the research question from the aim, identifying your wording as a reader’s formulation. Locate the numerical result and reported answer.
Identify the question’s mode and estimand. Distinguish the five-point estimate from that target.
Name one specific piece of supporting information to seek and a plausible documentary location. State one way the reported answer exceeds the record.





Exercise 2: Distinguish a procedure, a reason and a result (Foundational)
An invented report contains these passages:

M1: Twelve of 24 classes were randomly allocated to each feedback format.
P1: Random allocation supports comparing the assigned formats for the participating classes; uncertainty must reflect class assignment.
R1: The estimated eligible-cohort average assignment effect is 2.5 points, approximate 95% CI [1, 4].
D1: Assignment increased average assessed performance in these classes; practical magnitude remains uncertain against the two-point benchmark.


Identify the main statistical function of each passage and its location.
Explain why locating P1 in a protocol rather than the paper does not change its function. Is its location itself a judgment of adequacy?
In a variant, P1 says “Random assignment makes these classes representative of all schools.” Identify its function first, then explain the problem with the offered reason.





Exercise 3: Follow an interval into an answer (Integrative)
A separate invented workshop study randomly assigns 80 participants equally to two feedback formats. Everyone completes the same immediate 20-point quiz. The estimated assigned-group mean difference is 1.1 points, 95% CI [-0.2, 2.4]. The documented uncertainty procedure matches assignment. Before outcomes were examined, a 1.5-point difference was identified as potentially important.

State the estimate, uncertainty and substantive benchmark, explaining what each contributes. Does the interval describe individual participants’ gains?
Which directions and practical-size conclusions remain compatible with the interval? Write a bounded answer of no more than two sentences.
Explain what additional evidence would be needed to turn this answer about an immediate quiz into a claim about durable professional learning.





Exercise 4: Read incomplete or conflicting materials (Integrative)
In an invented feedback report, Methods says all 480 eligible students were included. A linked flow table says 460 supplied follow-up scores. The analysis code is unavailable. The protocol explains class allocation and equal-size weighting, but does not explain missing outcomes.

State what each source contributes and the specific unresolved difference. Which information would you seek next, and why?
Explain why the protocol is useful support even though it does not resolve this discrepancy. Do two references to the protocol create independent evidence?
Give a reasoned local evaluation and explain when “not assessable from the accessible record” is preferable to declaring the whole answer unsupported.





Exercise 5: Predict the consequence of a changed design (Integrative)
A supplied invented report gives a 2.5-point mean difference and 95% interval [1, 4] for 480 students in 24 classes, and concludes that assigning explanatory feedback improved average delayed performance in those classes. In Version A, classes were randomly assigned and uncertainty reflects that allocation. In Version B, teachers chose their preferred format; the numerical table is identical, and no adjustment or identification argument is supplied.

Predict whether the same causal answer remains supported in Version B. Explain which changed fact matters before referring to the interval.
Apply Justification adequacy and Claim calibration selectively. Distinguish a numerical difference from the support for its causal interpretation and its uncertainty calculation.
If you replace the causal answer with a description of the observed groups, are you only narrowing the same answer or answering a different question?
For Version A, change only the interval to [-1, 6]. Explain what changes in the conclusion about direction and the two-point importance benchmark.





Exercise 6: Read a documented construction history (Integrative)
An invented team makes these decisions about its planned delayed-assessment feedback study:
A. Before recruitment, a pilot reveals ambiguous instructions; the team clarifies delivery and realigns its plan.
B. During analysis, a verified duplicated score is corrected and the declared comparison is recalculated.
C. After viewing outcomes, the team chooses an immediate quiz instead of its planned delayed assessment because the result looks more favorable.
D. The declared analysis is completed, but its interval leaves meaningful benefit and harm compatible; the team reports that uncertainty.

Classify each decision as refinement within Phase 1, repair within Phase 2, a revised/additional cycle, or normal completion. Give a reason.
State what the record of C must preserve. Name one useful resource that can be reused and one status that does not transfer automatically.
If the delayed assessment was never administered, what should be recorded about the original question? Explain why an orderly final Methods section cannot establish that decisions were prospective.





Exercise 7: Locate the reasons, then judge the answers (Integrative)
The report below is invented for this exercise. It is the whole report; no assignment or sampling documentation accompanies it.
S1. We describe how average weekly study time relates to average test score in 60 secondary schools, using each school’s recorded averages for one term. School-average study time ranged from 2 to 6 hours a week, and every school had both averages.
S2. A scatterplot of the 60 schools showed a roughly straight upward pattern, so we summarized it with a least-squares line. We used a regression program, so the coefficient is a causal effect.
S3. The fitted slope was 4 test-score points per additional hour of school-average weekly study time.
S4. Across these 60 schools, schools with more average study time had higher average scores: the least-squares line summarized the pattern by about 4 points of fitted school-average score per additional hour over the observed 2–6 hours.
S5. Each additional hour a student studies raises that student’s score by 4 points.

Locate the reasons the report offers and its reported answers. Name the function each performs and the paragraph where you find it.
Before judging it, say what function the sentence “We used a regression program, so the coefficient is a causal effect” performs. Then apply Justification adequacy to it.
Judge S4 as the answer to a descriptive question about these 60 schools. Is it supported as stated? Does it need an interval?
Apply Transition fidelity and Claim calibration to S5. Is it supported? Explain whether replacing S5 with S4 narrows the same answer or answers a different question.

title: Part Two: Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling
text:
Part Two of Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral Research is about latent-variable modeling. The methods of Part One worked with variables that were recorded: a test score, a count, a group label. Here the variable of primary interest is one that no column of the data set holds. Twelve questionnaire items are recorded; the planning, the learning strategies and the sense of belonging those items are meant to register are not. Part Two asks what follows from taking that situation seriously, and answers through factor analysis: how observed responses represent latent variables, and how a measurement model is developed, specified, estimated, evaluated and extended.
It is written for postgraduate students and applied researchers who have read Part One or who already command the statistics it develops: variable form, variance, covariance and correlation; estimates, sampling uncertainty, intervals and tests, with the limits of a dichotomous decision; regression equations, residuals and conditional comparisons; nested model comparison and penalized in-sample criteria; held-out evidence; and reproducible work in R. Part One’s argument-based reading of a study is useful background rather than a prerequisite.
The first four chapters form the measurement foundation. Chapter 1, From Latent-Variable Modeling to Factor Analysis, is the general and conceptual presentation. Chapter 2, Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development, is the exploratory approach, conceptual and practical. Chapter 3, Specifying and Estimating Confirmatory Factor Models, is the foundational confirmatory approach, covering the general model, specification, identification, estimation and basic global and local evaluation. Chapter 4, Evaluating and Comparing Confirmatory Factor Models, develops comparison, revision, independent validation and the higher-order and bifactor extensions. The chapters after them carry the structural half of the subject, from relations between factors and indicators to relations among variables in a structural system; the last section here says what they cover and what they cannot confer.
Part Two asks for more mathematics than Part One did. Readers manipulate equations, count the moments a covariance matrix supplies against the parameters a model spends, and work with small vectors and matrices: a matrix product, a transpose, a symmetric matrix, a diagonal matrix. No previous course in factor algebra or matrix calculus is assumed; each new operation appears first in a scalar or two-variable case, substantive and graphical meaning comes before notation, and every symbol, index and dimension is defined before it is used. Calculus and proof-based mathematical statistics are not prerequisites, and the longer derivations, identification theorems and asymptotic arguments are placed so that a reader can pass over them without losing a definition, an equation or an assumption the main route needs.
The situation the four chapters share can be put in one sentence and one equation. Several recorded responses vary together, and the attribute used to explain their association is not recorded at all; the common-factor model writes each recorded response as a common part, shared with the other responses through a small number of unobserved variables, plus a residual part that the declared common variables do not represent. For \(p\) indicators and \(m\) factors, with \(\mathbf y_i\) the \(p\times1\) vector of responses recorded for unit \(i\),
\[
\mathbf y_i=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\eta_i
  +\boldsymbol\epsilon_i,
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)
  &=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\alpha,\\
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)
  &=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi
    \boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Theta,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(E(\boldsymbol\epsilon_i)=\mathbf 0\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\eta_i,\boldsymbol\epsilon_i)=\mathbf 0\). Here \(\boldsymbol\nu\) holds the \(p\) indicator intercepts, \(\boldsymbol\eta_i\) the \(m\) factors for unit \(i\), \(\boldsymbol\Lambda\) the \(p\times m\) loadings that relate the two, and \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_i\) the \(p\) residuals; \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) holds the \(m\) latent intercepts, \(\boldsymbol\Phi\) is the \(m\times m\) factor covariance matrix, \(\boldsymbol\Theta\) the \(p\times p\) residual covariance matrix, and \(\boldsymbol\vartheta\) the complete vector of free parameters. What the model produces is the implied pair: a mean structure \(\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)\) and a covariance structure \(\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)\). An analysis working from covariances alone sets the mean structure aside or profiles it out under stated assumptions, which is a choice rather than an absence. One notation serves all four chapters, and it is chosen to survive the move to structural models, so that later chapters extend the model rather than quietly changing what its symbols mean.
The covariance equation is what makes the proposal answerable. Declared loadings, factor relations and residual restrictions imply one particular covariance matrix, and that matrix can be held against the one a sample supplies. The comparison has force because a covariance matrix for \(p\) indicators holds only \(p(p+1)/2\) distinct entries: a model that spends fewer parameters than that makes claims which can fail. That counting is a recurring operation in Part Two, and it is kept separate from the further question of whether those moments determine the parameters at all.
None of this makes a factor identical to the construct that names it. A construct is a substantive idea belonging to the research question, and its meaning comes from theory, item content, response processes, the population studied and the use intended for the results, none of which a covariance matrix supplies. A factor is a random variable inside a statistical model, and an observed or estimated score is neither; the three are never treated as synonyms. The arrow a path diagram draws from a factor to an indicator states the direction of representation the model adopts, writing each response as a function of the factors plus a residual. It is not a finding that the factor produces the response, and it is the wrong direction for a construct whose indicators produce it.
The scope is narrower than the vocabulary might suggest. Part Two models continuous indicators and continuous outcomes; ordered categorical indicators, thresholds, polychoric correlations and ordered-response factor models are signposted where a reader would meet them and are taught elsewhere, and numeric category codes are not automatically continuous measurements. The boundary concerns the indicators rather than every variable in a study: categorical grouping variables and dummy-coded predictors stay in scope, and the later multigroup and MIMIC work uses them alongside continuous indicators. The measurement foundation is the reflective common-factor model with its higher-order and bifactor relatives, estimated by normal-theory maximum likelihood across exploratory and confirmatory work; principal components analysis answers a different question and is not a common-factor estimator. What the family cannot do is as settled as what it can. No factor analysis establishes that a latent entity exists, that a reflective direction is causal, that a scale is valid, or that a structural claim is warranted; higher-order and bifactor models are rival representations of an adequate core model rather than repairs for a weak one; and reliability follows a defined score, model, population and use, so it is not validity and does not mend a weak measurement representation.

title: Part Two: Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling
section: How the Chapters Build on One Another
text:
How the Chapters Build on One Another
The first four chapters make four connected moves on one covariance equation: represent a common-factor model and derive the moments it implies; explore a development record to settle dimensionality, orientation and interpretation; formulate and evaluate the resulting proposal as explicit restrictions on evidence that played no part in producing it; and compare, revise and extend the fitted model. The equation is the same throughout. What changes at each stage is the responsibility it carries and the evidence it must answer to. Figure 1 sets out that architecture; no chapter redraws it.








Figure 1: The four-chapter architecture moves from representation to exploratory development, foundational CFA, and advanced CFA.





Table 1 states what each chapter is responsible for and what it hands to the chapter after it.



Table 1: The four-chapter measurement sequence.










Chapter
Main responsibility
What it hands forward




1. From Latent-Variable Modeling to Factor Analysis
Separate an observed variable, a latent random variable, a fixed parameter and a residual, and a factor from the construct that names it; write one two-factor, six-indicator system as scalar equations, matrices, a path diagram and a sentence and check the four against one another; say what a scaling, sign, location or coordinate convention supplies and what it cannot decide; derive \(\boldsymbol\Sigma=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Theta\); and say what exact reproduction does not establish
The vocabulary the three later chapters use without redefinition, and the known-value six-indicator records on which the algebra is checked before any sample is read


2. Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development
Audit indicators, units, coding and missingness before reading a correlation matrix; state which matrix an extraction targets; compare observed eigenvalues with a matched permutation reference and read a structured retention profile across seven rules; count effective parameters and candidate degrees of freedom; transform loadings and factor covariance together and say what rotation preserves; and read pattern coefficients, structure correlations, factor correlations and communalities together, locating discrepancy in a residual matrix rather than an average
A frozen candidate specification with its named rivals, its retained cross-loadings, the retention evidence behind it and an explicit list of unresolved alternatives, settled before any confirmation evidence is inspected


3. Specifying and Estimating Confirmatory Factor Models
State one restricted model as words, equations, parameter matrices and a diagram and check that they agree; separate free, fixed, equality-constrained, bounded and defined entries; set a latent metric by marker or fixed-factor scaling and transform between them; trace a cross-loading and a residual covariance into the moments each changes; count moments, free parameters and degrees of freedom and say why the count is not identification; check convergence, admissibility, gradients and local rank; read estimates with uncertainty, a basic global-fit profile and local residuals; and compare raw-record and derived-summary inputs
A specification and evaluation record: the exact specification and parameter ledger, the active items in order, the moment and degrees-of-freedom audit, the estimator and scaling settings, the convergence and admissibility record, estimates with their uncertainty, the basic global/local evidence and its limits, and the rivals declared in advance


4. Evaluating and Comparing Confirmatory Factor Models
Reconstruct the discrepancy the estimator minimized under a named divisor convention; read the exact-fit test, RMSEA with its interval, CFI, TLI and SRMR as answers to different questions; separate the three residual scales; establish exact nesting, run a compatible difference test and say when AIC and BIC are eligible; specify, count, fit and compare the higher-order and bifactor extensions; read modification indices and expected parameter change as leads that change analytic status; and freeze one revision and evaluate it on untouched records
A calibrated measurement conclusion whose analytic history and unresolved strain stay intact, and the structural question the later chapters take up: which latent variables are endogenous, which directional restrictions enter, and how measurement uncertainty is carried forward






Using one model family repeatedly does not give every record the same inferential role. Part Two keeps the analysis history visible so that development, first evaluation and independent revalidation are not collapsed into one favorable account. Every decision is inherited, prespecified, a planned sensitivity, or post hoc, always in relation to a named body of evidence, and that status follows the timing and provenance of the decision rather than the name of the function that fitted it: a model developed after inspecting a record is exploratory with respect to that record whatever routine estimates it, and a record made exploratory by revision does not recover confirmatory status because the next command is named after confirmation. The samples are never pooled to manufacture a larger analysis, and availability is not permission to use a record early. Table 2 gives the principal roles.



Table 2: Records keep distinct analytical roles even when they illustrate the same model family.










Record
First permitted use
What it cannot establish by itself




Known-value six-indicator records
Chapter 1 reconstructs an implied covariance matrix entrywise from parameters declared in advance
Sampling behavior, an empirical factor count, a unique rotation, a best model, or the existence of the constructs the columns are named after


SLE Sample A, 360 cases, development
Chapter 2 audits the indicators, develops the exploratory solution, and freezes the candidate with its named rivals
Independent confirmation of any choice made while Sample A was being inspected


SLE Sample B, 360 cases, confirmation
Chapter 3 estimates and gives a basic global/local evaluation of the frozen candidate; Chapter 4 develops comparative evaluation and diagnosis
Independent support for a relation first noticed in Sample B, which stays exploratory until fresh evidence tests it


SLE Sample C, 360 cases, revalidation
Chapter 4 evaluates the one revision frozen after Sample B
General validity, measurement invariance, or permission to search Sample C repeatedly for a revision that survives


Known SLE generating moments
Chapter 4 discloses them only after the Sample B and Sample C sequence is complete, then computes the population optimum and the population discrepancies directly
Contemporaneous justification for an earlier choice, or a finite-sample conclusion from one realization beyond what the audit separates


Separate constructed examples
Chapters 3 and 4 illustrate specified models with declared populations: a six-indicator system and a four-factor higher-order comparison
The development or confirmation status of the SLE sequence, which they never join






The Student Learning Experiences (SLE) records are a synthetic course case: continuous simulated data, not observations from actual students and not a validated instrument. Three independent samples of 360 complete cases carry twelve indicators – four Planning, four Strategy and four Belonging – drawn from one declared population and distributed together in sle_continuous.csv beside the chapters. Each analysis uses only the sample its role entitles it to, Chapter 1 uses none of them, and the Chapter 2 appendix supplies the codebook, the sample manifest and the generating population, so that every reported value can be reproduced. The retrospective audit that closes Chapter 4 is possible only because that population is known, and it is disclosed only after the Sample B and Sample C sequence has run its course: first the evidence a researcher could actually have had, then the generating structure the candidate omitted. It adds no further sample, no new candidate, no successful revision and no after-the-fact justification for a choice made earlier; its value is that a reader watches a model stay coherent, reproducible and apparently well fitting while still owing a narrower conclusion than its name suggests – which no real study can show.
The stopping points are as deliberate as the moves. Chapter 2 does not relabel a developed pattern as confirmation. Chapter 3 does not treat convergence or admissibility as adequate fit: it proceeds to a basic reading of global and local discrepancy, keeping the limits of that evidence visible. Chapter 4 does not treat favorable fit as construct validation. Each chapter completes one responsibility and transfers a defined record, rather than carrying an unexamined conclusion forward under a new name.

title: Part Two: Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling
section: How to Read a Chapter and Use the Concept Reference
text:
How to Read a Chapter and Use the Concept Reference
Each chapter opens in the same way. A Chapter overview box summarizes the whole chapter in ordinary words: the route, and what a reader will be able to do at the end. The prose that follows it begins from a real measurement problem or concern in an applied study and states the question the chapter answers. Each chapter closes with a numbered Summary and reading bridge that gathers what has been settled and states the questions the next chapter owes. A short Key terms table follows where a chapter carries one, then exercises, then any appendices, which hold derivations, data documentation and extensions the main route does not require. A term is explained where it is first used, and the chapters carry the statistics themselves: a model appears as equations, as parameter matrices, as a path diagram and as an explanation, and every reported number is computed for the reader and read in prose and in named tables. Results are rounded to three decimals from full-precision computation, with trailing zeros dropped (3.1 rather than 3.100), unless a source’s own precision applies. Counts and degrees of freedom stay whole numbers, values shown together share one number of decimals, and a very small probability is shown as a bound, such as below .001, rather than as zero. Chapter 1’s exactly constructed values appear at their natural precision, and a few values carry the digits their purpose needs: a very small numerical check is written in scientific notation, and Chapter 4 shows its reconstructed discrepancy to six decimals and its population discrepancy to seven significant digits, so that the arithmetic can be followed.
The software is named where the methods need it rather than taught as a course of its own. Chapter 1 asks for none: its records are constructed, its results exact, and its conclusions readable without a computer. psych and GPArotation enter with the exploratory work of Chapter 2, and lavaan enters with the confirmatory fits of Chapter 3. A chapter names the software it relies on and states the consequential defaults in words – scale setting, factor covariances, mean structures, missing-data handling, standard errors and the test-statistic family – so that a reader who never opens R can still follow every model, every count and every conclusion from the printed evidence.
Part One’s argument vocabulary is reused rather than redefined, and Part Two does not re-teach the argument-based approach as a recurring apparatus. One optional section of Chapter 1 shows how evidence, justification, interpretation and claim boundaries change when a statistical variable is latent, applies the six quality-evaluation questions under Part One’s names, records at least one failed verdict and repairs the claim; a reader may skip it without losing a definition, an equation, an exercise or a prerequisite for the chapters that follow. Chapters 2 to 4 express prespecification, uncertainty, limitations and claim boundaries in the ordinary technical vocabulary of exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, and analytic status is the one Part Two term that carries the development, confirmation and replication rules set out above.
The Part Two Concept Reference publishes beside these chapters and holds the single vocabulary these chapters share. Its concept tables gather related terms into broad groups and give each term’s meaning or essential distinction, and a closing table records the notation; each row names the chapter and section where the term is principally explained, so a term met in one chapter can be traced to the place that teaches it. It is written for lookup rather than for reading through: consult it when a term or a symbol is unfamiliar, and return to the chapter for the explanation, the worked example and the reason behind the distinction.

title: Part Two: Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling
text:
What Comes Later
Chapters 1–4 are available on the website. Chapters 5–12 are not yet available; the following map shows how they extend the measurement foundation.
Chapters 5–12 extend the measurement foundation to research questions about relationships, comparisons, change and the design of a new study. The same principle continues: define what the model represents, show which observed patterns its restrictions imply, and decide what the evidence supports. Each case states its own question, data and assumptions, so a new topic does not depend on remembering an earlier case’s numerical results.



Table 3: The structural continuation of Part Two.









Chapter
Research question and development




5. Path Analysis and Structural Systems
How do equations and diagrams define an observed-variable system? Known populations and empirical cases connect parameter identification, estimation, fit, constraints and comparison, including recursive and feedback systems.


6. Causal Models, Interventions and Identification
Which intervention or counterfactual question do the data and assumptions identify? Causal assignments, adjustment, Simpson reversals and instruments separate an observed association from a proposed causal answer.


7. Structural Equation Models with Latent Variables
How does a measurement model become part of a structural system? Joint measurement comes first, followed by a full structural refit that retains all indicators and re-estimates both portions.


8. Indirect Effects and Conditional Relationships
How do relationships operate through intermediates or vary with another variable? Indirect effects, latent products, conditional slopes and their intervals keep measurement quality and causal assumptions visible.


9. Measurement Comparability and Group Comparisons
Which comparisons have a common unit and origin? Group means, variances and structural relations require measurement restrictions suited to the intended comparison, including sensitivity to anchors.


10. Incomplete Data and Robust Inference
What information remains when responses are missing or distributions depart from the working model? Incomplete-data likelihood, robust inference, auxiliary information and explicit sensitivity analyses address different problems.


11. Latent Growth Models
What changes over time, and for whom? Growth means, person variation, piecewise and parallel processes, and within-person lagged departures are distinct longitudinal targets.


12. Study Planning and Power Analysis
What should a future study be able to learn? Evidence-calibrated populations, power, interval precision, failures and plausible model departures inform a feasible design.






Raw records and published summary statistics provide complementary routes. Means, covariances and sample sizes often permit a declared Normal model to be fitted or a published result to be replicated. Raw records additionally support case resampling, factor-score prediction, response-pattern inspection and procedures requiring information beyond the ordinary moments. Matching an estimate across routes does not automatically match every diagnostic or uncertainty calculation.
For a model with several latent variables, the first step fits their measurement system jointly. The second adds the structural relationships, retains the indicators and re-estimates measurement and structural parameters together. Exporting estimated scores and treating them as error-free variables would be a different analysis. Suitable measurement support is also needed before interpreting latent group differences or construct change.
A structural model does not upgrade an associational design to a causal one. Its directional claims require evidence about timing, confounding, assignment and the process that generated the measures. Planning therefore considers whether better measurement or a different design is needed, as well as whether more participants would improve precision. Multilevel modeling belongs to Part Three; categorical measurement and item-response models, mixture models and Bayesian SEM lie outside this Part Two sequence.

title: From Latent-Variable Modeling to Factor Analysis
text:
Suppose a study of study skills reports that its six-item questionnaire “measures two distinct constructs, Planning and Strategy”, and supports the sentence with a correlation table whose items fall into two clean blocks. Sentences of that shape are written constantly, about reading tests, symptom checklists, job-satisfaction scales and course evaluations alike.
The table is real. The two constructs are not in it. No column of the records holds a student’s planning ability and none holds their strategy use; what the study has is a pattern among six recorded answers and a proposal about what produced it. Whether that proposal is a useful statistical account of the pattern, and whether it licenses the words “two distinct constructs”, are separate questions with separate answers, and a report that runs them together can be exactly right about its arithmetic and quite wrong about its conclusion.
So this chapter asks:
Part One asked what a set of records supports about variables that were recorded. Here the variable of primary interest was not recorded at all, so the first half of the answer is a model explicit enough to say what an unrecorded variable would imply for the recorded ones, and the second half is a limit on how far that implication reaches.
crumbs: From Latent-Variable Modeling to Factor Analysis

title: From Latent-Variable Modeling to Factor Analysis
text:
Observed responses, an unobserved account
Provisional answer. When several indicators covary, a common-factor model can represent their covariance through unobserved factors and residuals. Compatibility with that covariance supports the statistical representation. Interpreting a factor as a construct additionally requires a defensible account of the indicator domain, response process, population, and intended use. Naming a factor, obtaining a simple pattern, or even reproducing covariance exactly is not enough.
Behavioral and social research often concerns attributes that are not recorded directly. A dataset may contain responses to several planning items, but no column contains planning ability itself. A test records item scores, not error-free proficiency. Symptoms may be observed while the syndrome proposed to organize them remains a theoretical and statistical construction.
A latent-variable model does not turn the proposed attribute into an observation. Instead, it introduces one or more unobserved random variables and states how they are related to the variables that were recorded. The useful question is therefore not simply whether a factor can be named. It is whether the proposed model has observable consequences, and what conclusions those consequences support.
Answering that pair takes both halves: a covariance representation that can be checked, and a conclusion that stays within what such a check can establish. The first task is to distinguish the quantities that enter the representation.
Table 1 keeps four kinds of quantity apart.



Table 1: Four kinds of quantity in a factor model.










Quantity
Status
Example




Observed variable
Recorded for each unit
An item response \(Y_j\)


Latent random variable
Introduced by the model; not recorded
A common factor \(\eta_k\)


Unknown fixed parameter
A population quantity to be estimated
A loading \(\lambda_{jk}\)


Residual random variable
The part of an indicator the declared factors do not represent
\(\epsilon_j\)






A factor is not merely a parameter; it is a random variable in the model, with a distribution over units. A loading is not a hidden score attached to a person; it is a parameter describing how the model relates an indicator to a factor. A residual is unobserved too, but that does not make it a substantive construct: it collects whatever the declared common factors leave out.
Figure 1 shows the smallest interesting case. Three observed indicators are drawn as rectangles, one unobserved variable as a circle, and the single-headed arrows run from the unobserved variable to the observed ones.








Figure 1: A latent variable with three indicators. Rectangles are recorded variables, the circle is a variable introduced by the model, and single-headed arrows denote loading relations.





For three indicators, the picture summarizes equations of the form
\[
Y_{ij} = \nu_j + \lambda_j\eta_i + \epsilon_{ij},
\qquad j = 1,2,3 .
\]
The indicator \(Y_{ij}\) is observed. The factor \(\eta_i\) and residual \(\epsilon_{ij}\) are random variables introduced by the model. The intercept \(\nu_j\) and loading \(\lambda_j\) are fixed but unknown population parameters.
The arrows deserve care. They state a direction of representation: the model writes each indicator as a function of the factor plus a residual, not the reverse. That is a modeling choice with real consequences, and it is the foundational common-factor representation developed here. It is not, by itself, evidence that the factor causes the responses. A diagram is a compact statement of a model; establishing that a latent attribute produces observed behavior requires theory about the response process and a design capable of supporting the claim. Model fit does not supply either.
Two inferential links are easy to conflate. First, relations among predictors, exposures and outcomes require a design capable of supporting causal interpretation; sampling units from a target population bears mainly on population generalization. Second, relating a proposed construct to a set of indicators requires defensible coverage of the construct’s content or behavioral domain. This second task is often called domain sampling, although indicator selection is commonly systematic and theory-guided rather than a literal probability sample.
Domain coverage supports a broad construct interpretation, but it is not sufficient by itself: the response process, dimensionality, population and intended use still matter. Without such a warrant, a factor may remain useful as a statistical device - for example, as a method factor - without being interpreted as the construct itself. Likewise, drawing an arrow from a factor to an indicator states the model’s reflective direction; neither domain coverage nor the arrow alone establishes a causal effect.
Two matters here remain genuinely contested, and it is worth knowing that before the algebra makes them invisible. The first is what a latent variable is: whether it should be treated as a real attribute that produces the responses, as a summary construction with no existence beyond the model, or as shorthand for the measuring operations themselves (Borsboom et al., 2003). The algebra below is compatible with all three readings and settles none of them. The second is the direction just described. For some constructs - socioeconomic status is the standard example - the indicators arguably produce the construct rather than express it, and under that formative reading internal consistency stops being a virtue and the common-factor model no longer applies (Bollen & Lennox, 1991; Edwards & Bagozzi, 2000). This chapter takes the reflective direction as its common-factor representation, a choice rather than a discovery. Chapter 7 also considers causal indicators and the assumptions needed to identify that different representation.
Why introduce something that is not observed? Because the model has consequences for quantities that are. Under assumptions developed below, two indicators connected to the same factor have the common covariance contribution
\[
\lambda_j\operatorname{Var}(\eta)\lambda_k .
\]
When their residual covariance is zero, this is their entire model-implied covariance. Section 5 derives the complete result rather than asking the reader to accept this preview.
Only after the model and its terms are clear will we ask it to reproduce particular numerical patterns. The two six-indicator matrices in Section 6 are constructed, known-value teaching matrices. They are not sample correlations or evidence that particular constructs exist.
